articles.title: Russia Increases Jet-Powered Drone Attacks on Ukraine Eightfold, Launching 2,800 in August
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Increases Jet-Powered Drone Attacks on Ukraine Eightfold, Launching 2,800 in August
Russia sharply increased its use of jet-powered drones against Ukraine over the summer, putting growing pressure on Ukrainian air defenses with faster, harder-to-intercept systems.
Russia increased the intensity of its jet-powered drone attacks on Ukraine more than eightfold over the summer, launching around 2,800 such drones in August compared with roughly 350 in June, The Moscow Times reported on September 13, citing The Times.
Jet-powered drones travel significantly faster than older propeller-driven models, reducing the time available for Ukrainian air defenses to detect and intercept incoming targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Russia launched around 800 jet-powered drones over just four days in late August, with most of them targeting Kyiv. According to Ihnat, the drones are being deployed in combat almost immediately after leaving production lines, according to The Moscow Times.
Russia currently uses two main types of jet-powered strike drones. One is the Geran, based on Iran’s Shahed design. Its latest fifth-generation version can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour, carry a warhead weighing up to 90 kilograms, and travel approximately 1,000 kilometers.
The second system, the Banderol jet-powered drone, has been used since the summer. It can reach speeds of up to 595 kilometers per hour, has a range of up to 480 kilometers, and can carry a 114-kilogram payload.
Anatolii Khrapchynskyi, a Ukrainian Air Force reserve officer and head of an air defense company, said the systems effectively provide Russia with a lower-cost alternative to cruise missiles. Their increased speed has sharply reduced the reaction window available to Ukrainian mobile fire teams, the outlet reported.
According to Khrapchynskyi, crews previously had around one minute to detect and engage older Shahed drones. Against jet-powered models, that window has fallen to approximately six seconds.
The higher speeds have also affected interception rates. Ihnat estimated that Ukraine can intercept up to 95% of older Shahed models, while the interception rate for jet-powered drones stands at around 60%.
The pressure intensified further in late August and into September, when Russia subjected Kyiv to an almost continuous two-week drone barrage, striking warehouses, civilian infrastructure, educational facilities, and other sites across the capital and surrounding region.
As a result, Ukraine is increasingly forced to use more expensive air defense assets against the faster drones, including scarce Patriot interceptor missiles as well as F-16, Mirage, and MiG-29 fighter aircraft.
A Ukrainian fighter pilot previously said even an older MiG can shoot down roughly a dozen jet-powered Shahed-type drones in a single mission, underscoring the importance of crewed aircraft in Ukraine’s multi-layered air defense system.
“Financially it’s painful, but that’s our purpose,” the pilot said. “In a single sortie even an old MiG can take out a dozen or so. You have to understand that since there aren’t many other options, you end up relying on skill and experience.”
Despite the higher cost of operating fighter aircraft, the pilot said their use against such drones remains justified, as intercepting aerial threats is a core function of combat aviation within Ukraine’s broader air defense network.
At the same time, Ukraine aims to have its first FREYJA anti-ballistic defense system completed by the end of 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 10, as the country pushes ahead with developing a domestically produced defense against ballistic missile threats with support from an expanding group of international partners.

articles.title: Baltic export: The Insider identifies the Russian agents of influence working to destabilize Latvia's upcoming elections
articles.body:
Latvia's upcoming parliamentary elections, scheduled for Oct. 3, will feature fourteen political parties competing for 100 seats in the Saeima. Roughly a third of the candidates consider Russian their native language — some studied at Russian educational institutions, while others frequently travel to Russia. Moscow is closely monitoring the campaign, and pro-Kremlin propagandists are spreading a range of falsehoods in an effort to influence Latvian voters. The Insider has identified the figures in the Russian Embassy in Riga and the presidential administration who oversee the Kremlin's network of agents in Latvia responsible for election interference.
Vladimir Balobayev, the Kremlin’s Baltic handler
Sources identify 38-year-old Kaliningrad native Vladimir Balobayev as the Russian Presidential Administration's point man on issues involving Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania.
In 2015, Balobayev was general director of the Baltic Information and Analytical Center, which channeled funding to so-called independent journalists in the Baltic states. Among those who received payments from him was Andrei Solopenko, editor of the Baltnews portal, which is now banned in the EU. In 2025, a Riga court sentenced Solopenko to 280 hours of community service for violating anti-Russian sanctions.
In 2016, Balobayev became deputy director of the Center for Eastern European Studies at Immanuel Kant Baltic Federal University in Kaliningrad, where he published a paper titled “Transformation of Poland’s Political System.” In 2019, Balobayev moved from Kaliningrad to Moscow and joined the Presidential Administration. He soon became head of the Department for Interaction with Civil Society Institutions within the presidential office responsible for cultural ties with former Soviet states. In December 2020, Putin awarded him the rank of Active State Councillor of the Russian Federation, 3rd Class.
At the time, the “cultural” directorate's Baltic desk was headed by Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) colonel Yevgeny Umerenkov. In the 1990s, Umerenkov had used a Komsomolskaya Pravda press pass as cover to spy in the United States and Mexico, and in 2020 he returned to the Kremlin-friendly tabloid after effectively being sent into retirement. The desk was taken over by Umerenkov's aide, Vadim Smirnov, who reported directly to Dmitry Kozak.
In the early 2000s, Smirnov had trained at the Moscow office of the American Council for International Education, which is funded by U.S. taxpayers. He later worked for RIA Novosti, served as press secretary to Kaliningrad Region Governor Vadim Tsukanov, and became a political columnist for Kaliningradskaya Pravda. In 2013, Lithuanian authorities barred “journalist” Smirnov from entering the country due to suspicions that he was involved in espionage activities. In 2024, due to poor performance, Smirnov lost his position as the Presidential Administration's overseer of the Baltic states. Balobayev took his place.
In August 2025, following a series of spy scandals, Putin scrapped the “cultural” approach and created the Directorate for Strategic Partnership and Cooperation (USPS) in its place (as The Insider previously reported). In the new directorate, Balobayev oversees a range of Kremlin-backed organizations: the Foreign Ministry’s Third European Department, Rossotrudnichestvo, the Russian International Affairs Council, the Foundation for Support and Protection of the Rights of Compatriots Living Abroad, the Russkiy Mir Foundation, the Baltnews news portal, and a team of propagandists.
Among Balobayev’s better-known actors promoting narratives about NATO’s “cunning” plans to seize the Baltic Sea while spreading “Russophobia” in the Baltic states are propagandist Andrei Mamykin (who is internationally wanted at Latvia’s request), former Riga City Council member Ruslan Pankratov (who fled to Russia), Belarus-based blogger Roman Samul (formerly active in the “Antifascists of the Baltics” movement), “historian” Alexander Dyukov (who predicts the imminent extinction of the populations of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania), and Konstantin Khudoley (head of the Department of European Studies at St. Petersburg State University’s School of International Relations).
One of Khudoley’s students at St. Petersburg State University, Vyacheslav Morozov, moved to Estonia in 2016 to teach at the University of Tartu, where he gave numerous lectures on Russia’s role in the modern world before being caught spying for the GRU. During the investigation, Morozov admitted to working for Russian military intelligence; he was sentenced to six years and three months in prison.
SVR station chief in Riga Igor Sorokopud
In 2023, in the midst of Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine, Latvia downgraded diplomatic relations with Moscow and cut embassy staff by 60%. The ambassadors were replaced by chargés d’affaires. Today, the Russian embassy’s work in Riga looks more like the activities of a school patriotic club: on commemorative dates, diplomats visit the graves of Soviet soldiers and present certificates to the few surviving World War II veterans who have made it to almost 100.
But that is only the visible side. Closely monitoring the Saeima elections is the SVR station chief in Riga, 43-year-old embassy first secretary Igor Sorokopud.
Born in Moscow, Sorokopud studied Middle Eastern languages at Department No. 38 of the Military University of the Russian Defense Ministry (VUMO), an institution currently headed by Colonel Vladimir Bykovtsev, who spied in Yemen back in Soviet times. After graduating from VUMO, Sorokopud enrolled at the SVR Academy, where he underwent specialized training for work at stations in the Middle East.
In 2018, he was posted to Iran, where he worked under the cover of the embassy’s third secretary. The Insider obtained an invoice from the Peter Justesen store in Tehran — part of the international duty free chain serving diplomats — made out to Sorokopud. According to the invoice, in January 2020 the Russian official spent $2,944.45 at the store (the sale of alcohol is strictly prohibited in Iran, and it appears that Sorokupud resold bottles on the side).
In 2024, Sorokopud was transferred to Latvia, where he took charge of the local SVR station. His main operational interests are Latvia’s cooperation with NATO, Western military aid to Ukraine, and people with access to the country’s leadership, the Defense and Foreign ministries, and other centers of decision-making.
Sorokopud’s operational focus: Latvia’s cooperation with NATO, military aid to Ukraine, and people in positions of power
The SVR’s agent network in Latvia is made up primarily of former Soviet military personnel and Russian-speaking residents who are susceptible to pro-Kremlin propaganda due to dissatisfaction with their personal economic circumstances.
In Latvia, Sorokopud lives with his wife, Yekaterina Vostrikova, St. Petersburg native who previously worked as a financial analyst at Aton, a Russian company that manages the assets of private investors. Until 2024, Vostrikova went by the name "Gretchen" and the surname of her then-husband, American Chad Anthony.After divorcing him, Yekaterina reverted to her maiden name, Vostrikova, and joined Sorokopud in Iran. The Insider has found that Vostrikova herself has access to classified information, suggesting that she may be more than simply a spy’s wife.
The SVR is actively engaged in disinformation operations in Latvia. In May, for example, the agency claimed —falsely, by all available indications — that Ukraine had reached a deal with Latvia to launch strikes on Russia from Latvian territory: “Despite concerns on the Latvian side that it could become the target of a retaliatory Russian strike, the authorities in Kyiv persuaded Riga to approve the operation. The Ukrainians emphasized that it would be impossible to determine the exact launch site of the drones.”
However, Sorokopud does not appear to be responsible for producing that particular disinformation narrative. Instead, the false claim in question was apparently orchestrated by SVR press bureau chief Sergei Guskov, whom The Insider previously reported on.
The “Russian world” in Latvia
Since the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, support for the “Russian world” in Latvia has declined noticeably. Moscow, however, still appears to be betting on the Russian Union of Latvia (RSL), despite the high-profile espionage scandal involving former Latvian MEP Tatjana Zdanoka, who, as The Insider revealed, worked for Russian intelligence services for several years. (Notably, the RSL’s governing board also includes the aforementioned Baltnews “journalist” Andrei Solopenko.)
In Strasbourg, Zdanoka served as leader of the RSL, promoted claims that Russian-speaking residents of the Baltic states were being persecuted, and voted against resolutions condemning Russia over the annexation of Crimea, its war in Syria, and its aggression against Ukraine. Leaked correspondence indicates that since at least 2005 Zdanoka had been in operational contact with the FSB, received money from Moscow, and sent reports to her Russian handlers. She also advised Russian intelligence on how to intervene more effectively in the internal affairs of EU countries.
MEP Zdanoka advised Russian intelligence on how to interfere more effectively in the internal affairs of EU countries
In 2024, amid the espionage scandal, Zdanoka stepped down from the RSL leadership. The party was then taken over by co-leaders Andrei Pagor and Yevgeny Osipov. Pagor, a former police officer, was forced to resign after suspecion arose that he had been soliciting bribes from drug dealers. He is currently running for the Saeima on the Sovereign Power–Young Latvians ticket.
The other co-leader, Osipov, was responsible for founding the Latvian branch of the neo-Nazi Russian National Unity (RNE) organization back in the 1990s. Osipov says that he went underground at the age of 16 and spent his nights putting up RNE leaflets. In 2000, fellow members accused him of disloyalty to RNE leader Alexander Barkashov and expelled him from the organization, after which Osipov joined the Latvian National Democratic Party (LNDP). In 2013, he was sentenced to community service for desecrating the Latvian flag.
Elena Osipova, Osipov’s wife, is also on the RSL’s governing board and heads the Russian Community in Liepaja. In 2023, she ran for the European Parliament alongside Zdanoka but failed to win a seat. She is now a regular participant in RSL protests and has had repeated run-ins with police. In 2024, Elena challenged the results of the Liepaja municipal elections, demanding a recount; the court rejected her request.
“Not so fast!”
Another former Zdanoka aide, Anna Bondere, is running for the Saeima on the Sovereign Power–Young Latvians ticket — alongside former police officer Pagor. She presents herself as a defender of the Russian language and a fighter against neo-Nazism. Bondere regularly attends RSL rallies and is frequently quoted by the propaganda website of the Russkiy Mir Foundation, established by Putin’s decree.
“Do you think the Russian Union of Latvia has ceased to exist? No! Not so fast!” she wrote in a Facebook post.
Bondere graduated from Moscow State Industrial University in 2003. After returning to Riga, she worked in education before joining the RSL. Russian border-crossing data show that Bondere travels to Russia almost every year and has visited the country particularly frequently since the start of the so-called “special military operation.” While in Russia, she stayed at expensive hotels, citing “business” as the purpose of her trips and using a Sberbank card to pay for her expenses.
The Insider sent Bondere questions via social media, but she did not respond.
Among the other pro-Putin candidates running for the Saeima is Alexei Roslikov, founder of the Stability! party. However, Latvian authorities have opened a criminal case against Roslikov for inciting ethnic hatred, prompting him to flee to Belarus.
Roslikov was previously involved in business, and local journalists have reported that he evaded taxes and repeatedly set up new companies. Whenever one of his companies accumulated debts, he would promptly change its founders. Roslikov has served as a member of both the Saeima and Riga City Council, but in 2026 he lost his mandate for repeatedly failing to attend meetings.
While lying low in Belarus, Roslikov has been waging an anti-Latvian propaganda campaign, portraying Russian-speaking people as victims of discrimination in the Baltic states. In his statements, the fugitive candidate says that if elected to the Saeima, “Ukraine will not receive another cent.” In April, Roslikov also spread a false claim that Latvian schools had purportedly banned students from speaking Russian even during recess.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Foreign Ministry has joined the disinformation campaign. Grigory Lukyantsev, director of the ministry’s Department for Multilateral Cooperation in Human Rights, claimed that authorities in the Baltic states were preparing mass deportations of Russian-speaking residents. The “sensation” was picked up by all major pro-government Russian media outlets. Unsurprisingly, the news turned out to be fake.

articles.title: Ukrainian F-16s Shoot Down Jet Drones – But Is It Enough?
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine has been using US-made F-16 fighters to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones.
Speaking to a television channel during his recent visit to Canada, Zelensky said Ukraine has “sometimes” resorted to Western air-to-air missiles, such as the US-made AIM-9 and AIM-120, to shoot down newer, faster jet-powered drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We use the corresponding missiles on F-16s, shooting down jet drones,” Zelensky said, as reported by state media Ukrinform.
“It is expensive, but sometimes, when nothing can be done to shoot down a particular jet drone, human life is more important and more expensive, so sometimes F-16s were used against such drones,” he added.
Zelensky’s comments came as Canada announced a new $3 billion package for Kyiv, which includes an unspecified number of AIM-9s and AIM-120s.
Recent comments from Yuriy Ihnat, the air force’s spokesperson, suggest that Ukrainian F-16s have at times resorted to onboard 20mm cannons to down jet-powered drones, which he said poses major risks to the aircraft itself. Pilots would be closer to the drones based on their size at open-fire ranges compared to enemy fighters, bombers, or other crewed aircraft; this makes debris from the drones a follow-on hazard to the shooter’s aircraft.
Jet-powered drones, which blur the line between drones and missiles, have been increasingly used by Russia against Ukraine in recent attacks, posing challenges for Ukrainian air defenses as current interceptor drones struggle to catch up with their higher speeds.
Russian Drones Just Miss Former CIA Director David Petraeus: a View From a Train Near the Polish Border
While Ukraine has been developing jet-powered interceptor drones as a countermeasure, Zelensky’s remark suggests a potential gap in Ukrainian air defense, as the AIM-9s and AIM-120s are typically costlier than interceptor drones.
While the latest AIM-9X Sidewinder missile is estimated to cost over $450,000 per unit, Ukrainian Air Force F-16s almost always carry the AIM-9M which cost about $84,000 when originally purchased by the US Air Force (USAF). The AIM-120 is $386,000 per unit, according to the US Air Force – though TWZ reported that some variants can cost over $1 million per missile.
Ukraine began receiving the missiles as part of the armaments for its new NATO-standard aircraft donated by its allies, starting with the F-16 in mid-2024, though the total number received remains classified.
Ukraine’s demands for air-to-air missiles
The rise of jet-powered drones has exposed a gap in Ukraine’s layered air defense, with what was once reserved to counter cruise missiles now used to counter Russian drones.
Since 2022, Russia’s aerial threats against Ukrainian cities primarily consist of Iranian-designed, propeller-driven Shahed drones and their Russian variants, with the occasional cruise and ballistic missiles.
Those drones are often countered by machine-gun fire and electronic jamming or, more recently, by propeller-driven interceptor drones, with a 90% overall interception rate, whereas air defense missiles – both ground and air-launched – are reserved for cruise missiles, with the scarce and coveted Patriot systems reserved for the faster ballistic missiles.
But with more jet-powered drones flying over Ukraine, Kyiv has had to intercept them with the missile stockpiles reserved for cruise missiles – including the AIM-9s and AIM-120s, according to Zelensky.
Are the new pledges enough?
Ukraine has long struggled with the number of those missiles in its arsenal, with shortages reported in late 2025.
Kyiv’s allies have since tried to remedy the situation. On July 30, the Pentagon announced approval of a $3.5 billion contract to produce thousands of AIM-120s for countries worldwide, including Ukraine – while total production is estimated to reach thousands by 2031, it’s unclear how many were destined for Ukraine.
More recently, at the 36th Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting, Berlin said it would boost AIM-9 deliveries from Bundeswehr stocks – but again, the exact number is not disclosed.
But known deliveries – before Ukraine ran out in 2025 – suggest that numbers have been limited.
One publicized figure from Canada suggests it sent at least 12 AIM-120s, 43 AIM-9s, and 250 AIM-7s in 2023, excluding other components sent to Ukraine. Dutch monitoring site Oryx estimated 43 AIM-9s and 287 AIM-7s from Canada, with no AIM-120s mentioned.
At present, Russia is estimated to be launching 100-200 drones per day against Ukraine consistently, excluding cruise missiles, with the Air Force suggesting in late August that over half were jet-powered at times.
Assuming Russia launches only 50 jet-powered drones and cruise missiles at Ukraine per day, that would be around 1,500 targets for Ukraine to shoot down, AIM-120s or not.
The good news for Ukraine is that the industry is scaling up production of jet-powered interceptors, other air defense missiles are available, and Russia may be having trouble getting Chinese jet engines for the drones.
But the bad news is that it still needs to intercept over 1,000 jet-powered drones that fly like a missile each month, one way or another.

articles.title: Russia’s $100,000 Jet-Powered Weapons Are Outpacing Ukraine and the US, WSJ Reports
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s $100,000 Jet-Powered Weapons Are Outpacing Ukraine and the US, WSJ Reports
Russia has accelerated the development and mass production of a new generation of relatively inexpensive precision weapons, including the jet-powered Geran-5 drone and Banderol cruise missile, moving from testing to large-scale manufacturing faster than Ukraine and the United States.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Wall Street Journal on September 14, Russia has managed to develop, combat-test, modify, and begin serial production of the new systems within several years, highlighting Moscow’s ability to rapidly convert battlefield experience into weapons produced at scale.
The Geran-5 and Banderol represent an attempt to combine some of the capabilities of more expensive cruise missiles with the lower production costs traditionally associated with one-way attack drones. Both weapons are estimated to cost around $100,000 each, while US-made Tomahawk cruise missiles and comparable high-end systems cost more than $2 million.
WSJ reported that the weapons rely heavily on commercially available and dual-use Chinese components, including jet engines, navigation equipment, and communications electronics. Ukraine and other countries have identified Chinese-made parts in debris recovered from Russian weapons.
China has maintained that it regulates the export of technologies that could have military applications.
The Geran-5 marks a significant change from earlier Russian versions of Iran’s Shahed-series drones. While the original designs used propeller engines and traveled at relatively low speeds, newer Russian variants have incorporated faster propulsion, improved navigation, and communications systems intended to make interception more difficult.
Mike Monnik, chief executive of drone-threat intelligence company DroneSec, described the Geran-5 to WSJ as “essentially a poor-man’s cruise missile.”
The shift presents a new problem for Ukrainian air defenses, which have spent years developing methods to intercept slower Shahed-type drones. Faster jet-powered weapons can require different detection and interception systems and further complicate efforts to maintain a favorable cost ratio between incoming weapons and the interceptors used against them.
According to WSJ, Russian manufacturers have also benefited from an ability to move quickly from experimental designs to large-scale production once a system proves effective in combat.
Kateryna Bondar, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ Wadhwani AI Center, told the newspaper that Russian industry can move “very fast from idea and experimentation to production.”
Ukraine has also demonstrated an ability to rapidly develop new weapons, including jet-powered drones and long-range strike systems. However, WSJ reported that Ukraine faces greater constraints in production capacity and long-term industrial planning than Russia.
The challenge is also affecting the United States and other NATO members. Western governments are attempting to expand production of air defense interceptors, including missiles for Patriot systems, while shortening the time required to move new military technologies from development into mass production.
For Western militaries, that creates an economic challenge. High-end air defense missiles and fighter aircraft can successfully intercept drones, but repeatedly using expensive interceptors against weapons costing around $100,000 is difficult to sustain during large-scale attacks.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the US and NATO are consequently investing in cheaper counter-drone systems, including new jet-powered interceptors capable of engaging faster targets.
The technological developments have implications beyond Ukraine. Russia, Iran, and North Korea have expanded military cooperation and exchanged weapons and technical expertise, while lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine are increasingly shaping drone and air defense development in other theaters.
The production surge is already visible on the battlefield. Russia launched around 2,800 jet-powered drones against Ukraine in August, up from roughly 350 in June.

articles.title: Swedish centre-left opposition widens lead to three seats with 95% of votes counted – Europe live
articles.body:
Hej from Stockholm as the dust settles (a bit) after a hectic election night.
With 95% of votes counted overnight, the left-leaning opposition bloc – led by Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats – has widened its lead to three seats, leading 176 to 173 against the reigning centre-right coalition and their far-right partners in Sweden Democrats.
Formally, the result is not settled yet: there is only some 28,600 votes separating the two blocs, with 6% of the votes yet to be counted – and that includes some 200,000 votes expected to come and be counted only on Wednesday.
Still, the Swedish public broadcaster SVT said last night it was 90% confident that the opposition would clinch the victory, even accounting for all the votes yet to be counted.
There is plenty of time for early exploratory talks: the parliament won’t meet until 28 September, when its due to elect a new speaker, and any votes on who could be the next prime minister can only come after that.
But the process of forming the new government could take weeks if not months leaving Sweden in a state of political limbo at a time of unprecedented geopolitical uncertainty in Europe.
No doubt first text messages, frantic WhatsApp or Signals, and phone calls are already exchanged today.
I will be here to cover all this drama for you.
It’s Monday, 14 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
European leaders joined forces to highlight growing competition in the Arctic, where global warming is opening new shipping routes, governments are vying for vast natural resources and a Russian military buildup is heightening security concerns.
The leaders, mostly from Nordic and Baltic countries, put a spotlight on environmental challenges, economic opportunities and military vulnerabilities at a time of doubts about whether the United States, through Nato, will remain a bulwark against Russia.
“This region has become a geopolitical hotspot,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz told a joint news conference, insisting a new EU focus should complement Nato’s work. “Russia is building up its military capabilities here, and Russia uses its presence for hybrid activities every day.”
Prime minister Petteri Orpo of Finland, which hosted the meeting in the capital of Lapland that’s home to a Santa Claus village, noted “high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic” and a changing security environment.
“The Arctic has emerged as the central arena of great power competition,” he said.
The two-day gathering that began Sunday comes after a Norwegian seizure of a Russian vessel earlier this month in the remote Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at the request of Ukraine.
Finland joins France's nuclear deterrent initiative
Meanwhile, Sweden’s neighbour, Finland, has joined France’s initiative to extend the reach of its nuclear deterrent through collaboration with partner European countries, Reuters reported.
In response to US president Donald Trump’s expressions of concern about the US security commitment to Europe and to the security implications of the Ukraine war, France in March announced the Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative.
“The initiative is first and foremost about strengthening European security. It reinforces Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and helps prevent escalation,” Finland’s president Alexander Stubb said in a post on X.
Under the initiative, the French president alone has the authority to decide when nuclear weapons are used, in contrast to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which has a shared Nuclear Planning Group.
However, it offers joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Finland’s defence minister Antti Häkkänen said in a separate statement that the agreement was a “natural step” after other Nordic countries, such as Norway, Sweden and Denmark, joined the initiative earlier in the year.
Russian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief says
Jennifer Rankinin Brussels andCharlotte Higgins and Amy Hawkinsin Kyiv
Catching up with other news from across Europe, the head of Nato has said a Russian drone attack on a train close to Ukraine’s border with Poland would not deter Kyiv’s western backers.
Mark Rutte said the strike on a passenger train showed how desperate Vladimir Putin had become.
“He thinks that he can stops us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong. Our answer is to increase support,” the Nato general secretary said.
European leaders have condemned the strike in which a Russian drone hit a passenger train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday shortly after a convoy of high-level diplomats and former leaders had passed through.
The earlier train, which was carrying the former UK prime minister Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus and running ahead of schedule, may have been the target of the Russian drone strike, Ukrainian Railways has said.
Early signals are promising for the opposition bloc, as Social Democrats are seemingly encouraged by the Centre party’s openness to talk about the future government.
Foreign policy spokesperson Morgan Johansson said the party’s conditions on not letting fringes control the government (13:53) “sound very good.”
“It’s one of the pieces of the puzzle that needs to be in place to solve this,” he said, quoted by SVT.
“Everyone on this side wants to change the government. That’s the starting point,” he added.
But any formal talks are likely to start only after we know the official results later this week.
The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains - analysis
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
Since the party was founded in 1988, the story of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) has been one of such continuous growth that a triumph in Sunday’s general election seemed inevitable.
In 2022, they capitalised on electoral gains – and the desperation of right-leaning parties to form a minority administration – and almost made their way into government.
A supporting role in prime minister Ulf Kristersson’s Tidö coalition earned the party, which has neo-Nazi roots, huge influence and mainstream acceptance by the political establishment.
This year’s election had been billed as final confirmation they were no longer pariahs but serious political heavyweights.
Early in the campaign, Kristersson announced that, if his coalition were to win, the SD would take key ministerial positions.
But Sunday’s results suggestthe march of the far right into the heart of Sweden’s government has been halted – for now.
Having fallen from Sweden’s second biggest party to third place and, with the right-leaning parties unlikely to be able to form a coalition, the SD appear to have lost their route into government.
The Centre Party is expected to play an important role in any post-election talks.
Although aligned with the opposition, the party made clear this morning that potential coalition partners – including Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats – “will need to see the big picture”and not let fringe powers dictate policy.
The party has long been critical of its potential future government partner in the Left Party, which feels emboldened by its strong election result and expected to demand a shift leftwards and its policies to be reflected by any future administration.
The projected result “shows the voters neither want to an economic turn leftwards, not a large role for the [far-right] Sweden Democrats,” party secretary Hannes Hervieu told SVT.
“There is no demand for fringe politics, but a desire for political stability,” he said, adding that the party would bring these points to the Social Democrats.
Curiously, prime minister Ulf Kristersson made similar noises last night about building an alternative majority around centre-right economic policies, but do not read too much into this: it’s still a very long way to go before that means anything more than just early post-election talk.
While the Social Democrats are understandably raring to take a crack at forming the next government, it’s easy to overlook that, despite coming out on top again, the party has actually lost ground since 2022 – recording its lowest vote share since universal suffrage was introduced in 1921.
With 95% of votes counted, the party sits at 28.1%, down more than two percentage points from 2022 (30.3%) and below its previous low of 28.3% in 2018.
Leader Magdalena Andersson was briefly asked about it last night, but waved these questions away, at least for now, as the focus is obviously elsewhere.
But leading Social Democrats are not exactly impressed by Kristersson’s chill approach.
The party’s foreign policy spokesperson, Morgan Johansson, accused him to trying to “cling on” to power, saying it was an “unsightly” behaviour, Expressen reported.
“If [the governing coalition] Tidö no longer has a majority, he will probably have to face the consequences of that.”
But in a stark warning highlighting just how tricky the government formation process is likely to be, Kristersson also said that if all parties stick to their red lines, “Sweden will not have a government.”
It’s clear he has some appetite for exploring a different majority to the red bloc.
PM Kristersson wants to 'take it easy' and wait until final results
Perhaps we should all just channel the Swedish PM, Ulf Kristersson, who essentially said this morning he was “going to take it pretty easy” until the final results are in.
He says there are some conversations scheduled in the meantime – including with fellow coalition leaders this evening – but he essentially wants to see the final results show first.
He also repeats his last night’s suggestion of exploring alternative majorities in the parliament.
One possible option could involve the Centre party switching sides, but it’s not immediately obvious how Kristersson would get them to accept a government with the far-right Sweden Democrats with it.
Social Democrat leadership meets for talks after election win
Senior figures in the Social Democratic party are meeting this morning with party leader Magdalena Andersson to discuss next steps.
The party topped the polls – that is certain – and is most likely to have a first go at forming the next government, but it will have to navigate the complex and often openly contradictory demands of the left-leaning bloc.
It remains to be seen whether they can get the Left Party to work with the Centre Party in particular, given rumbles on both sides about the feasibility of such an alliance.
But today’s doorstep comments suggest there is no rush just yet: all parties will want to wait for the final results on Wednesday or Thursday before committing to exploratory talks.
Party secretary Tobias Baudin confirmed, however, that he has exchanged texts with colleagues in other parties, SVT reported.
Asked about potential differences, he told P1 that he was “completely convinced” the parties would give it out with some “give and take” for all involved.
Hej from Stockholm as the dust settles (a bit) after a hectic election night.
With 95% of votes counted overnight, the left-leaning opposition bloc – led by Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats – has widened its lead to three seats, leading 176 to 173 against the reigning centre-right coalition and their far-right partners in Sweden Democrats.
Formally, the result is not settled yet: there is only some 28,600 votes separating the two blocs, with 6% of the votes yet to be counted – and that includes some 200,000 votes expected to come and be counted only on Wednesday.
Still, the Swedish public broadcaster SVT said last night it was 90% confident that the opposition would clinch the victory, even accounting for all the votes yet to be counted.
There is plenty of time for early exploratory talks: the parliament won’t meet until 28 September, when its due to elect a new speaker, and any votes on who could be the next prime minister can only come after that.
But the process of forming the new government could take weeks if not months leaving Sweden in a state of political limbo at a time of unprecedented geopolitical uncertainty in Europe.
No doubt first text messages, frantic WhatsApp or Signals, and phone calls are already exchanged today.
I will be here to cover all this drama for you.
It’s Monday, 14 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: EXPLAINER - US-Iran war ushers in new era of missile warfare
articles.body:
The Iran-US war is putting a new generation of missiles into combat, as both sides deploy weapons capable of striking from farther away while giving defenses less time to respond.
The US has deployed its Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) for the first known time in combat, while Iran says it has used its Kheibar Shekan, a missile capable of reaching US military targets across much of the Middle East.
Though designed for different purposes, both highlight a growing challenge in missile warfare: Weapons can be launched from mobile platforms, strike targets at greater distances and leave defenses less time to respond.
So what makes these weapons different, how have they been used in the war and what do they say about the future of missile warfare?
The PrSM is essentially the US Army's new generation of ground-launched ballistic missile -- designed to fly farther than its predecessor while allowing troops to carry more missiles on launch vehicles already in service.
It is replacing the Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), a missile developed during the Cold War and first used in combat during the 1991 Gulf War.
The baseline PrSM has a range of about 500 kilometers (311 miles), compared with about 300 kilometers (186 miles) for the longest-range versions of ATACMS.
That means an Army unit could potentially strike a target from more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) farther away, allowing launch crews to remain at a greater distance from enemy forces and air defenses.
The program is also working toward a range of about 650 kilometers (404 miles), while later variants are intended to reach at least 1,000 kilometers (621 miles).
The PrSM can also be fired from HIMARS, a truck-mounted rocket launcher, as well as the tracked M270A2 launcher. That compatibility means the US does not need an entirely new fleet of launch vehicles to deploy the missile.
It can also carry more firepower. A HIMARS launcher that can carry one ATACMS missile can carry two PrSMs before it needs to be reloaded.
Guided by an inertial navigation system aided by GPS, the missile is designed to detonate above the target, dispersing thousands of high‑velocity metal pellets over a wide area, according to weapons experts.
Beyond the Iranian battlefield, the missile’s debut also has wider significance for US military planning. Its greater range allows mobile launchers to threaten targets from greater distances, while its speed makes it particularly suited to time-sensitive targets such as missile launchers and air-defense systems.
Future versions are also being developed to strike moving targets, including ships.
In June, The Defense Post reported that the US Army awarded Lockheed Martin an $8.4 billion contract modification to boost PrSM production capacity.
The Iran-US war appears to have given the PrSM its battlefield debut.
US Central Command released footage on March 1 showing a PrSM being fired from a HIMARS during what it described as the first 24 hours of its operation against Iran, which began Feb. 28.
But its use has since drawn scrutiny over deadly strikes in Lamerd, a city in southern Iran.
BBC Verify reported in March that weapons experts who examined footage of a Feb. 28 strike said the projectile was likely a PrSM.
Airwars, a UK-based watchdog that investigates civilian harm in conflicts, separately analyzed three apparent PrSM strikes in Lamerd, including in residential areas and near civilian facilities, including the Shahid Naimi sports hall.
Its investigation found that one apparent strike caused damage across a radius of at least 170 meters (558 feet), while civilians were recorded killed at least 50 meters (164 feet) from the estimated explosion site.
Airwars said at least 21 civilians were killed in the attacks it investigated, including seven children and two women, and up to 170 others were injured.
The US military has disputed responsibility for the Lamerd strikes.
According to Airwars, US Central Command said CCTV footage was consistent with an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile. Airwars, however, concluded that the weapons were PrSMs based on analysis of footage and the damage left behind.
Unlike missiles that detonate on impact, the PrSM is designed to explode above the ground, dispersing fragments across a wide area. Airwars said the Lamerd strikes left thousands of distinctive marks on buildings, roads and vehicles rather than large impact craters.
 
Iran's Kheibar Shekan, whose name translates roughly as “castle breaker,” serves a different purpose.
The Wall Street Journal described the Kheibar Shekan as "cheap, accurate and lethal” and the “workhorse” of Tehran’s arsenal.
Unveiled in 2022, it is a solid-fuel, medium-range ballistic missile developed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), with Iran claiming a range of about 1,450 kilometers (901 miles).
That range puts US military facilities across large parts of the Middle East within potential reach.
Iranian media has reported the missile can carry a warhead weighing about 449-590 kilograms (990-1,301 pounds).
But one of its most important features is how quickly the missile can be prepared for launch.
The Kheibar Shekan uses solid fuel. Unlike liquid-fuel missiles that may require more launch preparation, solid-fuel missiles can generally be stored ready for use and fired more quickly.
That gives an opponent less time to detect preparations and potentially destroy the missile before it leaves the ground.
Iran and analysts describe its re‑entry vehicle as highly maneuverable in the terminal phase, a feature intended to complicate interception by missile defenses by making the warhead’s final trajectory harder to predict.
Tehran has also said the Kheibar Shekan is lighter and can be launched substantially faster than earlier systems, although the benchmarks for those comparisons have not been publicly established.
Iran has repeatedly said it has fired Kheibar Shekan missiles at US military positions since the conflict began on Feb. 28.
The IRGC has released footage showing the missile alongside other Iranian ballistic missiles, including the Fateh-110, Zolfaghar and Emad, which Tehran says have been used against US military targets.
During an escalation in late August, Iranian authorities said Kheibar Shekan missiles were used in attacks against US assets in Jordan.
Iran has also claimed attacks against US-linked targets in Bahrain, Kuwait and Erbil in northern Iraq, although such claims can be difficult to independently verify.
The missile is part of a much broader Iranian arsenal comprising short-, medium- and longer-range ballistic and cruise missiles.
Systems such as the Emad, Ghadr, Khorramshahr and Sejjil give Iran the ability to threaten targets across much of the region.
Although the PrSM and Kheibar Shekan belong to different missile classes and were developed by countries with very different military-industrial capabilities, both reflect a broader shift toward mobile and increasingly precise long-range strike systems.
Through programs like PrSM, the US is fielding land‑based missiles that can strike increasingly distant targets with precision from mobile launchers already dispersed with ground forces
Iran, meanwhile, has invested in missiles that can be moved, prepared rapidly and launched against bases and other targets across the region.
In both cases, mobility makes the missile launcher itself harder to find and destroy, while greater range allows forces to strike from farther away.
And that creates an increasingly difficult problem for defense.
Ballistic missiles travel at extremely high speeds, particularly as they descend toward their targets. Defenders must first detect a launch, determine the missile's trajectory, decide whether it threatens a target and then successfully intercept it -- all within minutes.
The result is an increasingly complex contest between long-range strike capabilities and the air and missile-defense systems designed to defeat them.

articles.title: Chinese-made ballistic missile debris found in Yemen
articles.body:
- Open-source analysts say missile debris found in Marib Governorate, Yemen, came from a Chinese-made DF-15A, possibly fired by Saudi Arabia for the first time.
- Saudi Arabia has previously acquired medium-range DF-3A and DF-21 missiles from China, but no confirmed history of the shorter-range DF-15.
Open-source analysts say wreckage from a short-range ballistic missile turned up in northern Yemen this week, and they believe it points to a weapon type Saudi Arabia has never been confirmed to use before.
The debris, identified as the booster stage of a Chinese-made DF-15A, was found in the Raghwan district of Marib Governorate, according to social media accounts that track weapons in the region.
The find comes amid a sharp escalation in fighting around Marib. Houthi forces and Yemen’s internationally recognized government have traded strikes across multiple provinces since early September, and Saudi Arabia has continued carrying out airstrikes in support of government forces there.
OSINT analyst MenchOsint wrote online that “Saudi Arabia fired Chinese-made DF-15A Ballistic Missiles at Yemen last night, likely for the first time.” A second account, OSINTWarfare, described the debris more specifically, saying the booster stage came from “a Chinese-made DF-15A (Dong Feng-15A) ballistic missile operated by Saudi Arabia” that fell in Raghwan district.
The DF-15A is a short-range ballistic missile, with a range generally estimated at around 600 kilometers (370 miles), well short of the medium-range systems Saudi Arabia is known to have acquired from China in the past. Riyadh purchased roughly 60 DF-3A missiles from China in the late 1980s, and a U.S. congressional commission later confirmed reports that Saudi Arabia bought DF-21 medium-range missiles from China around 2007, with the U.S. having reportedly required the DF-21s be modified so they could not carry nuclear warheads. Neither country has publicly confirmed Saudi Arabia holds any short-range DF-15 variant.
That gap in the public record is why some analysts online have floated an alternative explanation: that the debris could belong to a Pakistani-operated missile rather than a Saudi one. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact in September 2025, declaring that an attack on either country would be treated as an attack on both, and the two militaries have a long history of cooperation, including Pakistani troops training in the kingdom for decades. Whether that relationship extends to Pakistani missile crews or hardware operating from Saudi territory has not been established, and no source has offered evidence tying Pakistan directly to the Marib debris.
For now, the origin of the missile wreckage in Raghwan rests on the assessments of open-source researchers rather than any government statement. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defense has not commented on the reported strike, and it remains unconfirmed whether the DF-15A theory, the Pakistani-missile theory, or another explanation will hold up as more information becomes available.

articles.title: Trump Calls on Ukraine to Lay Off Energy Industry Strikes on Russia
articles.body:
A US President Donald Trump call on his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to lay off attacking the Kremlin’s energy industry because diesel prices in the US are too high came in the wake of a record month of strikes by Ukraine against Russia’s energy sector, and about six hours too late to prevent waves of Ukrainian robot aircraft from setting two more Russian oil refineries on fire.
The US president, speaking to reporters on Sunday during a visit to the 2026 Amgen Irish Open golf tournament, said that Ukraine’s long-range drone raids against Russian oil refineries were the main reason world diesel prices had spiked, and called on Zelensky to call off the attacks.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia. Let him go after targets – but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel. This isn’t done by the Middle East. This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine. So we spoke to Mr. Zelensky about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel because that’s hurting the world,” Trump told a gaggle of Irish and international reporters.
One Ukrainian strike package launched in the early morning hours well before Trump stepped onto the Irish links flew some 300 kilometers (185 miles) through Russia-controlled air space to hit the Slavyansk-EKO refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, damaging a crude oil processing unit and fuel reservoirs. The plant’s main business is processing oil and gas condensate into refined fuels, including diesel.
Ukraine Has Leverage Over Trump Now
As Trump, wearing a navy-blue suit and a white “USA” baseball cap under overcast skies, made his comments at Trump International Golf Links & Hotel Ireland in Doonbeg, County Clare, the fire at the refinery still was burning and visible from space, Kyiv Post review of timelines and imagery published by the NASA world-wide fire watch agency FIRMS found.
Ukraine’s second kamikaze robot plane attack of the night penetrated 1,200 kilometers (750 miles) into Russian Federation territory to hit the Tatneft-operated Taneco refinery, in the upper Volga region of Tatarstan. The facility is one of Russia’s most modern and a top national producer of diesel. Recordings of major fires in progress at the center of the refinery appeared on local social media, but local authorities said that damage was minimal. Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) and military intelligence agency (HUR) took credit for the attacks. Ukrainian milbloggers, late on Saturday, reported that the country’s drone forces that night had launched more than 400 kamikaze aircraft to attack targets across the Russian Federation’s west and south. Russia’s Defense Ministry on Sunday claimed shoot downs of 389 fixed-wing drones nationwide.
On Monday, FIRMS imagery showed significant thermal signatures consistent with major fires still burning at both locations.
The attacks hitting Slavyansk-EKO and Tatneft-Taneco followed a week of near-daily air raids by Ukrainian drone swarms against Russian energy infrastructure including Sept. 7 strikes hitting refineries in Ryazan and Perm, Sept. 8 raids hitting a refinery in Saratov and a refinery and fuel storage in the Black Sea port Novorossiysk, a Sept. 10 attack setting an oil loading terminal on Russia’s Caspian Sea shore on fire, a Sept. 11 strike hitting another Saratov oil refinery, and Sept. 12 strikes hitting a third refinery in Saratov and the Oil Refinery and Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez facility in Perm, deep inside Russia near the Ural Mountains.
During their last full month of strike operations, August 2026, Ukraine’s drone forces set a new wartime record (21) for number of Russian oil refineries hit, according to data published by Ukraine’s national long-range strike data bank DeepStrike UA and strike statistics published by Ukraine’s USF.
Russian refineries attacked by Ukraine’s wide-ranging drone forces over that month were in Omsk (first time in war), Saratov (hit by drones 12 times before), Syzran (three times), Perm (first time in war), Yaroslavl (six times), Krasnodar (10 times), Samara (five times), Tatarstan (one time), Tyumen (first time in war) and Orsk (one time before), Kyiv Post strike records showed. The August 2026 numbers were a 50% jump over refineries hit in July (14), and double the strike pace by USF units in October 2025 with seven refineries taking confirmed hits in the month, according to that data.
Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s energy industry echoed early September remarks by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blaming Ukraine and its drone strikes against Russia for a global “energy shock” that, he claimed, was the cause of rocketing energy costs worldwide.
A US-Israeli war with Iran leading to the near total shut down of tanker exports via the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf, along with worsening Red Sea tanker export volumes following Houthi capture of the Sea’s southern exit, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, are the main cause for rocketing crude oil and refined fuel prices – currently between $106-$120/bbl – most energy industry analysts say.
As of Monday, US diesel prices were at record highs, exceeding $6 a gallon, and gasoline prices were near record highs, ranging from $4-$6 a gallon depending on the state, according to data published by the American Automobile Association.
Russian President Vladimir Putin in Aug. 22 comments aired by state-controlled media said of Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russia: ““How effective are they – are they effective at all? And do they have any impact on the situation along the line of contact as a whole? The ultimate result for the adversary turned out to be the exact opposite of what was expected. No turning point occurred.”
According to an Aug. 28 estimate by Bloomberg widely re-published in Ukrainian media, Ukraine’s drone strikes against Russia’s fossil fuel processing capacity has cut Russian Federation national production of gasoline, aviation fuel, diesel and other petroleum derivatives by more than 30%. Russian industry analysts likewise have said the reduction is close to a third and that bringing capacity back online will be difficult because Russian air defenses are struggling to stop the Ukrainian drones.
