articles.title: Houthis claim to launch large-scale missile, drone attack against Saudi Arabian air base
articles.body:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi terror group claimed Monday that it carried out a large-scale ballistic missile and drone attack on King Khalid Air Base in southern Saudi Arabia, as the group simultaneously expanded its control over strategic islands along the Red Sea shipping route.
The Houthis said dozens of ballistic missiles and drones targeted military infrastructure at the base in Khamis Mushait, including aircraft hangars, radars, runways and ammunition depots.
The group claimed the strikes caused significant damage to the base. The extent of the damage could not be verified immediately.
The Houthis stated that the operation was carried out in response to what they described as more than 300 Saudi airstrikes across Yemen during the previous five days.
The group said Saudi F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets carried out those strikes from Khamis Mushait and Taif airbases.
Saudi Arabia has carried out strikes against Houthi targets amid a sharp renewed escalation between the kingdom and the Iran-backed group, but the Houthi figure of more than 300 strikes was not independently confirmed.
The Houthis threatened further operations inside Saudi territory if the strikes on Yemen continued, saying they would respond to any additional escalation with larger attacks.
The Monday claim followed a major Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia the previous week, when the group used missiles and drones against Khamis Mushait and Saudi energy infrastructure. Saudi authorities said those attacks wounded more than 70 people and caused fires at oil facilities.
Houthis make territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast
At the same time, the Houthis have made significant territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and on islands near the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Yemeni government and Houthi officials said Monday that the rebels had captured Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish, two islands roughly 160 kilometers north of the strait.
The takeover followed the group’s seizure of Mocha and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim, during its rapid advance along Yemen’s western coastline.
The Houthis had reached the Hanish Islands several days earlier as government forces withdrew from positions in the area, according to Yemeni military sources.
Government forces backed by Saudi Arabia attempted over the weekend to regroup and launch a counteroffensive following the Houthi advances around the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

articles.title: Red Sea blitz: What Houthi gains mean for Yemen and the Iran war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Red Sea blitz: What Houthi gains mean for Yemen and the Iran war
In a highly consequential development for Yemen and the region, the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mocha from the internationally recognised Yemeni government, along with a strategic Red Sea island.
The lightning advance over the past week puts them in a prime position to close the Bab al-Mandab Strait more easily than ever before.
The loss of Mocha on 10 September cuts the government’s direct access to the Red Sea, while the capture of the strategic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, a day later enables them to effectively close the Bab al-Mandab in tandem with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The offensive, which displaced almost 50,000 people, represents one of the biggest strategic setbacks for the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in several years.
The Houthis captured Yemen’s capital Sanaa and the major port city of Hodeidah in 2014. The Zaydi Shia group fought the government, which relocated to the southern port city of Aden, and its Saudi backers in a devastating war that from 2015 until 2022.
Approximately 150,000 Yemenis have perished, and the country endured a severe humanitarian crisis that pushed it to the brink of famine.
A 2022 Saudi-Houthi ceasefire largely held until July, when fighting resumed after Riyadh attempted to block a direct Mahan Air flight from Tehran to Sanaa, the first since 2015.
The official purpose of that Iranian flight was to pick up and return a Houthi delegation attending the funeral of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Riyadh and the Yemeni government feared an unopposed air bridge would enable Tehran to conveniently fly military equipment directly to its Houthi allies.
The emboldened Houthis have since resumed striking Saudi infrastructure and energy sites with drones and missiles. The kingdom now faces Iran-backed militia attacks from Yemen to its south and Iraq to its north. The latest advance inside Yemen marks the most significant escalation with Aden and its Saudi backer in years.
Serious territorial gains
“The Houthi advance into Mocha is a strong indicator that Iran is seeking to undermine the US-led coalition in its strategic rear, which is the Bab al-Mandab,” Nicholas Heras, Interim Executive Director at the Middle East Policy Council and Senior Director at the New Lines Institute, told The New Arab.
According to reports, Iran told the Houthis to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, promising them more funding and weapons, and Tehran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) paramilitary directly guided the group’s coastal offensive.
“Saudi Arabia is a wavering member of the American coalition against Iran and the resumption of the war in Yemen with rapid Houthi gains is an embarrassing predicament for Saudi Arabia,” Heras said.
Ryan Bohl, a senior Middle East and North Africa analyst at the risk intelligence company RANE, pointed out that Mocha “certainly matters” to the Houthis since it expands the “buffer zone” for Hodeidah.
Additionally, it opens up a route for any subsequent attempts to encircle the southwestern city of Taiz, entrenches their influence over the Red Sea, and provides “new launch positions” for striking shipping passing through that vital but narrow Bab al-Mandab.
“I think the Houthis will continue to advance so long as there is military opportunism,” Bohl told The New Arab. “They can always trade away territory for a final settlement since there is the suggestion that they may only be interested in controlling those Zaydi portions of Yemen,” he noted.
“The most likely block on further advances will be the almost certain furious counterattacks by the IRG (Yemen’s Internationally Recognised Government) and the Saudis who will do whatever they can to prevent the fall of a major city like Marib or Taiz or an advance on Aden,” Bohl added.
More broadly, the RANE analyst noted, these advances certainly help the Houthis with their broader Red Sea strategy and potentially give them additional territory which they can trade for a future settlement with Riyadh and the Yemeni government.
Heras echoed this assessment. “The Houthis understand the limits of their power in Yemen beyond the core areas of Zaydi population concentration and are instead seeking to improve their ability to pressure the Saudis to pressure the Americans to support Iran,” he said.
“This Houthi campaign along Yemen’s coast is a declaration that the Houthis are key actors in global geopolitics who are able to undermine the US geostrategy in the Middle East.”
Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), assesses that these Houthi advances mark the “most serious territorial gain” the group has made in years, putting the entire Hodeidah governorate under its effective control.
“This is a major defeat for the IRG - which just a few days ago was boasting of military advances in the very same governorate - and a sign of the extreme unpredictability of the current escalation," he told The New Arab.
Saudi support
RANE’s Bohl expects Saudi air support will prove critical for blunting any further Houthi advance and supporting IRG counterattacks.
“At the same time, so will unity amongst the IRG's ground forces,” he said. “This latter element is the most critical because without a sense of unity these counteroffensives will be stuck being localised and unable to comprehensively roll the Houthis back.”
According to an Axios report, Saudi Arabia’s powerful Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called US President Donald Trump during the Houthi advance, requesting renewed US strikes against them.
Trump declined. Nevertheless, US military advisors in Saudi Arabia are providing expanded intelligence and targeting support for the kingdom’s operations against the Iran-backed group, according to a CNN report.
Bohl noted that Saudi Arabia is already responding to Houthi attacks and advances and is “likely to be drawn into further involvement” in the civil war raging over its southern border. That further involvement could potentially lead to a deployment of Saudi forces into Yemen alongside “enhanced airstrikes” against the group.
The escalation, and ongoing Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, come a little over a month after the kingdom signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan on 7 August.
Pakistan has already clarified that it hasn’t planned any military response against the Houthis for their attacks.
“There is no such thing under discussion right now … When the time comes (we) will act under the agreement,” Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said on 10 September, the same day Mocha fell.
“As for other members of the Mecca pact, they will remain wary of conducting military operations inside of Yemen given the distant geographies from Turkey and Pakistan, as well as the prospect of trapping their forces in an intractable conflict,” Bohl said.
“But most notably, the change in the Trump administration from the first to the second term may prove to be important.”
He recalled that in its first term at the end of the 2010s, the Trump administration focused on “containment and mitigating the humanitarian impacts” of the Yemen conflict.
Now, in its second term, it perceives Yemen as “part of the struggle” against Iran. Consequently, it may be more likely to support broader Saudi military operations against the Iran-backed group while making “fewer demands” to change tactics that could have a significant humanitarian impact.
Potential scenarios
ACLED’s Yemen analyst Ali sees several potential scenarios for Yemen after these latest Houthi advances.
“The Houthis may press their advantage and launch more attacks to seize the coast of Taiz governorate just south of Hodeideh, bringing the entirety of the Yemeni Red Sea coast under their control,” he said.
“Alternatively, IRG forces may regroup to carry out a counterattack and attempt to reclaim lost territories.”
Both scenarios would mean a “heightened level of violence” and “increased risk for civilians” in Yemen in the coming weeks in addition to “hundreds of military casualties” from “deadlier clashes” along other internal frontlines. Ali anticipates fighting focused in al-Jawf in the east, which borders Saudi Arabia.
Both sides are engaged in heavy clashes there, with strategic sites “changing hands” at a rapid rate.
“Alternatively, the Houthi blitzing may force Saudi Arabia - which is the IRG’s main backer - back to negotiating with the group to avoid further potential losses for their Yemeni allies in the IRG, which could mean an abrupt end to the current round of escalation,” he said.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs
Follow him on X: @pauliddon
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: ‘Attacks will be fully autonomous’: Russia, Ukraine race towards AI warfare
articles.body:
‘Attacks will be fully autonomous’: Russia, Ukraine race towards AI warfare
Automated AI drones are just one component of an ultimate chain of destruction both sides are building.
Tetiana Bubynets collapsed on the asphalt after a Russian drone exploded at a gas station in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.
Despite the violent shockwave and blast of drone shrapnel produced by the attack on July 6, the 18-year-old accounting student had no visible wounds except for a nosebleed.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US envoys meet Putin: What’s behind latest diplomacy on Russia-Ukraine war?
- list 2 of 3US envoys hold ‘substantive’ talks with Zelenskyy in first visit to Kyiv
- list 3 of 3Witkoff says peace talks have been ‘very meaningful’ in Ukraine
She was rushed to hospital and pronounced dead shortly after, alongside two other civilians, aged 41 and 48.
One of her lecturers, Tetiana Melikhova of Zaporizhzhia National University, said Bubynets was an only child and that her mother “lost the meaning of life” after she died.
“She couldn’t speak. At the funeral, she just lay on the coffin; she couldn’t let her child go,” Melikhova told Al Jazeera.
The strike that killed Bubynets was the first recorded case of Russia’s use of a fully autonomous attack drone powered by artificial intelligence (AI), according to a New York Times analysis.
While drone strikes have hammered Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukrainian officials who examined the wreckage found the unmanned vehicle to be unlike others.
In place of an antenna, it featured an AI-powered minicomputer sold commercially by US technology company Nvidia, which rendered it capable of directing itself to the type of target it was programmed to spot – likely propane tanks in this case – lock on to it and proceed to strike.
AI-powered drones are the tip of the iceberg as Russia and Ukraine race towards boosting tech infrastructure aimed at coordinating reconnaissance and attack, according to analysts.
“It’s not about a drone having AI in it, and then seeing something and striking,” Marina Miron, researcher at the defence studies department at King’s College London, said. “Rather, it’s the drone seeing something, communicating to a software complex which knows how to map the GPS coordinates on a live battlefield map, and notifying the closest artillery unit.”
Referred to as reconnaissance-strike architecture, these unified battlefield management systems act like a central command. They track the location of friendly forces and identify enemy positions.
AI acts as the accelerator, instantly processing massive amounts of data collected through sensors in drones or any other military products, including interceptor missiles or artillery units.
The tactical advantage on the battlefield is given by the system’s ability to compress the kill chain – meaning coordinating and distributing the intelligence to military assets on the ground to find, track and destroy targets in a matter of minutes.
In such an ecosystem, AI-powered automated drones are just pieces of a broader puzzle.
Ukraine is known to be developing its system, which it named DELTA. Following operational trials in late 2025, Russia has been rolling out its version, the Svod Tactical Situational Awareness Complex, to front-line units.
Both sides claim that once the battlefield data is processed, a decision support system (DSS) presents a military commander with options to choose from, keeping a human in the decision-making loop, said Miron.
“In how far that is true is, of course, impossible to find out,” she added.
Acknowledging full AI autonomy would provoke ethical and legal questions.
Even if humans were to retain final decision-making authority, research has shown AI systems subtly shape choices, predetermining outcomes.
“Under time and pressure, commanders often do as AI suggests,” said Miron, whose research focuses on military AI and remotely piloted and autonomous systems.
Towards full automation
Coordinated AI-powered military systems are the next frontier of modern warfare, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defence adviser on loitering munitions, known by his callsign Flash.
“That’s what it will all come to,” he posted on his Telegram channel on July 1. “Navigation, search for a target, and attacks will be fully autonomous.”
Drones with some autonomous capabilities are already being deployed at scale.
Heorhii Volkov, commander of Ukraine’s Yasni Ochi drone strike unit, said this is currently mostly used in the final phase of long-distance strikes, where first-person view (FPV) drones are likely to lose radio connection due to electronic warfare or the curvature of the Earth.
The use of AI in so-called last-mile operations solves this battlefield hitch. If the signal is lost, an integrated AI-enabled onboard module takes full control of the unmanned vehicle, autonomously locks on the target and carries the strike to completion.
Yaroslav Azhnyuk, founder of Ukrainian technology company The Fourth Law, which develops AI-powered autonomy software for unmanned vehicles, said Russia and Ukraine were working to deploy a wider range of autonomous systems.
“This is not simply a race to demonstrate a fully autonomous drone. It is a race to make autonomy reliable, affordable and deployable at scale,” Azhnyuk told Al Jazeera. “Electronic warfare, increasingly long engagement distances and the growing number of drones are making human-controlled systems less sufficient. Autonomy solves exactly these constraints.”
Azhnyuk believes autonomy will become a game-changer over the next six to 12 months.
“The decisive advantage will belong to the side that can deploy reliable autonomy across tens or hundreds of thousands of systems, not just demonstrate it in prototypes,” he said.
Kateryna Bondar, senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), noted the dangers of AI’s reliance on algorithms.
“The system doesn’t understand what it’s doing; it’s just following the algorithm and the rules which people created,” said Bondar, who works at the CSIS’s Wadhwani AI Center. “AI has to be trained to recognise targets and engage these targets,” but writing code that distinguishes between a bus and a tank is easier than between a Russian and a Ukrainian soldier.
Additionally, cost-effective FPV drones have low-quality cameras and their resolution can be lowered further by adverse atmospheric conditions.
Military units using autonomous systems therefore “delegate the decision to a very imperfect technology that cannot distinguish between a civilian and a military person, combatant or non-combatant”, Bondar said.
“This is why there is a conversation around who makes a decision and who has responsibility for mistakes and errors.”

articles.title: Ukraine Has Leverage Over Trump Now
articles.body:
Notable to hear President Trump announce that he had been in contact with President Zelensky of Ukraine to call on him to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. Trump suggested that these Ukrainian attacks had been behind the ramp up in diesel prices in recent weeks. This appeared to repeat a narrative from Treasury Secretary Bessent that it was Ukrainian attacks on Russia, and not the war effort on Iran, which had driven US diesel prices to record prices - over $6 a gallon.
Obviously, it’s politically useful for Trump to blame the war in Ukraine for the elevation in global energy prices since the war in Iran given the proximity of midterms.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It’s true that Ukraine has been increasingly successful in hitting Russian energy infrastructure. Ukrainian deep strike drone attacks have hit 30-40% of Russian refineries. It is hard to determine how much capacity has been taken out of action, but it’s been so significant that Russia, which was a significant diesel and refined product exporter, has banned exports. There have, meanwhile, been significant shortages at the pumps across Russia.
Trump might be eager to deflect blame for the global spike in energy, and particularly from the war in Iran, but he cannot escape from some of the blame even for Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Important here to note that under the Biden presidency when US was providing significant military support to Ukraine – particularly long-range HIMARS and ATACMSs systems – it had leverage over Ukraine. It could threaten to pull those systems unless Ukraine held to certain red lines – particularly limiting attacks on Russian assets with global market impact. Ukraine generally complied.
Russia Launches Kalibr Cruise Missiles Directly From Base, Ukraine Says
But things changed under Trump. He pulled financial support from Ukraine and limited delivery of key weapons systems. Ukraine was forced to develop its own – and therein put much effort into the development of deep strike drone capability to replace the US systems. These systems are now proving so effective against Russian energy infrastructure. And as they are home made Ukraine feels little need to ask for US permission to hit longer range targets in Russia.
Ukraine still exercised some restraint, however. Because it remained dependent on European financing, Kyiv was inclined to limit actions that could disrupt global energy markets and hurt energy-importing Europe. Ukraine held back.
But what changed with Trump’s attack on Iran was that Ukraine saw the US acted on its own interests – attacking Iran and forcing up global energy prices against the interests of key allies in Europe, and Asia. Ukraine saw that what was good enough for the US was good enough for it. States, like the US act in their own national interest, and Ukraine saw the green light to do the same, even though they were hurting the interests of allies. Ukraine took the gloves off.
So I would argue that in his management (or mismanagement) of support for Ukraine and then the attack on Iran, Trump cannot get away from significant blame for current high oil, energy and diesel prices.
And surely if Ukraine is to stop these attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, then the question is what Trump will supply in return? What’s the quid pro quo? Ukraine now has leverage, or cards. Ukraine will likely demand an uptick in delivery of key air defense systems –Patriot interceptors if it is to pull punches in attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.

articles.title: A fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse has burned in a Russian strike since the start of the month
articles.body:
Russia struck a fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse in two weeks on 14 September, setting fire to the Odesa depot of medicine distributor BaDM, Ekonomichna Pravda reported. Russian forces hit it during an attack they ran across the country through the night.
The fourth depot, and what Russia did to it
The BaDM complex stands on the edge of Odesa. The strike started a fire on the grounds, and the State Emergency Service worked at the site. It left significant damage to the storage buildings.
Preliminarily, nobody was hurt, sources on the pharmaceutical market told Ekonomichna Pravda. BaDM is one of the biggest wholesalers moving medicines to Ukrainian pharmacies.
The three depots Russia hit before it
- Russia opened the run on 3 September, when it damaged the Biokon logistics complex in Boryspil raion, Kyiv Oblast. That site counts as the country's largest specialized pharmaceutical warehouse.
- Overnight on 8 September, Russian forces attacked the Kyiv warehouse of Optima-Pharm with two ballistic missiles. They had already destroyed that site, which belongs to one of the largest distributors, in 2025.
- On 13 September, Russian forces struck Universal Logistic, the second-largest medicine warehouse in Ukraine. Four specialized sites in two weeks is a pattern, and Russia now hits medicine storage as it has hit food, construction materials, and parcels.
The attack the Odesa strike came in
Russia launched 108 strike drones from 18:00 on 13 September, Ukraine's Air Force said. The wave carried Shahed-type drones, among them jet-powered ones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoys. Air defense downed or suppressed 85 of them by 08:00. Ukrainian forces recorded hits at seven locations, and the Air Force said the attack was still running when it published that count.

articles.title: Houthis claim large-scale missile, drone attack on King Khalid Air Base in Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Yemen’s Houthis on Monday claimed to have carried out a large-scale missile and drone attack on a Saudi air base in the southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group targeted King Khalid Air Base with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
He claimed the attack targeted aircraft hangars, radars, runways, ammunition depots and other military facilities, causing “significant losses” at the base.
The Houthis said the operation came in response to Saudi airstrikes in Yemen, claiming Saudi F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets had carried out more than 300 strikes across several Yemeni provinces over the past five days.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi claims regarding damage at the air base.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense issued an alert in Khamis Mushait governorate but later said “the danger has passed.” It urged residents to continue following Civil Defense instructions and avoid gathering and filming.
The Houthis vowed to continue attacks inside Saudi Arabia as long as Saudi military operations in Yemen continue, warning that any new attacks would be met with “broader and more severe” operations.
The attack comes amid a sharp escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with the two sides exchanging attacks in recent days.
Saudi Arabia has intensified airstrikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen, while the Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks targeting southern Saudi cities and energy facilities.
Last week, Saudi authorities said 73 civilians were injured in Houthi attacks targeting Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, while attacks also caused fires and temporary disruptions at energy facilities in the kingdom.
The Houthis captured Yemen's capital Sanaa in 2014, and have been battling a Saudi-led coalition for more than a decade.

articles.title: Former Estonian president: Not enough air defense in the world to meet Ukraine's needs
articles.body:
Former Estonian president: Not enough air defense in the world to meet Ukraine's needs
Former President Kersti Kaljulaid told ERR that defense industry representatives say there is currently not enough air defense equipment in the entire world to meet Ukraine's needs and the situation for Ukrainians has deteriorated.
You've just returned from Ukraine and alarming reports have emerged in the media about trains heading toward Poland coming under attack. How did your journey home go?
That's right. Tiit and Taavi took the train before mine to scout things out. I was on the next train, the so-called Yalta Express for the Yalta European Strategy conference. I don't know whether that was the original plan, because even before we set off, there was talk that attacks on the railways were expected that night, particularly in western Ukraine. That information was already out there, but our train took a different route.
We did stop as well. I just checked the time of the news report and it looks as though we stopped because of the same overflight. We got to practice evacuating the train. But nothing as terrible happened to us as what happened to the train ahead of Tiit and Taavi's on its way toward Warsaw, whose locomotive was hit.
Tiit and Taavi are members of your team — Tiit Riisalu and Taavi Linnamäe.
They're not actually members of my team today, but that's how the Estonian state knows them, yes. They were primarily there to prepare for the Ukraine financing conference in January.
You, however, attended the international YES security conference in Kyiv. What was your mood when you came back and what were your main takeaways?
This was another one of those years when all the Westerners were saying, "See, look, you're not losing after all, everything is going very well, Europe is supporting you and you don't even need U.S. assistance." And then the Ukrainians were saying, "Listen, we're hanging on by our fingernails here and we actually need a great deal more help."
They're quite desperate about the fact that they're not being allowed to die, but they're not being allowed to live either. They still feel that more could be done.
For understandable reasons, the veterans' panels are still full of disbelief. One veteran asked the audience how many people there thought that if Ukraine had received the level of assistance it is receiving today back when Crimea was occupied, whether any of this would even be happening now. They're quite saddened by all of this.
Some of the messages genuinely made me angry. For example, during a panel with senators, someone asked whether anybody could tell Trump that Starlink should be allowed to operate on Russian territory so that Ukraine could strike Russia much more effectively. The response was that in America, it isn't customary to interfere in business.
Everyone understands perfectly well that if Trump told Elon Musk that this was what was needed, that's what would happen. And as for not interfering in business, even the British AI Security Institute wasn't given the latest model because the U.S. government wouldn't allow it. So that was such a ridiculous thing to say that people became genuinely angry.
Late last week and early this week, U.S. presidential special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited both Moscow and Kyiv. As far as we know at this point, what good has come of that, apart from people in Kyiv getting one peaceful night's sleep?
I don't think even the Ukrainians themselves know that at this point. Clearly, to some extent, they're returning to the proposal made around the time of the Davos conference, which the Ukrainians said at the time contained significant guarantees they could be satisfied with.
But both then and now, the unanswered question is what leverage there is to actually bring the Russians to the negotiating table. That leverage wasn't demonstrated then and it doesn't appear to have been demonstrated now either.
Kushner's message was clearly that the two sides have to reach an agreement. That wording shows that they still think of this as two sides that are quarreling with each other and, for some irrational reason, don't understand that they would be better off doing business together. That was essentially his message.
And he also said that if the Ukrainians gave up Donbas, everything would be fine. But we don't hear anything about what Russia might give up.
Exactly — Russia could give up the rest of Ukraine that it hasn't conquered yet, right? It was very bad. All of it was very bad.
But on the positive side, Europeans understand that we're paying for this war, but that it's also in our interests to make sure it doesn't end badly.
How seriously are the Ukrainians actually taking these peace talks now? Some kind of follow-up meeting is being planned for October, again in a trilateral format.
Well, how trilateral can it really be? Zelenskyy did suggest holding a meeting on the sidelines of the G20, but Moscow immediately said he should come there and beg.
Naturally, the Ukrainians aren't going to tell the Americans, "We're not going to try." And of course they want peace because what's happening is horrific. These attacks on civilian infrastructure ... I've been going to Ukraine throughout the war myself and people in Kyiv said that things were still relatively calm while we were there.
Things have clearly gotten worse for them. Right now, they don't have an effective weapon against the new types of drones. They're struggling with that somewhat. They don't have the air defenses they keep asking for. Representatives of the defense industry were there as well and said there simply isn't enough air defense equipment in the entire world right now to meet Ukraine's needs.
So in that sense, the situation is very bleak for the Ukrainians and, of course, they want peace. But the Americans haven't shown what cards they have to bring the Russians to the negotiating table.
Europeans — the United Kingdom, Germany and France — also took part in one round of talks. What approach should Europeans take toward this whole negotiation process?
That's right. Senior advisers to the German chancellor and the French president were there, as were representatives from Italy and the United Kingdom. I asked whether it would be conceivable for our participation to be based on some kind of formal mandate. For example, the European Union's Foreign Affairs Council could decide how Europeans should conduct these negotiations, who should represent us there and what their mandate should be.
Otherwise, what happens is that decisions are made and afterward Ukraine has to be admitted to the European Union, its reconstruction has to be paid for and perhaps its military will have to be supported in the future as well. The Ukrainians' proposal in January was essentially: We'll keep 800,000 troops under arms and you pay for all of it.
Europe will have to shoulder that burden, but those costs will be shared among 27 countries. For those of us who aren't among the E3 countries — and that's the majority of us — it would be important to show our publics that this process has been properly mandated.
Would that be improved if, for example, Poland or the Nordic countries were also represented?
No. I think in that case there would always be another large country left out that would then feel slighted. The most sensible solution would still be for the European Union to issue a proper mandate. The representatives could also be from Germany and France — I don't think anyone would have a problem with that — but there has to be a proper mandate.
The panel you chaired at the conference focused on corruption. How well is Ukraine's fight against corruption going right now? We're seeing searches involving some very prominent people and people being caught. What does that tell us?
We did indeed have the justice minister at the table, along with the head of NABU, Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau, the deputy prosecutor general and Taras Kachka, a former deputy prime minister and now the chief negotiator — the role Henrik Hololei once had in Estonia.
He and some members of parliament didn't particularly like it when shortcomings were pointed out. They say, "What we do, we do well, but we only have the capacity to deal with very large schemes, not small-scale bribery." They have to make choices because they don't have the resources.
You could see that the negotiators really didn't like that kind of criticism and it was actually somewhat difficult to keep the arguments on the panel under control. Most of the participants were Europeans. My aim, however, was to let everyone involved have their say and allow those around the table to decide for themselves from which angle each person was viewing the "elephant in the room." Nobody denies that the elephant is still there.
At the same time, we also have to understand that corruption exists everywhere. You simply have to make it as difficult and high-risk an activity as possible. If the risk of getting caught is high and the penalties are severe, there will be less corruption than when the risk is low. That's clearly the direction they're trying to move in.
At the same time, they had what you might call an "industrial accident" in parliament that seriously undermined European confidence when there was an attempt to reduce NABU's powers instead. It's clear that they're getting a great deal of good advice, but people don't think they're capable of implementing it quickly enough.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Aleksander Krjukov
Source: "Ukraina stuudio"

articles.title: Ukraine’s FLYCAT strike drone is built to fly without satellite signals. Its bigger new sibling is designed to reach 200 km behind the front
articles.body:
A Ukrainian company has unveiled a homegrown strike drone built to fly deep behind Russian lines, Militarnyi reported on 13 September. Octava Defence showed the new long-range aircraft—a bigger version of a drone already used in combat—at the MSPO 2026 defense expo in Kielce, Poland. The company says the smaller drone is built to keep working in electronic warfare conditions without a reliable satellite signal.
Russian jamming is one of the biggest obstacles to Ukrainian strikes deep in the rear, which is why Ukrainian makers keep building guidance that does not depend on satellite signals.
The workhorse is already in the fight
The base FLYCAT, presented in January 2026 by another Ukrainian firm, Venator Technologies, is a strike drone Ukrainian forces have used in combat since March. An improved model went into action in July and August and is now undergoing codification—entry into Ukraine's official weapons register.
Watch first naval battle in history fought entirely by drones: Ukrainian uncrewed boat spots, fires on, and sinks Russian one in Black Sea
The company says the updated drone can fly more than 80 km, stay in the air for an hour, and carry a warhead weighing up to 3.7 kg. It is built to hunt armored vehicles, artillery, radars, and air-defense systems, as well as lighter shelters and communications gear. It can pair with a scout drone that finds the target and passes the coordinates. Several FLYCATs can also strike a single target together or hit multiple targets at once.
Nearly everything on it is built in Ukraine—the communications, navigation, guidance, and warhead. Only the engines come from abroad. Its two cameras—day-only or day-and-night—feed a terminal-guidance module that picks out the target from 2,000 m as it closes in.
The one that reaches deeper
The FLYCAT SL is a bigger, longer-range version, and it is still in testing. The company says it is built to fly more than 200 km, stay airborne for over two and a half hours, and carry a heavier load of up to 7 kg.
That range is meant to let it go after command posts, armored vehicles, artillery, and air defenses far behind the front line.

articles.title: Europe hesitates as Russian attacks escalate
articles.body:
While European nations use strong words against the Kremlin and discuss future response options, the strategy for now is to “keep calm and carry on,” according to a senior NATO diplomat.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte speaks as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen listens during a press statement before a meeting at EU headquarters on September 2, 2026, in Brussels. | Omar Havana/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Despite Russia's intensifying attacks on European critical infrastructure and weapons factories, NATO countries remain wary of making immediate tough moves that could provoke the Kremlin.
European capitals are eyeing options including opening a debate about whether a so-called hybrid attack could trigger NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause, more unified communication in response to incidents and a greater push on protecting critical infrastructure, according to three NATO diplomats and one person familiar with the matter, who were granted anonymity to speak freely due to the sensitivity of the matter.
But so far, Europe is avoiding taking any drastic steps — in part over fears it could escalate into an all-out war with Russia.
Advertisement
“We have all the response options ... some of them will be public, some are not,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte told POLITICO on Monday. “I'm saying to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and everyone who wants to listen, if you continue doing this, we will not only have our response options .... we will also continue the support in Ukraine.”
The calls for action underscore growing anxiety around the increasing frequency of sabotage, cyberattacks and other actions that fall below the threshold of conventional war across Europe. Over the weekend, a Russian drone hit a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border shortly after top Western security officials passed through, while Bulgarian authorities launched investigations into two explosions at weapons storage sites in the country.
“The pressure is mounting in view of the events on the Polish border,” said a fourth, senior NATO diplomat. But for now, the strategy is “keep calm and carry on and … continue our support for Ukraine.”
The most serious incidents pinned on Russia — including an attempted attack on Leipzig airport last month — have so far been thwarted. But European officials are increasingly grappling with the prospect they may soon face a successful attack with casualties, and the backlash that brings.
“The secret services have done a good job” so far, said one senior European defense official. But “we have been lucky — there have been no big incidents … if we do not act, then things might get much worse.”
“We are too shy — definitely,” said German lawmaker Marie Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, who chairs the European Parliament’s defense committee. “Vladimir Putin never stops, he’s always coming closer … we have to show we’re willing to fight back.”
Advertisement
Opening a debate
Inside NATO, allies have not yet formally drawn up plans for responding to the uptick in incidents, two of the alliance diplomats mentioned above said. Controversial options like offensive cyber operations against Russia are typically handled by national intelligence services.
Informally, some allies are discussing the possibility of starting a debate on whether an accumulation of sub-conventional attacks could cross NATO’s Article 5 threshold, the three diplomats said. Clarifying where that line is would send a clear warning to Russia and show NATO’s unified opposition to such attacks, two of the diplomats said, but acknowledged so far there is no consensus on the issue.
The senior European defense official said opening the discussion was “worthwhile,” but cautioned it would need to be matched with clear “political will” for a military response — to avoid hollowing out the meaning of the collective defense clause.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated wavering on NATO and collective defense in particular also makes that debate more sensitive. “We have considered calling for Article 5,” said an Eastern European diplomat. “But we don't want to escalate and it could backfire, as it could show Putin that Trump is not ready to help.”
Countries are discussing how to formally, quickly and collectively attribute the attacks to the Kremlin, the three diplomats said. Allies could also be asked to spell out more clearly their spending on civilian preparedness and protection of infrastructure like hospitals, as part of their obligations to funnel 1.5 percent of GDP into civil defense by 2035, the diplomats said. So far, what spending counts toward that target has remained largely undefined.
Gerlinde Niehus, a former longtime NATO official and independent security expert, said the alliance should come up with “pre-agreed packages” in response to specific future attacks, coordinated with governments and intelligence agencies.
Advertisement
Today, “Putin … clearly plays on long decision processes [and] institutional inertia between NATO and the EU,” she said. If a serious Russian-linked sabotage incident was not matched with a clear NATO response, “that would undermine fundamentally the credibility of the alliance,” she said.
That's a concern Rutte brushed off on Monday. “I don't think [NATO] will be perceived as weak” in that scenario, he told POLITICO, while declining to comment on whether the alliance was drawing up new options.
EU not united
The EU is also discussing further measures — but so far there is little evidence that it too is planning an immediate response.
Defense and security is expected to be a key plank of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s annual policy address this week, which is likely to spotlight hybrid threats and the bloc's long-anticipated security strategy, according to two EU officials. The strategy is expected to be presented in the coming weeks.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas is also preparing new sanctions against 1,600 entities, but these were proposed before the latest incidents over the weekend.
Meanwhile, the European Parliament is this week set to adopt a nonbinding resolution led by the Lithuanian MEP Rasa Juknevičienė, with unusually strong language that singles out Russia as “the gravest hybrid threat facing the Union and its Member States.” It is also likely to pass another report calling for strengthening EU agencies’ capacity to act against hybrid activities.
Advertisement
Yet in a sign Europe is still not unified on a stronger response, EU capitals failed to extend the bloc's Russia sanctions against around 3,000 individuals and companies on Monday.
The European Commission didn't immediately respond to a request for comment by POLITICO.
Gabrielius Landsbergis, Lithuania's former foreign minister, said Brussels must immediately take measures like closing the Baltic Sea for Russia's illicit shadow fleet, help Ukraine double its drone production capacity and even move to cut off electricity in Russia with cyberattacks.
“We hide behind the word 'hybrid' hoping that it will shield us from any counter-action,” he said. “Stop with the non-measures, because they only invite Putin to escalate.”

articles.title: Germany Plans €3.4B Tomahawk Missile Purchase
articles.body:
Germany’s Defense Ministry plans to allocate nearly €3.4 billion for US-made Tomahawk cruise missiles and Typhon launchers, according to a report published on Friday, Sept. 11.
According to an internal government planning document seen by Politico, the estimate covers the broader procurement and is expected to be considered during preparations for Germany’s 2027 budget.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The amount could still change before the budget is finalized, and the proposed purchase requires parliamentary approval.
Germany’s Defense Ministry declined to comment on the figure, citing the ongoing budget process. However, a ministry spokesperson confirmed that “the procurement of the US Typhon system with Tomahawk cruise missiles remains intended.”
The acquisition would provide Germany with its first independently operated, ground-based long-range strike capability and form part of Berlin’s broader effort to deter Russia.
Why does Germany want Tomahawk missiles
Tomahawk cruise missiles manufactured by Raytheon have a reported range of approximately 2,500 kilometers (1,600 miles). They could allow the German military, known as the Bundeswehr, to strike missile launch sites, logistics centers and other military targets far behind enemy lines.
The missiles would be fired from Typhon mobile launchers produced by Lockheed Martin. Typhon, officially known as the Strategic Mid-Range Fires System, was developed for the US Army and can launch both Tomahawk cruise missiles and SM-6 missiles.
So You Want to Be a MilTech Millionaire?
Germany currently has no comparable ground-based long-range strike capability. The planning document reportedly envisages bringing the system into German service by the end of the decade.
In 2024, then-US President Joe Biden and then-German Chancellor Olaf Scholz agreed that American forces would begin deploying long-range weapons to Germany in 2026, including US-operated Tomahawks.
US President Donald Trump’s administration later canceled the deployment plan.
Berlin had separately approached Washington in 2025 about purchasing its own Typhon launchers and Tomahawk missiles. Trump and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz reached an agreement in principle on the acquisition during NATO’s July summit in Ankara, according to POLITICO.
Owning and operating the weapons would allow Germany to maintain the capability without relying on a permanently stationed US long-range missile unit.
Berlin seeks role for German industry
Berlin is also seeking a role for German defense companies in manufacturing and maintaining the weapons.
The planning document says the US government has raised “the prospect of industrial cooperation” as part of the procurement. Officials familiar with the negotiations told Politico that the talks include possible co-production and the integration of German companies into the Tomahawk supply chain.
No production arrangement or division of work has been agreed upon, however. Washington is also expected to retain control over sensitive US technology and intellectual property.
Potential German participation could expand a transatlantic weapons supply chain already struggling with large order backlogs. The US is also under pressure to replenish missile stocks depleted during its war with Iran.
NATO members have committed to spending 3.5% of gross domestic product on core defense requirements by 2035, driving further demand for missiles and other weapons.
The Tomahawk purchase is only one element of Germany’s long-range weapons buildup. Berlin is also pursuing European-developed systems and modernizing its existing Taurus air-launched cruise missiles.

articles.title: European spies regain powers denied for decades
articles.body:
For decades, European intelligence agencies were defined more by what they could not do than by what they could; in Germany, the Nordic countries, and much of Eastern Europe, post-war trauma, the legacy of authoritarian regimes, and a growing commitment to safeguarding civil liberties constrained the operations of spy agencies, reports Politico.
Now, as Russia expands its campaigns of hybrid attacks against critical infrastructure and Chinese espionage intensifies, Europe’s largely dormant intelligence organizations have been granted new powers to protect their interests. Over the past 18 months, the need for change has become more pressing amid growing concerns regarding the reliability of the United States under the Donald Trump administration.
While each country must address the specific combination of its own intelligence services, history, and geographical situation, a shared trend toward granting broader powers is evident. Sometimes this comes at the expense of privacy, but governments are assuming a greater role in safeguarding their security. In recent weeks, the governments of several European countries have granted their intelligence agencies broader powers to disrupt hostile operations and launch defensive cyberattacks, while also authorizing the exchange of intelligence with private companies.
David Omand, former head of the UK’s Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), stated that intelligence communities must be able to provide governments with an understanding of what is actually happening and seek to explain it. They need to determine whether Russian-backed criminal activities are underway or if the situation is something entirely different. Omand noted that this requires intelligence communities to truly function as a unified whole, integrating technical, digital, and human intelligence.
In Sweden, the government is preparing staff for the new Foreign Intelligence Service,
which is set to launch in January. In August, Stockholm announced the appointment of two senior officials to the service: Andreas von Beckerath will serve as the agency’s Director General, while Annika Brändström will be his deputy. Both will assume their new roles as soon as the service becomes operational. Von Beckerath currently serves as the European Union Ambassador to Serbia, whereas Brändström has a long career in government, including experience as a security advisor.
The Swedish government has indicated that separating civilian foreign intelligence from military intelligence will allow for a clearer distinction of responsibilities and improve the country’s ability to assess a wide range of security risks. This restructuring is taking place as Sweden continues to reshape its security architecture following its accession to NATO. This process has been largely driven by threats posed by Russia, which escalated sharply after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
On August 28, the Dutch government launched consultations on a proposal to grant its intelligence agencies broader powers under national security law. This would allow them to disrupt the activities of Russian hackers, Chinese spies, and Iranian agents without prior authorization, and enable the sharing of more intelligence with security companies and the military.
Significant legislative changes are also planned in Austria,
a country that has acquired the status of a global hub for espionage. Current laws allow foreign agents to operate with impunity on Austrian soil, provided their spying is not directed against Austria itself. The government is now working to close this legal loophole, thereby complicating matters for the estimated 7,000 spies believed to be operating in Vienna.
The most drastic changes are taking place in Germany. The country has a troubled history with both Nazi-era agencies and, later, the East German secret police, and has been very cautious regarding the powers granted to its intelligence services. Now, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government aims to give these services broader capabilities to counter threats from hostile states. Under the proposed reforms, set to take effect in January, the German foreign intelligence service (BND) will be authorized to conduct sabotage and offensive operations.
An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, remarked that this move was long overdue. Europeans had not anticipated that such threats would reach them, and this measure represents a response to the new threat landscape.
Until now, the BND’s activities were limited to intelligence gathering.
This reflected post-war restrictions deliberately put in place to prevent a recurrence of the abuses that occurred under Nazi rule. However, this also meant that Germany was largely ineffective in the digital realm, partly due to a lack of the necessary authority to access certain types of communications data.
In March, Germany’s data protection watchdog warned that it would be unable to adequately protect citizens from surveillance by intelligence agencies. Omend stated that Germany represents a classic case—it will need to rethink its traditional approach of balancing privacy concerns against national security interests.
The need for deeper intelligence cooperation among European nations became increasingly urgent after the Trump administration abruptly halted the sharing of military and combat-related intelligence with Kyiv in March 2025. The US President has also faced accusations of appointing loyalists with limited or no experience to lead these agencies. This has raised concerns among European officials that Washington might be unwilling to share intelligence that contradicts the administration’s political stance.
Ferdinand Gehringer, a senior hybrid threats analyst at FTI Consulting, said that these changes reflect both a growing awareness of threats to Europe and a shift in the methods used by Russian intelligence services, which are increasingly employing low-level agents to carry out acts of sabotage.
Read also: Spanish intelligence warned of refugee flow before Ceuta crisis

articles.title: Trump calls for an end to attacks on Russian oil refineries
articles.body:
While visiting Ireland, US President Donald Trump called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries amidst a rapid global rise in diesel prices, Politico reports.
When asked about the current surge in fuel prices—particularly for diesel—Trump insisted that the situation was being caused by Ukraine, rather than the war with Iran that he himself had initiated. It was this conflict, he claimed, that had reduced oil exports from the Middle East to near-zero levels.
Trump stated that officials from his administration had asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop launching drones and missiles at Russian refineries that produce diesel. While walking across a golf course, the American told reporters that Mr. Zelenskyy needed to do one thing: stop destroying Russian diesel supplies. He suggested that the Ukrainian president could choose other targets but should avoid diesel production facilities, as attacking them was creating a diesel shortage.
At the same time, Trump continued to insist that the conflict with Iran—which Washington had initiated six months earlier—had nothing to do with the dwindling fuel supplies. He stated that the fuel shortage is not driven by the Middle East but is caused by the war between Russia and Ukraine—a matter he reportedly discussed with Zelenskyy. While there are countless other targets, diesel facilities should be left alone, he argued, because targeting them harms the global community.
Ukraine’s increasingly deep strikes into Russian territory are viewed as a crucial element of Kyiv’s strategy to make the war significantly costly for Russia. Meanwhile, a high-ranking European official close to peace talks led by the US remarked that
the Trump administration is seeking scapegoats ahead of the midterm elections
scheduled for the 3rd of November. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the Trump administration is blaming Ukraine because it does not know how to handle the war it instigated in Iran; they added that Russian diesel and oil have never been significant for US consumption, making Trump’s premise absurd. Furthermore, everyone has heard Trump boast that the US can secure all the oil it needs domestically.
Trump is not the first US official to blame Ukrainian strikes on Russia for rising diesel prices. Last week, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright stated that the damage inflicted on Russian oil refineries has created a challenging situation in the diesel market. A few days earlier, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted that the US was experiencing energy price shocks primarily because the Ukrainians had decided to blow up Russia’s entire energy industry.
A European official stated that if Washington wants Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, it must ensure that Moscow stops attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Any cessation of hostilities would have to be mutual, but since Putin does not respect the US administration, no truce exists.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the news agency Vesti that Moscow would not halt attacks during negotiations. The Kremlin is reportedly open to talks, but the “special military operation” would continue while they take place.

articles.title: ‘We are not scared,’ says top EU diplomat after Russian strike on passenger train
articles.body:
The head of Nato has said a Russian drone attack on a train close to Ukraine’s border with Poland would not deter Kyiv’s western backers.
Mark Rutte said the strike on a passenger train showed how desperate Vladimir Putin had become. “He thinks that he can stops us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong. Our answer is to increase support,” the Nato general secretary said.
European leaders have condemned the strike in which a Russian drone hit a passenger train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday shortly after a convoy of high-level diplomats and former leaders had passed through.
The earlier train, which was carrying the former UK prime minister Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus and running ahead of schedule, may have been the target of the Russian drone strike, Ukrainian Railways has said.
A spokesperson forthe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, struck a similar note to Rutte, saying the attack “was a futile attempt by Russia to undermine our support for Ukraine. It will not deter us.”
The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said the goal of the attacks was “to intimidate Europeans, discourage and above all divide them”.
The EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy, Kaja Kallas, said the strike “was clearly a message to the western world”. Speaking on the sidelines of an Arctic conference in Finland, she said: “I think the question for us is what do we take from that message? I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared off, because otherwise, you know, Russia will just achieve what they want, which is the submission of Ukraine.”
A spokesperson for Kallas added: “We strongly condemn the latest Russian strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border, including the attack against the passenger train,” and referenced a recent EU decision to approve a €6.1bn tranche of the €90bn loan for Ukraine. “We are acting on the front to equip Ukraine better to defend itself, and we will continue to stand firmly with Ukraine and its right to defend itself against Russian aggression,” the spokesperson said.
Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.
Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.
The strikes, which prompted air raid warnings in Poland, came as EU diplomats met in Brussels on Monday for last-ditch talks on the rollover of the bloc’s sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian individuals and entities involved in supporting Vladimir Putin’s war. The sanctions are due to expire on Tuesday but their prolongation is being held up by a dispute about whether to remove an individual from the list.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram on Sunday: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”
Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries as well as Johnson, Petraeus and the former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.
The diplomatic train, Ukrainian Railways said, had left ahead of schedule and could have been the target of the Russian drone.
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.
“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.
He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.

articles.title: Europe Prepares for War as Germany Sends Up to 1,000 New Troops
articles.body:
Germany is preparing to order up to 1,000 active-duty soldiers to serve with its permanent brigade in Lithuania this fall as European NATO members strengthen their eastern defenses against the threat of a Russian attack, according to a report published on Monday, Sept. 14.
According to Bild, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has approved compulsory postings after the Bundeswehr failed to attract enough volunteers for the Lithuania-based unit.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The first mandatory assignments could begin this fall and affect fewer than 1,000 soldiers, several independent sources told the German outlet.
Germany’s Defense Ministry was expected to brief senior representatives of the Bundestag’s Defense Committee about the decision on Monday.
The measure is not a general mobilization or conscription of civilians. It concerns serving Bundeswehr personnel who could be assigned to Lithuania even if they did not volunteer for the deployment.
Only about 60% of the positions required for the brigade have been filled voluntarily. The most serious shortages involve IT specialists, logistics personnel, cooks and enlisted soldiers.
Bild reported that compulsory postings could currently affect as many as 20% of the brigade’s positions. The Bundeswehr hopes to reduce that figure to around 10% by the end of September by attracting more volunteers.
The German military has conducted recruitment campaigns and offered familiarization trips to Lithuania for soldiers and their families. However, the remaining personnel decisions must be made soon because affected soldiers need to be notified, and then may challenge their assignments through legal procedures, and require time to plan a possible relocation.
‘The Battlefield Has Gone Underground’: Khartiia Commander Reveals Ukraine’s Edge Over Russia
“Voluntariness remains the top principle,” Bild reported. “But to guarantee the brigade’s operational readiness, compulsory assignments can no longer be avoided.”
Germany reinforces NATO’s eastern flank
Germany plans to station 4,800 soldiers and around 200 civilian personnel permanently in Lithuania by the end of 2027.
The unit, officially known as the 45th Armored Brigade Lithuania, will be the first German combat brigade permanently based outside the country since the Bundeswehr was established in 1955.
According to the Bundeswehr, the approximately 5,000-person heavy maneuver brigade is intended to protect NATO’s eastern flank following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Once fully operational, the brigade will include thousands of soldiers and approximately 2,000 military vehicles, NATO said.
Lithuania borders Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. It is also close to the Suwalki Gap, a narrow corridor connecting Poland and the Baltic states that NATO considers particularly vulnerable in a potential conflict with Russia.
Pistorius had previously insisted that the brigade should be staffed primarily by volunteers. During a visit to Lithuania in June, however, he acknowledged that compulsory assignments might be necessary and estimated that fewer than 1,000 soldiers could be affected.
Tusk warns Russian escalation could reach NATO
Germany’s decision comes as Poland also strengthens its security posture following Russian attacks close to its border.
On Sunday, Sept. 13, a Russian drone attacked the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train at the Yahodyn railway station in Ukraine’s Volyn region near Poland.
Poland scrambled fighters during the attack, while Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened an urgent meeting with government ministers, senior military commanders and intelligence chiefs.
“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intense activity on the Russian side, and unfortunately, we cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory,” Tusk warned.
The Polish prime minister said Russia’s escalating actions were becoming an immediate security concern for NATO countries bordering Ukraine, reinforcing calls for stronger military readiness across Europe.

articles.title: ‘Our Victory or Defeat’: Ukrainian Top Commander Reveals What Could Force Russia to Reconsider the War
articles.body:
Ukraine’s success or failure in the coming months will largely depend on whether it can defend its skies against Russian ballistic missiles and faster jet-powered attack drones, Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky said at the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv.
“Our victory or defeat will depend on whether we can protect Ukrainian skies this winter,” said Biletsky, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He said Ukraine must counter two principal threats: ballistic missiles and jet-powered attack drones, including Shahed- and Banderol-type weapons.
If Ukraine withstands Russia’s winter air campaign and prevents further battlefield advances, Moscow could face a fundamental decision over whether to continue the war, Biletsky said.
“If we pass this test with dignity and effectiveness, I think March or April will confront Russia with an existential question: Why and how should it continue the war if it has not achieved any of its strategic objectives?” he said.
That moment could create an opportunity for negotiations and a lasting peace largely on Ukraine’s terms, Biletsky added.
The commander said Russia is pursuing two main strategic objectives: completing its occupation of Ukraine’s Donetsk and Luhansk regions and weakening the country’s ability to resist through attacks on civilians, energy facilities, industry, and the economy.
Europe Prepares for War as Germany Sends Up to 1,000 New Troops
According to Biletsky, Russia’s political leadership has demanded that its forces seize the entirety of the two eastern regions by the beginning of 2027, while Russian military commanders have set a deadline of mid-April.
“Russia’s political leadership is demanding that they finish it within the absolutely unrealistic timeframe of the beginning of 2027,” the commander said.
Russia has repeatedly set new deadlines for capturing all of the Donetsk region, a central war objective that its forces have failed to achieve despite years of costly offensives.
Ukraine is preparing for intensified fighting around Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, two key cities in its remaining defensive belt in Donetsk. Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, commander of the National Guard’s 1st Azov Corps, are among the commanders overseeing the region’s defense.
Biletsky said the situation on the front remains difficult but is not the worst Ukraine has faced during the war.
“It is not easy. It is difficult. But the front is not going through its hardest period compared with previous years,” he said.
Ukraine has “every chance” of holding advantageous defensive positions, preserving its belt of fortified cities, and improving its position in parts of the Donetsk front, he said.
“I think that in the near future, within a month, we will demonstrate these improvements to the entire world, and they will be undeniable,” Biletsky said. He did not provide operational details.
The 22nd YES Annual Meeting was held in Kyiv on Sept. 11-12 under the theme “Peace Through Strength NOW!” It brought together about 700 politicians, diplomats, military personnel, veterans, business leaders, activists, and experts from 28 countries.

articles.title: 13 km inside Lebanon: How IDF commandos seized Hezbollah stronghold Khiam in 36 hours
articles.body:
Nearly two years after the battle, the IDF has revealed details of one of Maglan’s most significant operations during the Northern Arrows campaign, when commandos advanced some 13 kilometers (8 miles) into southern Lebanon and fought their way through Hezbollah’s defenses in Khiam.
According to the military account, Maglan forces dismantled successive Hezbollah defensive and command positions and gained control of the town in less than two days.
“You don’t forget the cold of November nights in Lebanon, no matter how much time passes, even if you’re in the commandos,” recalled Lt. Col. Z., who commanded Maglan at the time.
“It was freezing,” he said. “I grew up on the ethos that you don’t fight in Lebanon during the winter because the conditions are simply too difficult. But during Northern Arrows, we had to reach Khiam at exactly that time.”
Maglan’s mission was to take control of the northern part of the town, neutralize Hezbollah command centers there and eliminate anti-tank capabilities that threatened Metula, roughly 13 kilometers to the south.
It was the unit’s final battle of the campaign after dozens of special operations.
“We came into it as veterans of three battles, but this one was different from all the others,” Z. said. “It combined depth with the front line.”
Maglan’s ‘secret sauce’
Lt. Col. A., a reservist who commanded Maglan’s detection-and-strike element, said the unit was selected because the mission required a combination of stealth, intelligence gathering, special operations and maneuver warfare.
“Traditionally, we stand on three legs: detection and strike, special operations and maneuver,” he said. “Khiam is a complex target at tactical depth that has to be reached covertly. Only when you use all the components correctly and add the ‘secret sauce’ does all the magic come together.”
The detection-and-strike method, he explained, allows the same force that identifies an enemy to close the targeting cycle within seconds.
“It is a technique that lets us actively expose the enemy,” A. said. “The same team discovers the terrorists and closes the circle on them within seconds, with zero bureaucracy.”
The capability began developing inside the unit in the 1990s during operations including Grapes of Wrath and Accountability, relying on close coordination with the Israeli Air Force and advanced technology.
“It becomes part of your soul, hunting the enemy,” A. said. “It requires a rare combination of patience, terrain analysis, understanding and the fusion of intelligence.”
Four days of preparation around Khiam
For the troops who entered Lebanon, the depth of the operation was evident almost immediately.
“We hadn’t been out of regular service for very long when we were called up to Lebanon,” recalled Staff Sgt. G., a reservist in one of the teams. “We put on our gear, waited for the vehicles and crossed the border. It took 40 minutes to reach the drop-off point. I remember us looking at each other and saying, ‘Wow, we’ve gone really deep.’”
The area had proved difficult for the IDF during the Second Lebanon War. This time, commanders chose a different approach: drive as far as the terrain allowed and then continue on foot across the hills and mountains, with the goal of reaching northern Khiam in a single night.
Khiam lies between two mountain ridges, and at the time of the operation the surrounding areas were under Hezbollah control, according to the IDF.
“To deal with that, we deployed teams at different ranges on the hills around the town four days before the first ground entry,” Z. said.
After what G. described as an hours-long climb, the teams reached their positions and divided responsibilities.
“We stopped at one point and began observing,” he recalled. “I sat with the Negev machine gun on my knee and noticed a wooded hill about 70 meters away.”
His squad commander told him another Israeli force was positioned behind the trees and that nobody should be moving between the two positions.
“As soon as he finished speaking, I saw three figures in the background,” G. said. “They were walking strangely and carrying weapons. There was no room for doubt. I cocked the Negev and opened fire.”
Other troops immediately joined the firefight.
“There was a special synchronization between us. We just did what we had practiced,” he said. “I remember the guys shouting throughout the encounter until we killed the other two as well.”
Only the next morning did he realize how close the Hezbollah terrorists had been.
“We passed the place where the encounter happened and suddenly understood that it hadn’t been anywhere near 70 meters,” he said. “They had been seven to 10 meters away from us, and even so we managed to take control of the situation very quickly.”
The first 36 hours
For Maglan’s commanders, the central challenge was turning intelligence collected before the operation into an accurate battlefield picture while events unfolded.
“You are constantly racing against time to locate and eliminate the right terrorist cell,” Z. said.
The IDF’s 7th Armored Brigade approached from the south, while commando forces operated from the north and west, supported by intelligence collection at both close and long range.
A. recalled one incident in which several Hezbollah terrorists were spotted fleeing from Khiam’s old quarter toward a nearby wadi.
“One of our forces locked onto them and eliminated them,” he said. “We could have said, ‘Mission accomplished, we’re done here.’ But what did the team do? We redeployed and concentrated effort on that point because the indication was correct. We waited, more terrorists appeared, we engaged them and they were eliminated.”
According to Z., Hezbollah repeatedly attempted to ambush the advancing troops but instead found its own forces being attacked.
“The enemy tries to surprise you, but finds itself surprised instead, and within 36 hours from the start of the battle it is defeated,” he said.
“They did not expect to encounter a force moving that sharply and precisely. We simply waited for the terrorists to make a mistake and attacked them with missiles, drones and additional capabilities until most of the local command chain had been eliminated.”
For A., the operation represented the culmination of decades of experience.
“Twenty-five years led me to this battle,” he joked. “When it ended, I said, ‘That’s it, I’m retiring at the top.’”
He said individual soldiers rarely grasp the full scale of an operation while it is underway.
“One soldier fired 12 mortar rounds, another encountered a terrorist face to face and a third was clearing houses in the town,” he said. “Only when they hear the full picture do they fall silent and understand the power of what they accomplished, step by step.”

articles.title: Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,700 Troops, 74 Artillery Systems and 2,124 UAVs in One Day
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,700 Troops, 74 Artillery Systems and 2,124 UAVs in One Day
Russia sustained an estimated 1,700 personnel losses, along with 74 artillery systems and 2,124 operational-tactical UAVs over the latest 24-hour period, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
As of September 14, Russia’s cumulative personnel losses since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, stood at approximately 1,508,600.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The latest tally also included one tank and one armored combat vehicle, bringing Russia’s total estimated losses in those categories to 12,345 tanks and 25,331 armored combat vehicles.
Another 74 artillery systems were recorded as lost, pushing the cumulative figure to 49,752. Russian forces also lost seven multiple-launch rocket systems and two air defense systems, bringing their respective totals to 2,127 and 1,637.
Estimated aircraft and helicopter losses remained unchanged at 442 and 356, respectively.
The General Staff also recorded the loss of 12 Russian unmanned ground vehicles, increasing the overall total to 2,615. Another 2,124 operational-tactical UAVs were added to the tally, bringing cumulative drone losses to 516,441, while the number of cruise missiles remained unchanged at 5,111.
Russia also lost an estimated 548 vehicles and fuel tankers and two pieces of special equipment over the past day. Cumulative losses in those categories now stand at 148,807 and 4,683, respectively. Naval losses remained unchanged at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Meanwhile, fighting remained intense along the frontline, with Ukrainian forces recording 208 combat engagements during the latest reporting period.
Ukraine has also continued targeting Russian military-linked infrastructure beyond the frontline. Satellite imagery recently revealed extensive damage to Russia’s Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant following a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile strike, including the destruction of part of the facility’s main production building.
