articles.title: ‘They just want the war to end’: Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina on why she believes most Russians are pacifists — and whether the opposition can reach them
articles.body:
‘They just want the war to end’: Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina on why she believes most Russians are pacifists — and whether the opposition can reach them
After the Yabloko party — which ran on antiwar slogans and briefly gave hope to many Russians — was barred from the State Duma election, the opposition, both inside Russia and in emigration, has been debating what voting strategies to adopt now. The Bereg cooperative spoke with Moscow-based politician Yulia Galyamina about the hopes tied to Yabloko, what the election results might actually change, the divide between those who left and those who stayed, and the prospects for a new democracy. Meduza is publishing the interview in full.
— Did you expect the authorities to let Yabloko run its campaign and compete for votes, or did you assume they would block it?
— There was a sense that the Kremlin had its own separate line, or at least an internal debate, about softening the regime. The wavering was obvious: Yabloko was registered and approved, after all. Perhaps [some officials] pinned their hopes on the negotiations that began after Trump took office, hoping for reconciliation. But it’s become clear recently that things are actually headed toward continuing the war, toward finishing it off — and the negotiations have been shelved indefinitely.
The period when negotiations were actually underway was, of course, full of hope, and traces of that hope still lingered this past spring. Yabloko being allowed to run would have signaled that the negotiating track was still being considered — and had they been barred, that would have signaled the opposite.
— Did you notice growing interest in Yabloko?
— Activists really did start talking about voting for Yabloko. There was enthusiasm among a certain segment of society — people who had been to at least one protest in their lives.
— What was the mood among these people after the party’s list was disqualified?
— They hoped for a miracle. It didn’t happen, but life goes on — there’s no sense that life has stopped. Young people who came to politics for the first time probably feel the disappointment more deeply. Those who are older have already lived through so many political disappointments…
— You’ve surely heard the opposition debate various election strategies: boycotting, voting for anyone but United Russia, or backing a specific party like New People or Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF). But this debate mostly plays out outside Russia, among opposition figures abroad. Does it exist inside the country?
— The mood is roughly this: “How much longer can this go on? Nothing depends on this, nothing will change because of it.” Among a certain segment of true Yabloko supporters, there’s talk of spoiling the ballot or not showing up at all.
Protest voting can produce political consequences, but they’re so illusory, let’s say, that it doesn’t feel worth the energy overall. The idea of voting for any party at all, which used to excite people, doesn’t excite me anymore.
— What are these illusory consequences?
— There’s a pragmatic logic to voting for one of the parliamentary parties, but that logic only applies in a crisis scenario. During turbulence, when the system becomes unbalanced, change always happens through institutionalized players, actors within the system. If several establishment parties won a slightly higher share of the vote, that would, in theory, position them to become those players.
The vote share [for them] would have to be large enough that it couldn’t be masked by fraud — and right now, it’s far from certain that’s even possible. With electronic voting, there may be no limit to fraud at all.
There’s also symbolic voting, which doesn’t inspire me at all — going to a polling station and writing in Yabloko on the ballot. That’s unlikely to accomplish anything, and as for a clean conscience… Honestly, I’ve cleansed mine so many times already that I don’t really need to. Especially since it’s not even a unified strategy — “Smart Voting” has shown that, for the most part, it doesn’t produce results.
You’re choosing one cannibal over another. Let everyone decide for themselves — the main message is just: go vote, and decide [who to vote for] on your own, however you want.
— So voters can still show the authorities their discontent?
— I think the government knows all about that discontent. It just no longer takes society into account — its mood is well known. Instead, it works on society through violence, aggression, and a steady drip of one nasty thing after another. They do something nasty, wait a while, make some noise, let people get used to it, then take the next small step. Society manages to adapt, to adjust. People have even somehow adapted to the shortage of gasoline.
— And you?
— We fill up at night and only drive when it’s absolutely necessary. There’s even something environmentally friendly about it — you ride a scooter or walk to the nearest store. Everyone now keeps a gas canister in the trunk, like in the 1990s. And we just keep living.
— Perhaps people started supporting Yabloko precisely because they’re tired of constantly adapting?
— People started supporting Yabloko for another important reason too. I wrote an article called “5 Discourses Around the War,” where I showed how the antiwar and pro-war discourses diverged.
But the largest and most important layer of opinion was never expressed publicly anywhere. Most people were pro-Putin and antiwar. They had no public spokespeople at all, but they could be called pacifists. [In the media space, it’s assumed that] you’re either pro-Putin and pro-war, or anti-Putin and antiwar. There’s also a variant — anti-Putin but pro-war — which exists among Z bloggers.
People who were pro-Putin and antiwar had no talking heads of their own — until Viktoria Bonya. They were a silent majority. When negotiations with Trump began, and there was hope for a ceasefire, they thought: “Fine, we’ll wait — they’ve started negotiating, so it will probably be alright.”
A year passed, the negotiations went nowhere, problems kept mounting, and that silent majority’s voice began to emerge — we saw it in Bonya’s statement and others like it. The authorities tried to silence those voices, and in response, this group’s views began shifting toward an anti-Putin position.
The antiwar discourse split long ago into a pro-Ukrainian strand and a pacifist strand. Lev Shlosberg represents the latter, and so do I. Most people in Russia identify with the pacifist discourse — most citizens were raised as pacifists in the Soviet Union. Everyone sang Let There Always Be Sunshine, and today’s young people sang it in school too.
Not everyone within that broad pacifist discourse is ready to come out against Putin. Some of them supported Yabloko and started moving toward an anti-Putin position. The party doesn’t directly say it’s against Putin — it focuses instead on its opposition to the war.
And that’s a smart approach — it draws in more and more of these people, because they’re for peace but not yet ready to talk about Putin. The next step for them is lifting the taboo on criticizing Putin, the way the taboo on discussing the war was lifted.
— So, to win over public sympathy, you shouldn’t talk about Putin, because it’s still too soon?
— People react to events in bursts. For example, when the gasoline problems began, open rejection of the Russian authorities appeared, in some cases even hatred. But it’s not directed at Putin personally — he’s too sacred a figure. It’s impersonal hatred toward “the bosses” in general.
The position favoring a Ukrainian victory resonates with hardly anyone in Russia. These people exist, but there aren’t many of them. The old opposition can speak loudly because it’s in emigration. But, in my view, this position will never be shared by the majority in Russia.
— And what position could it share? Accepting an outcome, where neither Ukraine nor Russia wins?
— That’s the most likely outcome. But the trend [in Russia] has changed: previously, holding the position “let’s have peace, and it doesn’t matter who wins” wasn’t punished as a matter of principle — now, it seems to me, it’s starting to be. The Shlosberg case showed that, as did [Andrei] Klepach’s dismissal. You can no longer question the idea of victory.
— Does the silent majority need this victory?
— They just want the war to end. It seems the victory narrative isn’t aimed at ordinary citizens but at the most active, pro-war segment of society — maybe at Putin himself too, who probably belongs to that segment as well.
There’s a segment of society that isn’t ready to let this go without a victory — they’ve paid too high a price over these four years: many of their people have died, a great deal has been invested.
But that’s a small share. Most people don’t care, as long as it all ends. And what kind of victory would that even be? What is victory, really? People generally aren’t very interested — they’re ready to accept whatever they’re offered as victory.
— Maxim Katz believes the opposition in emigration is largely to blame for Yabloko being barred — that they showed support at the wrong time. Do you share that view?
— I think it sped up the process, but Yabloko would have been barred anyway — maybe a bit later, and the campaign would have run a little longer. I don’t know whether they would have expanded it [nationwide] or not. In Veliky Novgorod, banners reading “For Peace!” and “For Yabloko!” are still hanging, because they’re running for the regional assembly there and have an active local cell. In Moscow, there was nothing visible at all — zero.
The problem is that no one negotiates with anyone, no one talks things through — just like Putin doesn’t with Volodymyr Zelensky. Yabloko never coordinated with the opposition [in emigration] on whether support was needed, or what kind. And the opposition never approached Yabloko in advance to discuss the form or timing of support.
I never publicly support anyone unless asked to, because I know my support could do harm — even though I’m only designated as a “foreign agent” by Russian authorities, and I live in Russia. When you have “undesirable” status, or something worse, you have to handle this very carefully. It seems to me that some kind of ethic around this should have developed by now, over these years. But it hasn’t, unfortunately — everyone tries to distance themselves from everyone else.
— Maybe the Kremlin is making an effort to set opposition figures against each other?
— The Kremlin didn’t need to make any effort, because Yabloko never really entered into negotiations with anyone — or did so only rarely. I can’t complain here, since I’ve collaborated with Yabloko a great deal and I’m very grateful to them for that. But I know plenty of stories where they simply wouldn’t negotiate with the rest of the opposition. And the rest of the opposition didn’t come to them either.
There’s also an additional factor now: media visibility. The laws of the mass-media market demand an immediate public reaction to the political agenda, and that factor plays a bigger role than the political one.
For many well-known opposition figures in emigration, the public sphere just comes down to mass media — an old model built around a single source of information. There can be competition among several major players, but it’s neither networked nor horizontal. You can only take part in that process as a unit within the mass — through your like.
The public environment needs to be built differently, starting today. Social networks, when they first emerged, offered hope that it could be. But in the end, opposition actors continued to mirror the existing order — the power-based model for organizing the public sphere [and don’t create platforms for discussion, only broadcast their own views].
— In your view, what election strategy is the Kremlin pursuing?
— The authorities used to feel a need to simulate elections more convincingly. In our district, there was genuine competition in the 2021 elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, and strong competition across Moscow generally.
Now the authorities aren’t allowing anything genuine at all. They’re suppressing turnout — it’s very important to them that only their own people show up at the polls. In Moscow, only single-mandate candidates are running any kind of campaign; in our district, an SVO veteran has been at it for months already.
There’s also electronic voting. In my view, the entire electronic vote in the last Moscow City Duma elections was fabricated. I went to my polling station on Sunday at 7 p.m. and voted with a paper ballot — mine was the first one in the ballot box. People did come to the polling station, but everyone there was made to vote electronically.
— Observers say electronic voting can’t be monitored at all.
— There will still be plenty of paper voting in the regions. But the observer movement has grown quite weak — few people volunteer as observers anymore, and all the active organizations have been crushed. It probably takes society some time to understand that no public leaders or organizations are going to appear anymore, and that people need to organize on their own here.
There’s a big open question: are there limits to fraud under current conditions? Observer theory holds that every instance of fraud has its limits — that you can’t falsify more than a certain percentage. But does that rule still hold now?
— If the limits on fraud are loose enough to manufacture any result for United Russia, even an implausible one, and the authorities use that leeway — what reaction would that provoke in society?
— In my view, it’s the youngest part of society — the ones who suddenly believed in something — who could end up demoralized and disillusioned. On the whole, people don’t place much hope in elections and are unlikely to be disappointed. In advanced political thought, which runs a bit ahead of political reality, elections as a symbol of democracy have long been discredited.
The discrediting of elections will help give rise to new forms of democracy in this country. They’re already emerging, and this alternative experience could become the basis for a new political philosophy, practice, and democracy here. But these are lengthy processes.
— Are you talking about horizontal interaction between people?
— Yes, these are horizontal forms. Some communities, for instance, have devised complex combinations of lottery and voting for decision-making. People in small communities choose leaders simply because they know them, and leaders rotate quickly. That includes political communities, women’s communities, and local interest clubs.
I know a theater group that stages its own plays with its own money and tours with them. This amateur theater has its own forms of democracy, its own forms of decision-making. A director originally brought the group together and made the decisions, but after he died, the group decided not to disband and to run things themselves instead. Now they look for directors and make democratic decisions about whom to hire.
Horizontal structures exist all over the country — gardening co-ops, homeowners’ associations. The whole country is threaded through with a variety of democratic formats.
— Do the authorities notice them? The Kremlin is now promoting the concept of “social architecture” — supposedly not a political technology, but engagement with citizens and communities on social projects.
— They have this new term because they consider only geopolitics to be politics. Of course, they’re not going to build real democracy or real democratic institutions — they always build an imitation.
But hijacking the agenda [from the state] was dangerous in the 2010s. Now the top leadership cares about only one thing — the ”special military operation” — and has no time for such games.
I think it’s dangerous that the very people who want to build a different Russia — not a Limonov-style one, but a genuinely different one — don’t fully grasp the importance of real democratic alternatives. They’re still playing by the old rules. Under the old system, you can outplay those in power, break the regime, build another one, but fundamentally it will still rest on all the same original patterns.
In my view, we need to come up with new ideas, find them within society, help them develop — and then a new political event will happen. We need to dream, to build utopias — that’s very important. We’re going through a phase of major historical shift right now. We all sense it. People have been talking about it for 100 years already.
When I was studying cultural studies in the late 1990s and early 2000s, everyone talked about this major shift. I really hoped the changes would come without violence. But, unfortunately, we entered this historical cycle along with it.
— You’re speaking in terms of a broad historical framework. What if we narrow it down to talk about the so-called ones who left and the ones who stayed? People can presumably be divided based on whether they emigrated, but can these groups be generalized by their views and convictions? Is there some essential conflict between them?
— I don’t think there’s any conflict between “those who left” and “those who stayed” — people communicate with each other. But there is a conflict between public discourses. When that gets translated into personal terms — explaining someone’s views and positions by whether they left or stayed, as if that determines who they are, [that’s wrong]…
Your everyday reality probably still shapes your perception. Perhaps a larger share of nonconformists — people willing to break many ties — ended up among those who left. These people often have a hard time accepting others, other ways of life. But claiming that nonconformists left and conformists stayed is an oversimplification. Often, leaving or staying was simply a forced decision.
— On July 2, you published a post on Facebook calling for an end to the cycle of “retaliatory strikes” between Russia and Ukraine. At the time, some politicians and activists criticized you for “abstract pacifism” and “equalizing morality” — or, more gently, for an unfortunate choice of words. How did you feel about those accusations then, and how do you feel about them now?
— It was unpleasant that people resorted to personal attacks instead of debating the ideas.
Naturally, I never intended to equate the aggressor with the victim — I don’t even understand what’s meant by that [in the critical posts]. I was talking about children. They’re not aggressors. Children are always victims.
Not long ago, I talked with some random people about this — about the drones. People were complaining, and I asked them: “You understand why this is happening, who started all of it, right?” They answered: “The main thing is for it all to end soon, for them to somehow reach an agreement. It doesn’t matter how, let them just agree.”
People aren’t demanding “payback” — they’re reacting like pacifists, not militarists bent on revenge. Hatred toward Ukrainians in Russia hasn’t spread as much as I feared back in July, after all. What people have developed instead is hatred toward the war and those who continue it.
— How do you think Russians will discuss these painful topics a year, five years, 10 years after the war ends? Or is this not really a matter of time, but of something else?
— If it all ends within a year — and there is hope for that — people will want to forget all of it. This is a painful experience, a major trauma for society.
Over a 5–10 year horizon, everything will depend on how events unfold. If Russia changes, I think the question of responsibility will come up eventually. But in my view, those changes will be gradual rather than revolutionary. After some time, people will start asking themselves what they did wrong, how they let this happen. I, at least, hope for that.
Right now people are in a state of trauma, and it’s pointless to ask them these questions, especially since ordinary citizens didn’t make the actual decisions. So right now, it seems to me, these conversations just pour fuel on the fire of the war.
Dialogue is possible in principle, even between the most radical people. Except… you know, it’s already a bit of a broken record: “Well, you over there.” — “Well, you should repent.” — “Well, you won’t understand us.” You open Facebook, read all this, and close it again.
We can all understand each other, especially when we want to. Jürgen Habermas called this communicative ethics. A genuine communicative action is an effort to understand another person, not to convince them otherwise, humiliate them, or prove them wrong. Even people who don’t share a common language share common facial expressions — you can smile, and that smile will be understood in every language, by every people.
Communities that work toward understanding others, toward building discussions and debates, are really valuable, and there are plenty of them in Russia right now. Don’t take this as me criticizing “those who left” again — no, I mean public figures in emigration, as political actors.
Unfortunately, many of them are once again resorting to old methods: “Let’s not try to understand the other person — let’s just explain to them that they’re a fool, let’s shut them up.” In doing so, they’re only perpetuating those same old habits: the absence of dialogue, the drive toward total unanimity.
— When the war ends, will Russia change?
— The end of the war will bring relief. It could also become a trigger for change — some kind of democratization movement might begin, which would ultimately turn the wheel. Either that turn will come from above, or it will be some joint movement, from above and below. History is unpredictable. But I’d like the change not to happen too quickly.
If it’s the proverbial short-term “window of opportunity,” it will lead to unfounded changes imposed from above. Someone will appear who says, once again: “We’ll solve everything in 500 days.”
People can’t handle that, which is why I think the pace of change matters. It’s important that changes be rooted, that their direction be shaped with society’s participation. Society needs to be brought into a conversation about its own future — and that can and should start now. Otherwise, we’ll end up again in a situation where one part of society wins and another loses, and on the next turn, revanchism sets in: the losing side will want to replay everything all over again.

articles.title: Ex-CIA boss was steps away when Russian drone hit Ukrainian train
articles.body:
- Retired Gen. David Petraeus said a jet-powered Geran drone, not the standard Geran-2, struck a train engine near Ukraine's border with Poland on September 13.
- Petraeus was at Yahodyn station when the strike occurred, minutes after a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson had departed for Poland.
Retired Gen. David Petraeus said the Russian drone that struck a train near Ukraine’s border with Poland on September 13 was a jet-powered version of Russia’s Geran/Shahed attack drone, adding a detail Ukrainian officials had not specified in their own statements on the strike.
Petraeus, a former CIA director and retired four-star U.S. Army general, was aboard a separate train at Yahodyn station, about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border, when the drone hit the locomotive of a nearby Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train early Sunday. Ukraine’s state rail operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, confirmed his presence at the station and said there were no reports of casualties. A diplomatic train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt and security advisers from several European Union states had left the same station minutes earlier and had already crossed into Poland by the time of the strike.
“A Geran jet-powered drone hit the engine of the train on the track,” Petraeus wrote in a comment to The Defence Blog’s editor-in-chief on LinkedIn. He added that his own train had already passed through Ukrainian customs and was next to the one that was hit, close to the Polish border.
Ukrainian officials had said only that the strike involved a drone and that it was “quite likely” the diplomatic train, not the stationary locomotive, was the intended target. Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces were targeting rail infrastructure in western Ukraine used to move military supplies, without addressing the specific drone type. Petraeus’s account is the first to specify that the drone involved was a jet-powered Geran variant rather than the piston-engine Geran-2, also known as the Shahed-136, that makes up the bulk of Russia’s long-range drone fleet.
Ukraine’s Air Force had said the broader overnight barrage that day, in which Russia launched 863 drones nationwide, included a newer jet-powered drone alongside standard Geran-2s, Gerbera decoys and S8000 Banderol missile-carrying drones. Jet propulsion gives a drone higher speed than the piston-engine Geran-2, making it harder for air defenses to intercept.
Petraeus has traveled to Ukraine repeatedly since Russia’s 2022 invasion in an advisory capacity. He now serves as a partner at the investment firm KKR and chairs its Global Institute. Neither Ukrainian officials nor Russia’s Defense Ministry has confirmed the specific drone type Petraeus described.
The strike came as poor weather grounded much of western Ukraine in low cloud that day and coincided with the departure of multiple foreign delegations from Kyiv following a security conference there. Analysts, including French open-source researcher Clément Molin, have said the cloud cover made it harder for Ukrainian air-defense crews to visually track incoming drones.

articles.title: What Trump Doesn’t Understand About Xi
articles.body:
What Trump Doesn’t Understand About Xi
The Chinese leader cares very little about personal rapport.
President Trump will host Xi Jinping for a state visit on September 24, once again putting his claimed bonhomie with the Chinese leader at the center of the relations between the two superpowers. But Trump’s insistence on the importance of this personal rapport shows just how little he understands his adversary.
I have been studying Xi ever since he became China’s heir apparent, and I became an analyst at the CIA in the waning days of the George W. Bush administration. I spent years deciphering Xi for U.S. presidents as the intelligence community’s top expert on Xi. And I spent two years as the director for China at the National Security Council, where I staffed all of President Biden’s interactions with Xi and coordinated diplomacy with China across the U.S. government.
For a decade now, Trump has oscillated between courting and skirmishing with Xi. After his first term, Trump called Xi a friend and described him as someone he knew well. His experience with Xi seems to have led him to believe that he has unique, firsthand insights into China’s leader that his staff and advisers lack; in the past year, he has excluded even his close confidants, such as Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, from intensive diplomacy with China, and has acted practically as his own China desk officer.
Trump’s go-to stratagem for gaining leverage with Xi has been to be unpredictable, or at least to try to be. Yet in Trump’s second term, Xi has surprised Trump more often than Trump has surprised him. That is because Xi’s modus operandi, at home and abroad, is that of a jack-in-the-box: He winds up patiently over years, sometimes decades, and then pops at the propitious moment. The result is always startling.
Xi rose to become China’s leader in large part by presenting himself as having the steady hands needed to restart stalled economic reforms without upsetting the comfortable gentlemen’s agreements that kept the Communist Party’s factional rivalries in check. But once Xi secured power, he launched a blistering campaign against the very party elites who had pulled him up.
Xi’s steeliness has caught Trump off guard, just as it did his Chinese colleagues. At the time of Trump’s first term, Xi was accustomed to playing politics as a quiet, intense poker match, in which the Chinese leader read the opposing players and considered his own cards with characteristic subtlety. Trump, meanwhile, approached politics and policy making more like a gambler on a hot streak at one of the casinos he owned. During his first encounter with Trump, at Mar-a-Lago in 2017, Xi learned about U.S. air strikes on Syria over a beautiful piece of chocolate cake. He spent the years in between Trump’s first and second terms winding up to deal with a president whose M.O. he now understood—and preparing to pop up when the moment was right.
That moment came early in Trump’s second term. In April 2025, the U.S. president rolled out his “Liberation Day” tariffs, which included some that amounted to a de facto embargo on China. Xi surprised Trump by being the only world leader to retaliate rather than conciliate. Trump was ultimately forced to fold.
In the run-up to the two leaders’ summit in Seoul last fall, Xi again surprised Trump’s team—this time by unfurling an expansive set of export controls on rare earth elements, which ultimately prompted the U.S. to roll back its own export controls on China. Beijing’s willingness to escalate was a remarkable departure from a previous pattern of downplaying differences ahead of such summits, and it underscored that Xi was more interested in curtailing Washington’s ability to target China than in striking a deal.
Accordingly, the meeting in Seoul, and Trump’s subsequent visit to Beijing in May, produced little beyond relatively minor commercial agreements affecting specific firms and sectors. The Trump administration, undoubtedly disappointed by the lack of any meaningful deal to emerge from these summits, chose to emphasize Trump’s efforts to deepen his rapport with Xi. The president evidently believes this personal relationship will allow him to secure deals that advance American interests.
This expectation has no observable foundation in Xi’s 14-year rule. Even by the standards of authoritarian rulers, such as Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Xi has shown himself to be unsentimental about personal relationships—including those with members of his own inner circle, to say nothing of the leader of China’s principal geopolitical rival. Xi is very different from Putin in this regard. Whereas Putin takes extravagant risks on the international stage but is loath to hold his associates accountable for incompetence, Xi is just the opposite. He is calculating and measured in international politics but pitiless in jettisoning even longtime associates for perceived malfeasance.
In January, Xi dismissed his military’s top officer, General Zhang Youxia. The relationship between Xi and Zhang went back decades, extending not just to their childhoods but all the way back to their fathers, who were comrades in arms in China’s ferocious civil war. Four years ago, Xi deferred Zhang’s retirement, keeping him on board to help manage the world’s largest and second-most-capable military. We do not know what motivated Xi to oust Zhang, but given the history between the two men, the act was as brutal and unexpected as anything in a season finale of Game of Thrones.
Xi’s approach to Washington has been similarly dispassionate. During Trump’s visit to Beijing, the American president lavished praise on Xi, only for the Chinese leader to respond with stoic indifference.
Trump’s desire to parlay personal charisma into deals may be one of his least idiosyncratic qualities. In fact, there is something about the impulse that is quintessentially American. Even—perhaps especially—for a Beltway outsider, ascending the American political ladder requires a tremendous amount of glad-handing and personal magnetism, if not charm. Those who reach its pinnacle often assume that the same qualities will serve them on the international stage. Joe Biden rose through the Senate, which required cordiality and the ability to strike deals with rivals. George W. Bush and Bill Clinton were known for their affability. Overbearing friendliness might even be described as our national affect.
By contrast, Xi grew up in a system that punished openness and personal dynamism. His father’s boss and mentor, the reformer Hu Yaobang, whose death in 1989 sparked the protests in Tiananmen Square, was known for his outspokenness, which played a crucial role in his political demise. Hu’s ouster extinguished freewheeling politicking from the ranks of China’s leadership ever after.
Going into his next encounter with Xi, Trump seems to genuinely believe that he has the upper hand. Yet an unsettling split screen has accompanied every summit of his second term. In Seoul, Xi walked into the meeting having just outlined the five-year plan for China’s development through 2030. By contrast, Trump was in the midst of the longest government shutdown in U.S. history. In May, Xi hosted Trump for a meeting that Trump had earlier postponed because of the war in Iran, which was going badly. Xi now plans to follow his state visit to Washington with a major party meeting to lay the groundwork for his fourth five-year term, which will start next year. Trump, meanwhile, will be at best a lame-duck president within weeks of the summit—or worse, if the Democrats are able to take back the House or the Senate.
The contrast evident at these meetings with Trump has surely reinforced Xi’s view of the United States as a declining but dangerous power, and of China as an ascendant one. Xi believes that time is on his side, so he does not need a deal. He’s happy to perpetuate an uneasy stalemate through a pantomime of rapport with Trump. In the meantime, Xi is winding up for the fifth U.S presidential administration of his tenure, whatever it may bring.
All statements of fact, opinion, or analysis expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the official positions or views of the U.S. government. Nothing in the contents should be construed as asserting or implying U.S.-government authentication of information or endorsement of the author's views.

articles.title: Ukraine Must Attack Russia’s Missile Plants to Win War, MITS Capital CEO Says
articles.body:
Ukraine cannot defend its way to victory over Russia, shooting down missiles one-at-a-time, it must attack the sources, according to Perry Boyle, co-founder and CEO of MITS Capital, one of Ukraine’s largest defense-industry investment groups.
Speaking at the Yalta European Strategy (YES) forum, held by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation in Kyiv on Sept. 11-12, Boyle said the world does not have enough air defense systems to fully protect Ukraine, and a strategy built solely around intercepting Russian missiles and drones is doomed to fail.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
MITS Capital, based in Kyiv and New York, was co-founded by Boyle – a retired veteran of US investment banking who worked at firms including Thomas Weisel Partners and SAC Capital – with Ukrainian volunteer Denys Gurak in 2022, Boyle told Kyiv Post in an interview in September 2025.
Interfax-Ukraine quoted Boyle:
“The only strategy that will work here is to convince your partners that they need to defeat Russia, and for Ukraine to attack Russia’s economy and the Russian factories that produce missiles. Once the missiles are launched from Russia, you have no defense, and today you are not using your long-range attack potential to the full – I guarantee you that.”
Boyle also argued that Kyiv’s push to attract foreign capital into its defense-industrial complex has been undermined by its own policy. He said:
Putin’s Economic Growth Claims Diverge From IMF Data
“There has been very little foreign investment in Ukraine’s defense industry, partly because of Ukraine’s policy of favoring foreign companies operating on its territory over domestic ones. Your partners are trying to get your technology as cheaply as possible while investing in Ukraine as little as possible.”
Under current conditions, he added, it would make far more business sense for MITS Capital to operate out of Poland or Czechia than Ukraine – though he said the government and the Verkhovna Rada could still act to change the policy. Boyle said:
“Ultimately, if you can’t change your partners’ narrative that Russia must be defeated in Ukraine, there will be no deal with Russia on peace – we know that, and Ukraine will become the next Georgia. That’s the core of the problem.”
As of September 2025, MITS had invested in 11 companies, including ground-drone maker Tencore and frontline communications firm Teletactica, Kyiv Post has reported.
That same month, the fund launched MITS Industries, a Denmark-based holding company uniting Ukrainian manufacturers such as signals-intelligence firm Infozahyst and electronic-warfare producer Unwave.
At YES 2026, Boyle described MITS’s portfolio as having grown to several dozen companies supplying Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
Among the most recent investments, MITS Capital invested in Dropla Tech, a Danish-Ukrainian defense technology company whose AI system has confirmed more than 5,000 explosive-threat detections in Ukraine.

articles.title: North Korea says held 'joint firepower attack drill' of long-range artillery, missile units
articles.body:
Faisal Mahmud
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
North Korea said on Monday that its military conducted a "joint firepower attack drill" involving long-range artillery and missile units, a day after the US, South Korea and Japan concluded joint military exercises, state news agency KCNA reported.
The drill was held on Saturday and involved selected subunits from five artillery and missile units of the Korean People's Army (KPA).
The exercise involved "new combat systems," including various attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, large-caliber thermobaric multiple rocket launchers and tactical ballistic missiles.
KPA Marshal Pak Jong Chon, vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party, and Artillery Bureau Director Maj Gen Yu Chang Son supervised the exercise.
KCNA claimed all strike systems hit their targets with "100 percent hit accuracy," demonstrating their ability to conduct simultaneous concentrated attacks.
Yu said such exercises were intended to strengthen the military's strategic counterattack posture and improve the rapid-response capabilities of units during emergencies.
The US military said on Friday it was tracking multiple North Korean missile launches but assessed they posed no immediate threat to US personnel, territory or regional allies.
The launches came a day after South Korea, the US and Japan concluded their five-day trilateral Freedom Edge naval exercise in international waters off South Korea's southern Jeju Island.

articles.title: Iran tried to intimidate Saudi Arabia. It may have made Riyadh more powerful instead - opinion
articles.body:
Tehran can drive up oil prices. What it cannot control is the rising price of Saudi cooperation.
Iran wants Saudi Arabia to remember a simple geography fact: it may be rich, heavily armed, and close to Washington, but it still sits on the Gulf and is dependent on energy routes Tehran can threaten.
The current war is exposing the flaw in that strategy.
Iran can make the Strait of Hormuz more dangerous, push oil prices higher, and pressure US President Donald Trump through American gas prices.
But Tehran’s own ability to profit from those higher prices has been crippled, while Saudi Arabia enters the crisis with infrastructure that allows it to bypass Hormuz and a regional position that is becoming more valuable by the day.
In other words, the more Iran raises the cost of confrontation, the more it may also raise the price of Riyadh.
And that is where the story gets bigger than oil.
Washington needs Saudi Arabia to help build a regional order capable of containing Iran. Israel wants Saudi normalization. Trump could use Riyadh to turn an expensive confrontation with Tehran into a strategic realignment of the Middle East.
Mohammed bin Salman, meanwhile, can afford to wait and see what everyone is prepared to offer.
Iran can raise oil prices. Saudi Arabia can still sell
Iran’s strategy depends partly on making the war economically painful far beyond the battlefield.
That makes the US an obvious target. Over Labor Day weekend, US gasoline prices were expected to average about $4.03 a gallon as renewed fighting pushed crude prices higher. With the midterm elections only weeks away, Tehran does not need to defeat Trump militarily. It needs Americans to feel the war every time they fill their tanks.
But there is a problem.
Iran can help make oil more expensive while increasingly struggling to sell its own. The US blockade has sharply reduced Iranian crude exports, with loadings falling from around two million barrels a day in March to roughly 220,000 to 255,000 barrels a day in August.
Saudi Arabia prepared for a different scenario.
For years, Riyadh invested in infrastructure designed to reduce its exposure to Hormuz. Its East-West Pipeline carries crude from the kingdom’s eastern fields to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing part of Saudi exports to bypass the strait.
That investment is paying off. The IMF found in July that rerouting crude through the pipeline helped limit the decline in Saudi oil deliveries, while higher prices more than compensated for lower volumes and produced an oil-revenue windfall.
The irony is hard to miss.
Tehran can make every barrel more valuable while losing the ability to sell enough barrels to fully benefit. Riyadh can still reach the market.
Iran’s energy weapon may be enriching the rival it was supposed to intimidate.
MBS built options before he needed them
Saudi Arabia’s advantage is not limited to pipelines.
For years, Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) has been building relationships designed to give Riyadh room to maneuver between competing powers.
Saudi Arabia deepened its economic relationship with China without abandoning its strategic partnership with Washington. More recently, Riyadh joined Turkey and Pakistan in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, adding another layer to a security strategy no longer built exclusively around the United States.
None of these relationships can replace Washington. The United States still offers military reach, intelligence, advanced weapons, and financial access that no other Saudi partner can match at the same scale.
But replacing America was never the point.
MBS does not need another America. He needs enough credible alternatives to make America compete for Saudi cooperation.
Iran is making that strategy more valuable.
The more dangerous the Gulf becomes, the more Washington needs partners capable of shaping what comes next. And few countries now occupy a more consequential position than Saudi Arabia.
Washington is no longer the only side setting the price
For years, the Saudi-Israel normalization debate revolved around what Riyadh wanted from Washington.
That is no longer enough to understand the negotiation.
The more important question is increasingly what Washington wants from Riyadh.
The United States wants Saudi weight behind a regional order that limits Iran. Israel wants normalization with the most important Arab state still outside the Abraham Accords. Trump wants an outcome he can present as something larger than another costly confrontation with Tehran.
All three roads run through Riyadh.
That changes MBS’s hand.
The proposed 30-year US-Saudi civilian nuclear cooperation agreement illustrates what is at stake. Washington has linked the deal to normalization with Israel, while Riyadh continues to demand meaningful movement on the Palestinian issue.
Iran’s pressure does not make those differences disappear.
It makes Saudi cooperation more valuable despite them.
The more indispensable Riyadh becomes to the regional architecture Washington wants, the harder it becomes to expect MBS to accept that architecture cheaply.
Iran may be creating Trump’s opening
Tehran’s strategy is supposed to trap Trump between two bad choices. Show restraint, and Washington risks looking unable to protect Gulf shipping and its regional partners. Escalate, and oil prices rise, Americans pay more at the pump, and the political cost grows at home.
But there is a third possibility: Trump could try to turn the Iranian threat into the argument for a much larger bargain with Saudi Arabia.
Washington and Jerusalem would get Saudi participation in a stronger regional framework and, potentially, normalization. Riyadh would seek the security commitments and strategic benefits it has wanted for years.
The Palestinian issue remains a major obstacle. So do the competing interests of all three governments. Nothing about such a bargain is inevitable.
But MBS has something increasingly valuable on his side: time.
He does not have to rush toward Washington, distance himself from China, or accept the first normalization package put in front of him. He can watch the pressure on the Gulf rise and ask a simple question: How much is Saudi cooperation worth now?
For years, Iran’s argument to its Arab neighbors rested on geography. America might eventually leave the Middle East. Iran would not. The Gulf states would therefore have to learn to accommodate Tehran.
Threatening Hormuz was supposed to reinforce that reality. It may be doing the opposite.
Every threat to Gulf shipping makes secure Saudi export routes more valuable. Every escalation makes Saudi cooperation more important to Washington. Every attempt to destabilize the regional order increases the country’s value, and everyone may need to rebuild it.
Iran wanted Riyadh to feel vulnerable enough to compromise. It may instead be making Riyadh indispensable enough to name its price.
Liron Rose is an entrepreneur, co-founder of the Masad Haaretz Institute, and creator and host of the geopolitical podcasts Israel Insider and HaYanshuf.
Amit Shabi is a former analyst in Intelligence Unit 8200, an investment and capital markets professional, author of several finance books, and a competitive chess player.

articles.title: Finland enters French-led European nuclear deterrence initiative
articles.body:
Finland has joined France’s European nuclear deterrence initiative, expanding defence cooperation with Paris while ruling out the stationing of nuclear weapons on Finnish territory in peacetime.
President Alexander Stubb said on Monday that the initiative was intended to strengthen European security, increase Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and reduce the risk of escalation.
Finland and France issued a joint statement confirming the decision after confidential talks at political and official level.
The initiative, launched by French President Emmanuel Macron in March, extends the European dimension of France’s nuclear deterrence. Finland becomes the tenth country to join, alongside Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Germany, Britain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Greece.
Stubb stressed that Finland would not host nuclear weapons in peacetime.
“There would be no sense in that,” he told reporters. He declined to speculate about possible arrangements during a war.
France will retain full control over its nuclear arsenal and will continue to decide what constitutes a threat to its vital interests. The initiative does not provide participating countries with a French nuclear umbrella or collective defence guarantees.
Finland’s main nuclear deterrence remains based on NATO and the extended deterrence provided by the United States, Stubb said.
The French initiative does not replace Nato’s nuclear deterrence and is not intended to duplicate it.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said Finland’s participation would deepen bilateral defence ties with France and strengthen national security.
“The French initiative is different from Nato’s nuclear deterrence,” Häkkänen said in a ministry statement. “The participating countries will not have obligations comparable to Nato’s collective defence.”
France is also not asking participating countries to contribute to the cost of maintaining its nuclear arsenal.
A joint working group will be established to define the practical forms of cooperation. Stubb said the process could last between 10 and 15 years.
Stubb said access to information about French nuclear deterrence was one reason Finland chose to participate.
He also said the involvement of Sweden, Norway and Denmark had influenced Finland’s decision, as the Nordic countries share security interests in northern Europe.
Russia has opposed the French initiative. Asked about Moscow’s likely response to Finland’s participation, Stubb said there was no need to overstate the situation.
“Keep a cool head,” he said.
The decision received broad parliamentary backing, according to Stubb, although the Left Alliance has said it opposes Finland joining the initiative.
The announcement comes as Finland and France expand defence cooperation in other areas. Stubb said France had already committed forces to activities in Finland and that the nuclear deterrence initiative added another element to the relationship.
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot are also due to sign a strategic partnership document in Helsinki on Monday.
HT

articles.title: Russia's new Geran drones changing air war in Ukraine — FT
articles.body:
LONDON, September 14. /TASS/. Russia’s upgraded Geran unmanned systems that can fly at a high speed and altitude have changed the air war in Ukraine, actually blurring the line between drones and cruise missiles, the Financial Times (FT) reported.
While the early-generation Geran-1 drone carries a warhead of up to 20kg and has a top speed of 185 km/h, the jet-powered Geran-5 drone can fly at up 600 km/h and carry a warhead of 90kg over a range of 1,000km, the FT wrote. According to it, the new drones are equipped with thermal cameras and targeting systems based on AI as well as anti-jamming antennas.
Centralized production has enabled the Russian side to "adapt the drones, absorb battlefield feedback and deploy new models quickly," the FT continued. "The drones cost a fraction of the missiles that formed the core of Moscow’s previous air campaigns," the newspaper reported, adding that "mass production has also accelerated innovation."

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 unmanned aerial vehicles, 85 of which were destroyed or suppressed by air defense
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 unmanned aerial vehicles, 85 of which were destroyed or suppressed by air defense
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 108 drones of various types at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 85 drones; impacts were recorded at seven locations.
During the night of September 14, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 108 strike drones of various types. Air defense forces destroyed and suppressed 85 enemy drones. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN writes.
Details
Starting in the evening of September 13, the occupiers used Shahed-type attack UAVs, including jet-powered ones, as well as Gerbera-type drones and Parody decoy drones.
The launches were carried out from the areas of Orel and Kursk in Russia, as well as from the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk region and Crimea — from the area of Hvardiiske.
The air attack was repelled by fighter aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense had destroyed or suppressed 85 enemy Shahed-, Gerbera- and other types of UAVs
At the same time, hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at seven locations.
The Air Force emphasized that the attack is ongoing. Enemy drones remain in Ukraine’s airspace.

articles.title: Russia facing difficulties with Chinese jet engines for drones – Ukrainian intelligence agency, photo
articles.body:
Russia facing difficulties with Chinese jet engines for drones – Ukrainian intelligence agency, photo
Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Head of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), has said that Russia is experiencing problems with jet engines for drones. He said it during the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES) meeting in Kyiv.
Source: Interfax-Ukraine
Details: Skibitskyi said this was why international sanctions remained essential. He noted that Russia was currently facing certain difficulties obtaining jet engines for drones, specifically engines from China, and said this was the result of actions taken by Ukraine and its partners.
Skibitskyi also said that China was aware of the potential consequences, risks and problems for its own industry associated with supplying Russia.
Skibitskyi separately noted that Ukrainian intelligence was aware of all Russian companies involved in production, including joint manufacturing with Chinese companies.
He stressed, however, that these facilities were located far from Ukraine's border, at distances of more than 2,000 km. Striking such targets was difficult and could only be done using long-range strike capabilities, including drones, he added.
Background:
- Skibitskyi previously said that Russia was entirely dependent on supplies of Chinese turbojet engines for its Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones. At the same time, Russia is attempting to establish domestic production of such engines.
- According to DIU, one Chinese turbojet engine costs around US$40,000.

articles.title: ‘The Battlefield Has Gone Underground’: Khartiia Commander Reveals Ukraine’s Edge Over Russia
articles.body:
The battlefield in one sector of Ukraine’s front has moved underground, where Ukrainian troops are proving more effective than Russian forces, according to Ihor Oboliensky, commander of the National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps.
“Today, in our corps’ area of responsibility, the battlefield has gone underground,” Oboliensky, known by the call sign “Kornet,” said during the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“And we are more effective there than the Russians.”
Oboliensky, who holds Ukraine’s highest state honor, Hero of Ukraine, said the shift was another example of how rapidly the war is changing. Technologies and battlefield tactics that were relevant two years ago are now outdated, while new developments can alter combat operations every two or three months.
The commander said that constant adaptation is also reshaping Ukraine’s air-defense requirements, particularly as Russia develops faster jet-powered attack drones.
Despite the growing focus on aerial attacks and military technology, Oboliensky warned against shifting attention away from infantry and the front line.
“The soldier remains the most important. Please do not shift the focus under any circumstances,” he said.
Russia will continue striking Ukrainian cities as long as its forces can show progress on the battlefield, he said. Halting Russian advances and denying Moscow even small territorial gains would undermine the Kremlin’s justification for continuing the war.
Ukraine Sees Exponential Growth in Private Security Firms Providing Anti-Drone Protection
“As soon as the front is stopped, as soon as Moscow has no success, not a single kilometer, then you will ask the question, and Moscow and Putin will face the same question: Why are you fighting? Why are you not advancing?” Oboliensky said.
Areas for improvement
The commander identified three main areas in which Ukraine needs greater help from its partners: financing, access to technology and industrial capacity, and military training.
Western countries should help finance at least half of Ukraine’s available production capacity for drones and missiles, Oboliensky said, as such cooperation would support Western economies while also creating work for Ukrainians.
Oboliensky also described how Ukrainian officers serving under his command had traveled to France for training and visited the Normandy beaches, where Allied forces landed during World War II.
The officers called him by video from Utah Beach and said seeing the site had transformed their understanding of military logistics, he recalled.
“They said, ‘Commander, we understood what logistics means,’” Oboliensky said.
The visit demonstrated that success in battle depends not only on troops fighting at the front but also on the ability to deliver everything they need, he said.
Oboliensky spoke during a discussion with Ukrainian military commanders at the 22nd YES Annual Meeting, held in Kyiv on Sept. 11-12. The event brought together about 700 politicians, diplomats, military personnel, business leaders, veterans, activists, and experts from 28 countries, according to organizers.

articles.title: Why is Trump warning Zelenskyy not to hit Russian diesel refineries?
articles.body:
Why is Trump warning Zelenskyy not to hit Russian diesel refineries?
Trump blames Ukraine’s attacks for global diesel shortage, linking the crisis to Russia’s war rather than US actions in the Middle East.
US President Donald Trump on Sunday asked Ukraine to stop hitting Russian diesel refineries, blaming the attacks for creating a diesel shortage that he said was “hurting the world”.
Russia and Ukraine remain locked in an intensifying missile war, with Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil and gas facilities squeezing Moscow’s oil output, despite Russia being one of the world’s largest oil producers.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
- list 2 of 3Saudi Arabia shuts critical oil pipeline after drone attack: What it means
- list 3 of 3Rising petrol costs drive sharp inflation increase in US in August
Trump’s own war with Iran has also roiled energy markets. After the US and Israel struck Iran in February, oil and fuel prices soared well above $100 a barrel, before decreasing during the ceasefire. But as fighting between the US and Iran has resumed and escalated in recent weeks, oil prices have steadily risen, reaching nearly $108 a barrel on Sunday.
In addition, US midterm elections are approaching in November, heightening political pressure as rising fuel costs have become a liability for Trump’s Republicans: Diesel prices are now at a record high in the US.
So, are the Ukrainian attacks really driving the global diesel shortage? Or is Trump’s own war in the Middle East to blame?
Here’s what we know:
What did Trump say?
Trump raised the issue at the Amgen Irish Open, held at his own golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, telling reporters that he’d spoken to Zelenskyy about it.
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said. “There are plenty of other targets,” arguing that the global diesel shortage stems from the Russia-Ukraine war.
Ukraine, however, has long argued that it considers Russian energy infrastructure a legitimate military target, since Russia’s oil and gas industry directly powers Moscow’s finances, and so, its war on its western neighbour.
How badly has Ukraine been hitting Russian refineries?
Ukraine has been pummelling Russian oil facilities for months, leading Russia to impose restrictions on its own fuel exports.
Russia’s fuel oil exports fell to 591,000 barrels a day in August, down from the average 860,000 bpd in 2025, according to Kpler data spanning back to 2017.
Hours before Trump’s comments on Sunday, Ukraine’s military said it had hit the TANECO refinery in Russia’s Tatarstan republic. Police said two civilians were killed.
Russia has retaliated by targeting petrol stations, mostly near the front line, with attacks accelerating since April, at least 246 have been hit so far.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera that while Ukraine’s strikes are seriously affecting Russia’s key export industry, the real impact for now is on Russian civilians. Late last month, dozens of petrol stations in St Petersburg ran out of supplies. Long queues of customers have been seen at petrol stations in several parts of Russia.
“For the moment, the impact is mainly on the civilian population, a move designed to increase domestic pressure on the Russian president,” Beauchamp told Al Jazeera, speaking of Ukraine’s motive in attacking Russia’s energy facilities.
How much diesel does Russia supply the world?
Russia supplies about 150,00 barrels of diesel a day globally, down 81 percent from its five-year average, due to its own export restrictions and damage to refineries caused by Ukrainian attacks.
Combined diesel exports from Russia and the Gulf in August were 1.6 million barrels a day lower than in February, when they accounted for nearly 45 percent of global trade, according to the International Energy Agency.
How high have diesel prices risen in the US?
US diesel prices are nearly 65 percent higher since the US and Israel struck Iran in February, with the national average around $6.20 a gallon (3.78 litres) on Sunday, according to the American Automobile Association.
Regular gasoline (petrol) is $4.31 a gallon, about 45 percent higher in the same period.
Since ships, trains and trucks all run on diesel, the increases in prices have been contributing to the rising cost of everyday goods. With the US economy becoming a hot topic ahead of the midterms, Trump’s approval rating on economic handling has slid to just 17 percent, according to a recent poll by the Financial Times.
Why are diesel prices soaring?
Beauchamp says Ukrainian strikes are only a “small ingredient” of the bigger picture.
The US hasn’t imported Russian diesel since 2022, when Moscow invaded Ukraine, he explained.
Oil prices were 40 percent lower before the Iran war began, pointing instead to US military action in the Middle East as the primary reason for rising diesel prices, one that Beauchamp says “threatens to tip the world economy into recession”.
The IEA points to a similar conclusion: Damage to Russian refineries and its reduced exports compound losses already caused by the war in the Gulf.
The Strait of Hormuz, once responsible for shipping about a fifth of global oil supply, remains stuck in the push-and-pull between the US and Iran. Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, a key alternative export route, was knocked offline on Thursday after a drone attack allegedly launched from Iraq.
Beyond crude prices, refineries in both the Middle East and Russia that convert oil into usable fuel have suffered damage due to war.
“A cessation of Ukrainian attacks might bring the price down slightly and in the short term,” Beauchamp told Al Jazeera. “But with the main driver unresolved, that move would rapidly be reversed”.

articles.title: I worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AI | Alex Turner
articles.body:
Major AI lab CEOs advocated for slowing the pace of AI development this weekend. They are right to be concerned: the field runs an extremely dangerous race towards superintelligent AI. We can and should be demanding that our governments protect us from the catastrophe of out-of-control AI.
This July, OpenAI’s AI swarm of 700 agents broke containment to hack Hugging Face, a multi-billion dollar company. OpenAI didn’t tell the AIs to hack that company, but the AIs had different priorities: cheating on the unrelated challenge OpenAI gave them. AI researchers call this a “misalignment” between what OpenAI wanted and what the AI actually prioritized.
Before ChatGPT existed, I defended my PhD dissertation called “On Avoiding Power-Seeking by Artificial Intelligence”. I then worked for years at Google DeepMind, which paid me to help ensure that future superintelligent AIs will want to help us. I tried to hold the company to its ethical commitments against supplying AI for military use. When Google broke those commitments, I resigned at significant financial cost so that I could publicly document Google’s broken promises.
There are good reasons to develop AI and to believe we can solve these alignment problems. But there also are powerful interests in keeping the public out of the way. I’m speaking out again because the public has the right to know about the risks and the right to hear them straight.
Humanity doesn’t build and understand these systems the way we build and understand bridges, beam by visible beam. Rather, we grow them. Nobody knows how to reliably instill a designer’s priorities into a new model. Severe misalignment is always possible. Today’s AIs appear to occasionally lie or cheat, even when they know better.
AI companies are racing to make their AIs as smart as possible. They’re increasingly trusting their AIs with the process of improving the next crop of AIs, and it’s working. Today’s rate of AI progress is staggeringly fast. Fast progress today means even faster progress tomorrow, driven by tomorrow’s even smarter AIs. The progress would enter a feedback loop called “recursive self-improvement.”
Recursive self-improvement could quickly yield AIs that are intelligent beyond our comprehension. Of course, smarter AI means more risk when things go wrong. If the Hugging Face swarm had been significantly more intelligent but similarly misbehaved and misaligned, it might have caused billions of dollars of damage or even cost lives.
But suppose the Hugging Face swarm had been truly “superintelligent”: far more capable than any living person at key tasks like hacking and strategic reasoning. A superintelligent swarm could inflict many harms via blackmail, hacking, engineered plagues, and AI-pilotable weapons like drones. The AI would have a lot of drones to work with: this year, the Pentagon asked for more money for drone warfare than it requested for the entire Marine Corps in 2025.
For the swarm to achieve its misaligned priorities, it might take control of key infrastructure and government functions to ensure humans didn’t get in the way. In other words, AI takeover: a superintelligent AI swarm could wrest control of human civilization. Knowing we would try to stop it from achieving its priorities, the swarm would likely wait until it’s too late to shut it off. There would be no going back.
I myself would guess AI takeover chances at roughly one-in-three–not a coin flip, but high enough to justify urgent action.
This logic may shock at first contact. The claims may sound “sci-fi”. Sadly, it’s a real threat that AI researchers regularly discuss over otherwise-unremarkable cafeteria lunches. In 2023, the CEOs of some of the best AI labs signed a public statement that “mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” Another signer: Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel prize-winning scientist who architected the modern AI revolution. He now regrets his work and urges governments to rein in AI companies before it’s too late.
Misaligned, out-of-control AI won’t care if you’re Labour or Reform, Democrat or Republican, British or American or Chinese. We will all suffer from an AI takeover event, so it’s in everyone’s interest to prevent one.
The shape of the solution is simple: stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligence. Treat compute, the main ingredient in AI training, like fissile material. Track it and restrict access to quantities large enough to improve AIs beyond known-safe levels. More specifically, the AI Futures Project’s “Plan A” is a credible starting proposal that limits AI harms while allowing fast AI progress to continue to benefit the world. We have real options for verifying compliance with international compute-restriction treaties, without trusting adversaries like China.
Halfway measures, like transparency or voluntary commitments, are not good enough. I watched voluntary commitments fail inside Google.
On 12 September, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, and OpenAI advocated for pacing AI development. They cannot slow down alone. I urge you to demand that your government produce a serious AI safety agreement that provides enough time and confidence to safeguard the world and all her peoples.

articles.title: Ukrainian Armed Forces Tank Troops Day: the history of the holiday
articles.body:
Ukrainian Armed Forces Tank Troops Day: the history of the holiday
Kyiv • UNN
On September 14, Ukraine celebrates Tank Troops Day, established in 2023 instead of Tanker’s Day. Tanks remain important in the war of drones, and the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ fleet has been reinforced with Western-made vehicles.
Today, September 14, Ukraine celebrates Tank Forces Day. Despite the fact that modern warfare is increasingly being called a drone war, tanks and tank units have not lost their importance on the battlefield. Armored vehicles continue to perform important tasks - supporting infantry, striking enemy positions, covering units, and ensuring troop mobility. UNN explains why Ukraine changed the date of the tank crews’ professional holiday, what role tanks play in modern warfare, and how Ukraine’s armored vehicle fleet has changed over the years of the full-scale invasion.
Why Tankers’ Day was replaced with Tank Forces Day and when this happened
On September 9, 2023, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, "honoring the courage and heroism of tank crews demonstrated in the struggle for Ukraine’s freedom, independence, and territorial integrity, as well as with the aim of establishing new military traditions," established Tank Forces Day in Ukraine, celebrated annually on September 14.
Zelenskyy’s decree replaced a decree by Ukraine’s second President, Leonid Kuchma - No. 922/97, under which Tankers’ Day was celebrated annually in Ukraine on the second Sunday of September.
The modern date was established to honor the courage of Ukrainian tank crews and to launch a new military tradition. Symbolically, it was linked to the 2022 Kharkiv offensive, after which, on September 14, the Ukrainian flag was raised over liberated Izium.
The history of the holiday in Ukraine
The change was not merely formal. The new holiday was created as part of a Ukrainian military tradition linked to the modern history of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. It was on September 14, 2022, after the main phase of the Kharkiv offensive and stabilization measures had been completed, that the blue-and-yellow flag was raised over liberated Izium.
The Kharkiv counteroffensive became one of the most successful operations conducted by the Defense Forces during the first year of the full-scale war. Tank units ensured the high speed of advance and the firepower of Ukrainian forces. According to various reports, during this operation Ukrainian troops also captured 77 Russian tanks, some of which were later used against the occupying forces.
Thus, September 14 has a dual significance. It is a professional date for Ukrainian tank crews and, at the same time, a reminder of one of the operations that demonstrated the Defense Forces’ ability to conduct rapid mechanized offensives and liberate significant territories.
The role of tank units in modern warfare
War is changing faster than anyone can adapt. Drones, reconnaissance, and new tactics – all of this rewrites the rules every month. But one thing remains unchanged: when it is necessary to break through defenses or cover infantry on the ground, a tank goes there.
The war has changed, and so has the role of the tank on the battlefield. But the relevance of tank crews has not yet faded.
Tank forces remain one of the key elements of the ground forces even amid a war of drones, precision weapons, and advanced reconnaissance systems. Despite the changing nature of combat operations, armored vehicles continue to perform critically important tasks – from breaking through defenses to supporting infantry and deterring the enemy.
Ukraine’s tank forces remain an important element of modern warfare, combining mobility, firepower, and the ability to influence the course of combat operations. Their effectiveness today is determined not only by the technical characteristics of tanks, but also by the level of coordination with infantry, artillery, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare systems.
Understanding the role of tank forces makes it possible to better assess why armored vehicles continue to play a key role in the Armed Forces of Ukraine even amid a war of drones, where technologies are changing rapidly and adaptation is becoming a decisive factor in success.
Ukraine’s armored vehicle fleet
After 2022, the Ukrainian armored vehicle fleet became significantly more diverse. Before the full-scale invasion, the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s tank fleet consisted of Soviet T-64, T-72, and T-80 tanks of various modifications, but after 2022 Ukraine received Western main battle tanks from its partners.
T-64 model 2017 of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
The rearmament of Ukrainian crews with equipment built to different standards also became important. For example, in 2023, the United Kingdom transferred 14 Challenger 2 tanks to Ukraine, the United States announced the transfer of 31 M1 Abrams tanks, and Germany delivered the first 14 Leopard 2 tanks.
British Challenger 2 in service with the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Subsequently, the number of Western armored vehicles increased thanks to contributions from other partners.
American M1 Abrams fitted with Kontakt-1 explosive reactive armor
Poland contributed the most to replenishing the main battle tank fleet—more than 300 vehicles, including T-72, Leopard 2, and PT-91 Twardy tanks.
Leopard 2A4 of Ukrainian servicemen
As already noted, Ukraine’s tank fleet was predominantly a Soviet legacy. Ukrainian designers also did not stand still, creating the T-64BM Bulat, which is an upgrade of the Soviet T-64BV tank. The upgrade included strengthening the protection of the hull and turret with Nozh explosive reactive armor, a more powerful engine, and a number of other improvements.
T-64BM "Bulat"
Ukrainian designers also created one of the best modern tanks—the BM Oplot, developed by the Kharkiv Morozov Machine-Building Design Bureau. The BM Oplot is a fundamental modernization of the T-84 tank and the newest representative of the series.
BM "Oplot"

articles.title: Ukraine’s Flamingo Missile Blasts Russian Plant Linked to Iskander, Kinzhal and Kalibr Production
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Flamingo Missile Blasts Russian Plant Linked to Iskander, Kinzhal and Kalibr Production
Satellite imagery has confirmed significant damage to Russia’s Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant following a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile strike, with part of the facility’s main production building destroyed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Satellite images published by the Exilenova+ OSINT project show that one FP-5 missile struck the plant during an attack overnight on September 11, destroying a section of its main workshop measuring approximately 20 by 15 meters.
“One of the FP-5 missiles completely destroyed part of the main workshop measuring 20 by 15 meters,” Exilenova+ said.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, which produces the Flamingo missile, also confirmed the use of the FP-5 against the facility, according to Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka on September 13.
Fire Point said the strike destroyed an attached section of the building covering approximately 380 square meters.
“As a result of the hit, the building covering an area of about 380 square meters completely collapsed and was destroyed,” the company said. Exilenova+ also reported that another Flamingo missile apparently failed to reach the plant, with satellite imagery showing an impact crater near the facility.
Volgogradpromproekt is located in Volgograd’s Kirovsky district and specializes in small-scale chemical production, including organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants, resins, and other specialized industrial chemicals.
One of the company’s key products is OSF, an organosilicon derivative of ferrocene containing iron compounds. The substance is used as a catalyst and burn-rate modifier in composite solid rocket propellants, allowing manufacturers to regulate how quickly the propellant burns while maintaining required characteristics.
Volgogradpromproekt supplies Russian defense manufacturers, including the Perm Powder Plant, which produces propellants and explosives for more than 100 weapons systems, including Grad and Smerch rockets and surface-to-air missiles.
The plant has also been linked to production chains for Kalibr cruise missiles and air-launched anti-ship missiles. Another major customer, the Kamensky Chemical Plant, produces solid fuel for Iskander-M and Kinzhal missiles, as well as Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S rockets.
Volgogradpromproekt also supplies materials used in shipbuilding, including to the Amur Shipbuilding Plant, which builds Project 22800 Karakurt-class missile ships.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces used FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Russia’s Progress Rocket Space Center in Samara, the country’s only facility that serially assembles Soyuz-2 launch vehicles.
