articles.title: Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones
A Russian Navy corvette stationed at Kronstadt has been painted to resemble a waterfront building and fitted with protective netting, as Moscow continues adapting its Baltic Fleet vessels against Ukrainian drone attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on September 14, photographs published by military observer Massimo Frantarelli show a Project 1331M corvette, known by NATO as the Parchim II class, with painted outlines resembling windows and doors across its hull. Netting has also been installed above parts of the deck as a physical barrier against incoming drones.
The vessel was photographed at the Leningrad Naval Base in Kronstadt on August 22. Frantarelli said the ship could be either the Zelenodolsk or Kazanets, although its exact identity has not been confirmed. Russia operates roughly six of the East German-built anti-submarine corvettes, each displacing about 800 tons.
The modified vessel is part of a broader effort to alter the appearance of Russian warships based at Kronstadt. Naval analyst H I Sutton has documented several Baltic Fleet ships using black-painted bows and sterns, checkerboard patterns, and other disruptive designs since mid-2026.
Two Project 22800 Karakurt-class missile corvettes, Mytishchi and Burya, were also seen in July with unusual paint schemes and anti-drone netting.
The measures followed successful Ukrainian strikes against Russian naval assets in the Baltic region. On June 3, Ukrainian forces struck the corvette Boikiy while it was undergoing work in dry dock at Kronstadt, causing significant fire damage. Ukrainian officials said the vessel may have been damaged beyond repair.
In March, Ukrainian drones also sank the Russian patrol ship Purga near Vyborg, northwest of St. Petersburg. According to Defence Blog, neither vessel had protective anti-drone netting installed when it was targeted.
Similar techniques have historical precedent. During World War Two, warships were sometimes painted to distort their outline or blend into nearby infrastructure. Germany’s battleship Tirpitz reportedly carried a scheme during fitting-out at Wilhelmshaven that included painted features intended to make the hull resemble buildings along the waterfront.

articles.title: Iran lashes out at US for crimes committed against civilians
articles.body:
Speaking at his weekly press briefing among reporters on Monday, Spokesman for the Iranian Foreign Ministry Esmaeil Baghaei pointed to the US attack on the Iranian city of Lamerd, in Fars province on February 28, 2026, emphasizing that the attack on the city of Lamerd was a clear example of a US war crime committed against the noble nation of the country.
Americans detonated 2,000 kilos of explosives over the city of Lamerd within 35 seconds with the aim of intimidating the people, the spokesman deplored.
The people of the Iranian city of Lamerd, particularly the families of martyrs and veterans—are true embodiments of patience and insight in the arena of defense and resistance against criminals, Baghaei underlined.
Referring to his recent visit to the Iranian city of Lamerd, Fars province, he paid tribute to the city's residents and families of the martyrs and the disabled veterans who were victims of the American atrocity, stating, "What we witnessed firsthand in Lamerd far surpassed the impression we had previously formed through the media; the sheer brutality involved in this crime is incompatible with any human standard or principle."
That a small town of about 30,000 people, the city center and its civilian areas, become a testing ground for the latest weapons is not compatible with any human standards and principles.
Detailing the nature of the attack committed by the United States on Lamerd city, Baghaei stated, The use of a missile packed with three- and four-gram shrapnel—specifically the firing of four missiles, each weighing approximately 500 kilograms and containing a total of 180,000 pellets, followed by their detonation over the stadium of the city, residential areas, the vicinity of the Blood Transfusion Center, and educational facilities and schools—constitutes a definite war crime.
This heinous action constitutes a war crime, both due to the use of a prohibited weapon—specifically a missile classified as a cluster munition—and because it targeted civilian areas and neighborhoods, he said, adding that the US committed this crime in the city in order to instill terror and intimidate people.
On the first day of the military aggression committed by the US and the Zionist regime jointly against the Iranian people—the very day Tehran and numerous other cities, including Minab and the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School, were targeted, approximately 2,000 kilograms of explosives detonated over the city of Lamerd within a span of 35 seconds, Baghaei underlined.
Turning to the victims of this attack, Baghaei stated, "Twenty-one innocent people, including an Afghan national, were martyred during the attack. The pain and suffering of those left disabled by this incident are also indescribable."
Elsewhere in his remarks, Baghaei referred to the recent US attack on a vessel near Hengam Island, noting, "I take this opportunity to offer my condolences to the family of the latest martyr of the Iranian resistance against American crimes."
The US attack on the Iranian vessel near Island of Hengam, led to the killing one, injuring several others, he said, emphasizing that two Pakistani citizens among those wounded in US attack on Iranian ship near Island of Hengam.
"This incident is yet another indication of the fact that the United States has deployed military forces to our region—thousands of kilometers away from its own borders—and, while claiming to be concerned about the safety and security of shipping, attacks Iranian vessels right off our coasts and borders."
Regarding the understanding between Iran and Oman on establishing safe maritime routes, Baghaei stated that the two coastal states reached an agreement—on a matter concerning them exclusively—following weeks of negotiations, and intended to present this understanding at a meeting attended by regional countries, in line with a responsible and far-sighted approach.
Iran-Oman deal set safe navigation routes through Hormuz with respect for sovereignty of both, he added.
* US claim of construction in Iran's Pickaxe Mountain are part of Washington's psychological warfare.
* Hormuz policy will not be 'dictated' by outside forces.
 
 * Austria's visa denial to Iranian delegation for IAEA conference is breach of its international obligations.
Rejecting any Iranian interference in Yemen’s affairs, Baghaei pointed out that Yemenis independently make decisions concerning their country, calling for equal maritime security for all countries.
Noting that Iran and Oman had created a suitable opportunity for dialogue among regional states, he stated that regional countries are expected to recognize the sensitive moment and seize the value of such opportunities created, he continued, adding, “If we truly believe that—as permanent neighbors, and despite all the legitimate grievances we hold regarding the conduct of certain nations—we ought to sit at the same table and discuss establishing a secure region free from the interference of destructive foreign actors, then this meeting presented an excellent opportunity.”
Regarding the postponement of the aforementioned meeting, Baghaei also stated that the has been raised is accurate; Saudi Arabia has requested that the meeting not be held for the time being.
He confirmed that Saudi Arabia was the side that requested the postponement of the planned meeting between Iran and the Persian Gulf states on possible Strait of Hormuz arrangements.
The continued war among Muslim countries only serves Israeli regime's goal of regional insecurity, he opined.
The foreign ministry spokesperson emphasized that the Islamic Republic of Iran has consistently declared—and demonstrated in practice—its readiness to assist in resolving disputes among regional countries, enabling them to reach an understanding on their issues without any interventionist role by Iran in the process.
"We are well aware that the continuation of war in the region among Islamic countries has only one winner—the Zionist regime; a regime that seeks to perpetuate tension and insecurity in the region and among Islamic nations, so that this issue must be taken into serious consideration by the regional states,” Baghaei maintained.
In response to a question regarding US efforts to isolate the Islamic Republic of Iran and the role of the BRICS group in countering this policy, the Foreign Ministry spokesperson stated, "A country that stands up for itself and has garnered the admiration and praise of many nations will not be isolated—even if some countries, due to considerations regarding the United States, do not explicitly voice this sentiment."
The international community, including countries in the region, has rightly recognized that US actions have undermined international norms that are not only desirable but essential for the maintenance of international peace and security, he stressed.
The United States has turned the United Nations into an instrument for its own objectives and has largely reduced the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)’s position to a political tool, he said, adding that the United States has also violated the most important principles and foundations of the United Nations Charter, including the principle prohibiting the use of force.
In response to a question about the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) claims regarding Iran’s Mount Kolang (Pickaxe) near the Natanz nuclear enrichment facility in central Iran, Baghaei said Iran has provided the agency with all information required under its safeguards obligations, dismissing the allegations as media speculation.
“Remarks about Mount Kolang are part of the United States’ media and psychological warfare,” the spokesman said.
He explained that new allegations are repeatedly raised in an effort to justify false narratives, adding that such claims sometimes mislead observers and public opinion.
The IAEA said on Thursday it has observed construction activity at Iran’s Mount Kolang, with its director general Rafael Grossi claiming that new activity at the complex had been spotted in remote imagery.
“There are some indications that there is activity around this construction site,” Grossi told Bloomberg Television.
“We don’t have any concrete information as to activities that may be taking place there,” he added.

Denmark Prepares Priests for 20 Military Funerals a Day as Europe Braces for Major War
Denmark is preparing parish priests across the country to handle large numbers of military funerals in the event of a major war in Europe, with planners considering scenarios in which 10 to 20 Danish soldiers could be killed on the worst days.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Danish broadcaster TV 2 on September 12, the initiative was launched by Thomas H. Beck, head of Denmark’s military chaplains, amid concern over the possibility of a military confrontation on NATO’s eastern flank, including the Baltic states where Danish troops are deployed.
“In the event of a major war, I can easily imagine that we will have 10-20 casualties on the worst possible days. It is important that we are prepared to handle that situation,” Beck told TV 2. “The chaplains will not be able to undertake this task alone,” he added.
Denmark currently has around 95 military chaplains, while approximately 2,000 parish priests serve across the country. Beginning in January, military chaplains are expected to conduct training sessions for civilian clergy on how to receive fallen soldiers, conduct military funerals, and notify relatives of deaths.
The training will also cover military traditions surrounding funerals, including the use of Denmark’s national flag, military headgear, sabers, and medals. The program, called “People’s Church and Defense,” has received 1.8 million Danish kroner in funding from Denmark’s Ministry of Defence.
Beck said Denmark’s experience in Afghanistan involved far fewer casualties than those that could result from a larger war in Europe. “During the Afghanistan war, we only had a few deaths per year, which the Danish Armed Forces chaplains could easily handle,” he said.
“Learned from the experience of the war in Ukraine, we may face much higher casualty figures in the future. And then there will be a need for the country’s other priests to also be able to receive fallen soldiers and conduct a military funeral,” Beck added.
TV 2 reported that the casualty estimate applies to a possible military confrontation abroad rather than fighting on Danish territory. Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service currently assesses that “there is currently no threat of a regular military attack against the Kingdom of Denmark.”
The preparations come as Denmark strengthens its military presence in the Baltic region. Danish forces have deployed a combat battalion to Latvia as part of NATO’s eastern defenses.
TV 2 also reported that Danish chaplains participated earlier this year in a Swedish military exercise involving a scenario with 500 dead soldiers. The drills included procedures for identifying bodies, placing fallen troops in body bags, and organizing burials.
“We have a lot to learn from both the Swedes and the Finns when it comes to larger exercises,” Beck said.
Sweden has also developed broader wartime burial plans. On the island of Gotland, church authorities have prepared procedures for burying as many as 3,000 people in wartime, including the possibility of using temporary graves before bodies are later transferred to their home parishes.
Beck stressed that Denmark’s figures remain estimates rather than an official casualty forecast. TV 2 noted that Danish authorities rarely discuss potential wartime losses publicly because such scenarios are generally treated as sensitive military planning.
Poland has also stepped up preparations for a possible confrontation with Russia. In August, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said Warsaw was “preparing for war,” warning that a major Russian provocation could occur within months as Poland strengthens its military, critical infrastructure, and defenses along NATO’s eastern flank.

articles.title: Russia Launches Kalibr Cruise Missiles Directly From Base, Ukraine Says
articles.body:
Russia has been launching its naval-based Kalibr cruise missiles directly from port via its missile carriers for four months in a row, according to Ukraine.
Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk noted the new trend on television, according to state media Ukrinform on Monday, Sept. 14.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Even the use of cruise missile carriers that launch Kalibrs takes place directly at the base, that is, right in the harbor. This is a trend that has been observed for the fourth month in a row,” Pletenchuk said.
The Kalibr, with a reported range of 1,500-2,500 km (932-1,553 miles), is the mainstay in the Russian Navy’s arsenal and have been frequently used against Ukrainian cities since 2022.
The missiles are typically launched at sea by Russian warships and submarines, with Ukrainian channels closely monitoring their movements ahead of potential missile strikes.
Pletenchuk noted the peculiar nature and difficulty in launching them from the harbor, before warning that the missiles’ danger should not be overlooked.
“Submarines, for example, are also not so easy to use. To do this, they need to dive. I still can’t imagine how they can use them in the mode in which they are currently launching them,” Pletenchuk continued.
“Let’s not downplay the danger: we are assuming the maximum – four carriers, but realistic figures would probably be two surface carriers,” he added.
Canada Considers Joining EU €90 Billion Ukraine Loan
Pletenchuk also estimated that Russia has four vessels capable of launching the Kalibr missiles from the Black Sea – two Buyan-M-class warships and two Varshavyanka-class submarines.
On Sept. 9, Ukraine claimed to have hit the Admiral Essen, a Russian Admiral Grigorovich-class frigate capable of launching Kalibr missiles, at Russia’s Novorossiysk.
Pletenchuk also noted the decreased frequency of Russia’s cruise missile launches, saying that two had been documented this month, compared with a summer high of three.
Based on Kyiv Post’s tallies, Russia launched at least 251 cruise missiles in July, with massive strikes documented on three days (July 2, July 6, and July 30), where 40, 55 and 65 cruise missiles were launched, respectively, based on the Ukrainian Air Force’s morning updates.
The rest of July consisted of occasional cruise missile launches of up to 16 per day.

articles.title: Finland joins France’s nuclear deterrent initiative
articles.body:
Finland joins France’s nuclear deterrent initiative
- Finland has joined France’s Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative to strengthen European security amid concerns over US commitment and the Ukraine war.
- The initiative keeps French presidential authority over nuclear use but promotes joint exercises and potential deployment of nuclear-capable assets among partners.
- Finland follows Nordic countries joining earlier and emphasises the programme complements NATO without hosting nuclear weapons in peacetime.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – Finland has joined France’s initiative to extend the reach of its nuclear deterrent through collaboration with partner European countries, the heads of both countries said on Sept 14.
In response to US President Donald Trump’s expressions of concern about the US security commitment to Europe and to the security implications of the Ukraine war, France in March announced the Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative.
“The initiative is first and foremost about strengthening European security. It reinforces Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and helps prevent escalation,” Finland President Alexander Stubb said in a post on X.
Under the initiative, the French president alone has the authority to decide when nuclear weapons are used, in contrast to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which has a shared Nuclear Planning Group.
However, it offers joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Finland's defence minister Antti Hakkanen said in a separate statement that the agreement was a “natural step” following other Nordic countries, such as Norway, Sweden and Denmark, that joined the initiative earlier in 2026. In total, 10 countries participate, including Finland.
Stubb said the programme does not replace NATO’s nuclear deterrence and that Finland does not intend to allow nuclear weapons to be stationed on its territory in peacetime. REUTERS

articles.title: Fury after Russian strike on Ukraine train nearly catches dignitaries
articles.body:
European leaders expressed outrage Monday, a day after a Russian drone strike targeted a train near the Ukraine-Poland border, shortly senior visiting officials, including the former prime ministers of the U.K. and Sweden, passed through.
According to Ukrzaliznytsia, a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson, Carl Bildt and security advisers from several European Union states had purposely left the station at Yahodyn ahead of schedule. The visitors were on their way back from a security conference in Kyiv.
"It is highly probable that the Russian drone's intended target was in fact the diplomatic train, which had departed the station earlier than scheduled," the company said in a Telegram post.
Bildt, the former Swedish PM, shared a video on X of the attack at Yahodyn station, near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland.
"This wasn't our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing," Bildt said. "It was evacuated as the Russian drone approached and no one was hurt. Very good safety system. Our train just had an evacuation warning."
Bildt, Johnson and fellow passengers had been in Kyiv for the Yalta European Strategy conference, which is an annual gathering of leaders and experts across politics, business, security and media.
Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to Ukrzaliznytsia.
There were no immediate reports of casualties on any of the trains.
Ukrzaliznytsia said it "constantly adjusts train schedules" to guard against strikes.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Monday that Russian drone strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border would drive the military alliance to increase its support for Kyiv, calling the attacks on Sunday a sign of growing desperation by the forces under Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The strikes yesterday on trains in Ukraine close to NATO territory again show Putin's desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror," Rutte said at NATO's political headquarters in Brussels. "Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine."
Rutte pledged to increase support for Ukraine and bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defenses along its long eastern border with Russia.
"He thinks that he can stop us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong," the NATO chief said of Putin.
Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said Monday that the drone attacks near Poland's border were "clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine."
"We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared," she said.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Monday that Russia seeks to "divide" and "intimidate" Kyiv's European allies after a drone attack near a train carrying European officials in Ukraine.
"These attacks have a very clear objective: to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and, above all, divide them," Barrot told reporters on the sidelines of the European Arctic Summit in Finland.
He pointed out that the strikes occurred "as Ukraine was hosting a major economic support forum, attended by a large number of business representatives and diplomatic officials from around the world, particularly from Europe," according to broadcaster BFMTV.
Meanwhile, the office of U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that Russian strikes were aimed at undermining international support but Britain would not be deterred.
A spokesperson for his Downing Street office told journalists that the attack "was a futile attempt by Russia to undermine our support for Ukraine. It will not deter us."

articles.title: FACTBOX: Russian strikes hit Kievstar mobile provider building, railway facilities
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. Russian strike drones hit the Kievstar mobile provider’s building, which also provides services to Ukraine’s military, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
Russian forces also hit locomotives and military trains carrying supplies for Ukraine’s army in the Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, Poltava, Nikolayev, and Odessa regions.
TASS has compiled the key details of the strikes.
Targets in the Kharkov and Sumy regions
- Russian pilots used aerial bombs and X-39 missiles to hit temporary deployment sites and drone command posts in the communities of Fyodorovka in the Kharkov Region and Zemlyanoye in the Sumy Region, respectively.
- The Defense Ministry released footage showing the strikes.
- Russian Aerospace Forces crews carried out the strikes using FAB-500 500-kilogram guided aerial bombs equipped with universal planning and correction modules, as well as two LMUR Kh-39 long-range air-launched missiles.
Railway transport
- Russian forces used Geran-4 Seeker strike drones to hit locomotives and military trains in the Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, Poltava, Nikolayev, and Odessa regions.
- The trains were used to carry various military supplies across Ukraine.
Strike on Kievstar building
- Russian drone operators from the Varyag Separate Brigade of Unmanned Systems carried out a precision strike on the Kievstar building in Ukraine.
- Kievstar is a telecom company providing mobile and internet services to Ukraine’s military.
Strike on gas station in Kiev
- Drone operators from the Varyag Brigade used a Geran strike drone to hit a gas station in Kiev.
- The gas station was used to serve Ukraine’s military, including its command, the Defense Ministry said, releasing footage of the strike.
Ukrainian unmanned boat assembly facility
- Russian forces hit a facility for assembling Ukrainian unmanned boats in the settlement of Grigorovka with a drone.
Situation in Ukraine
- Power outages were reported in the Dnepropetrovsk, Sumy, and Kharkov regions after energy infrastructure was damaged, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry reported.
- Some residents in the three regions were left without power.
- The ministry urged Ukrainians not to use high-power electrical appliances in the evening to prevent grid overloads.
- Electricity supplies were cut off in Kiev-controlled Kherson, the city’s head of the administration appointed by Ukrainian authorities, Yaroslav Shanko, reported.
- According to him, specialists are working to determine the cause of the power outage.

articles.title: “Fairly disciplined workers”: Russia’s prison service is replacing penal colonies with forced labor centers — and making money from it
articles.body:
As the military recruitment of prisoners reduces the population of penal colonies across Russia, the country’s Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) is expanding another branch of its system: correctional centers for convicts sentenced to forced labor. By the end of 2025, Russia had created 400 of these centers, with space for up to 50,000 people. This past June, FSIN even unveiled a “quickly deployable” center that can be installed directly at businesses nationwide. The new system is more profitable than traditional penal colonies, providing FSIN with fresh revenue streams and companies with access to a workforce almost entirely devoid of rights.
You’re not prisoners, but you can’t leave
Russian law does not classify forced labor as imprisonment, but a person sentenced to forced labor is nevertheless obligated to live in a closed FSIN facility. They must work wherever the administration sends them and cannot freely leave the correctional center.
“You can sit there and not go anywhere for a year,” Olga [name changed], a former convict who spent time in correctional centers from Perm to Volgograd, told The Insider. After a penal colony, Olga said, a correctional center can genuinely feel “almost like home.” People there can wear their own clothes, use a phone, read the news online, and communicate with relatives every day through messaging apps. But the relative improvement in quality of life that Olga experienced only applies to those who have previously spent time in a penal colony, where prisoners must wear standardized uniforms, communication with relatives usually happens by letter, and phones are banned.
For someone sent to a correctional center directly from life outside prison, the experience looks different: living by a schedule set by the FSIN, leaving the center only with permission, working forced overtime, and being subject to the administration’s will.
“People who were sent to a correctional center straight from home were somewhat shocked,” Olga recalled.
“A model correctional center with a sports ground and park”
According to Olga, life becomes especially hard when a correctional center is set up directly at a production site — with a dormitory next to the workshop and the employer working together with the administration to reduce inmates’ lives to moving between bed and the workplace. That is exactly the model FSIN now wants to replicate: fast-deployable correctional centers that can be built next to enterprises.
“At the St. Petersburg International Legal Forum, FSIN presented a model correctional center with a sports ground and a park. The project was sent to the regions as a recommendation,” TASS wrote in late June. In FSIN photographs, the model does not look like a prison but like a tidy workers’ dormitory: a long two-story modular building, lawns, bushes, streetlights, a separate sports ground, and a walking area with benches.
The TASS report also listed other elements of the project: a parking lot, a diesel power station, a transformer substation, and a separate yard where those who have violated prison rules can still get a chance to walk. But the presentation itself showed that the most attractive parts of the image — the park and sports ground — aren’t mandatory. A FSIN representative clarified that they are only “optional facilities.”
In other words, what was sent to the regions was not a plan for a center with a park but an easily replicable solution for quickly housing people sentenced to forced labor. The FSIN website describes it even more directly: the facilities can be built quickly “at any enterprise,” and the project can be used by representatives of large and medium-sized businesses interested in creating dormitories for convicts at their facilities.
That detail is crucial, Olga explained. She served her sentence both in a correctional center where she had to walk down the street to get to work and in a center where the dormitory was effectively on the production site.
“If it’s a closed-system correctional center, then the employer works in very close coordination with FSIN. No one’s getting away from them. FSIN plays the way the employer needs it to,” Olga said.
Employers work in very close coordination with FSIN in closed-system correctional centers
In that model, a person does not simply live near work — work becomes an extension of the prison regime.
“The conditions were always more lenient where the employer wasn’t in the same building as the dormitory. But where you live right in the workshop, right at the production site, that was where things were the hardest,” Olga recalled.
At one correctional center in the Moscow region, Olga said, the living quarters resembled a hangar or garage, with a workshop on the floor below. The facility had poor ventilation and was plagued by dirt, rats and cockroaches.
“It's legalized slavery,” she said. “They force people to work and use every tool of pressure and punishment available to make sure they keep working and don’t complain.”
30,000 workers with no rights
Forced labor as a new type of criminal punishment began to be used on Jan. 1, 2017, when FSIN opened its first four correctional centers and seven sections attached to its penal colonies, with a total capacity of fewer than 900 people. The first convicts arrived in March of that year. Now, a small network of facilities that was previously being tested as an alternative to colonies has turned into a separate and growing branch of the penal system.
By the end of 2025, according to FSIN Director Arkady Gostev, Russia had created 400 correctional centers and sections operating as correctional centers, with capacity for 50,000 people — and more than 30,000 convicts were actually being held there.
Given the overall decline in Russia’s prison population, those figures are especially notable. In May 2026, Gostev said that since the end of 2021 the number of people in places of detention had fallen from 465,000 to 282,000. About 85,000 of them were held in pretrial detention centers (SIZO) and PFRSI, a Russian abbreviation for facilities operating as pretrial detention centers, leaving about 197,000 in penal colonies and prisons.
The rise of correctional centers, whose inhabitants are not counted among the country’s prison statistics, do not explain that decline. Instead, the main reason for the drop in the population of penal colonies was the recruitment of prisoners for the war in Ukraine — first by the Wagner private military company, then by the Defense Ministry. In May, FSIN itself acknowledged for the first time that “efforts to recruit contract soldiers” for the armed forces was affecting the number of prisoners.
But at the same time, the agency is expanding the part of the system that is formally not considered imprisonment — exploiting the labor of convicts rather than simply isolating them away from society. The more than 30,000 people actually held in correctional centers already amount to about 15% of the current number of people under FSIN’s jurisdiction. The centers’ total capacity — 50,000 places — is comparable to about a quarter of that population.
The agency is expanding the part of the system focused not on isolation, but on exploiting convicts’ labor
At the same time, legal changes are making it easier to fill correctional centers. Since 2026, forced labor can be imposed as a standalone punishment, without a prior sentence involving imprisonment. The penalties under dozens of articles of the Criminal Code have also been expanded to include forced labor.
A “dormitory” behind a fence: What life is like in a correctional center
Russia’s Penal Enforcement Code describes correctional centers as special institutions for people sentenced to forced labor. They can exist separately, as sections attached to penal colonies, or directly at enterprises that use convict labor. Inside such centers, internal rules apply, and convicts are kept under supervision.
In correctional centers, people are allowed to have money, wear ordinary clothes, use a phone, access the internet, and keep personal belongings. At the same time, a convict must remain on the correctional center’s grounds, they may not leave without permission from the administration, they must carry an ID card at all times, they must follow internal rules, and they must take part in unpaid maintenance and improvement work for up to two hours a week. The person and the room where they live may be searched, and their belongings may be inspected. In effect, it is the same kind of closed institution as a penal colony, only with a softer internal regime.
The word “dormitory,” which is used to describe the living quarters in correctional centers, says little about the real conditions. Russia’s Penal Enforcement Code uses the same word for the places where convicts live in general-regime, strict-regime, and special-regime colonies. In practice, these are usually not separate rooms for a few people but buildings divided into large sections, each housing several dozen people. Even in the model FSIN showed at the St. Petersburg International Legal Forum, a large room with rows of beds can be seen inside the modular building. It looks more like a barracks-style sleeping hall than a regular dormitory.
Olga said conditions varied widely by region. In some places, the administration turned a blind eye to the rules, while in others, it used them as a tool of pressure. Still, the routine in forced labor facilities, she said, resembled the “Groundhog Day” rhythm of life in a penal colony:
“Wake-up, breakfast, go to work, a little lunch at work, and then at around 8 or 9 p.m. we come back from work, wash, have a bite to eat, and go to sleep. That’s basically every day.”
In some correctional centers, Olga said, people could go into town for a few hours on weekends. However, on others, people had to go months without leaving the grounds.
“If there are no problems, if the employer does not say they are working badly, then everything goes normally,” she said. “But if someone starts, for example, filing complaints against the employer, then the administration first of all restricts outings.”
Grigory Mumrikov, an artist who served a forced labor sentence in Zelenograd, just outside Moscow, after being convicted of participating in the organization of an anti-war protest, shared similar impressions. Compared with pretrial detention, the correctional center seemed to him like “great happiness,” even if he was still in captivity. From evening to morning, he was in the correctional center, and from morning to evening, he worked as a laborer at Aksakovo, a sanatorium run by FSIN. Mumrikov spent the couple of free hours he had after work walking around a lake.
“I could simply sit on a bench, just to avoid being on that territory,” he said, referring to the correctional center.
That was possible because the convicts worked outside the correctional center and traveled to and from Aksakovo on their own. But by 8 p.m., Mumrikov had to return to the center for the evening roll call.
“Everyone was rounded up and told to work weekends”
Under the law, people sentenced to forced labor must work wherever the correctional center’s administration sends them. Formally, their labor is supposed to be regulated by labor law. But convicts do not have the key right of a free worker: the right to refuse a particular job and leave for another employer.
Convicts do not have the key right of a free worker: the right to refuse a particular job and leave for another employer
In some correctional centers, Olga said, there was still some choice — the administration could offer two or three potential employers, and the person would choose where to work based on their skills and health. But that was not the case everywhere. In the correctional center in Leninsk, in the Volgograd region, where she was held in the winter of 2023-2024, there was only one employer: a canned goods factory.
“You cannot refuse to work, because that is considered a malicious violation,” Olga said.
According to her, people worked 10 to 12 hours a day, and weekends could be turned into workdays. However, if inspections began, the employer would show a normal schedule.
“The employers drew up a good schedule and pretended that no one had been forced to come in on weekends and that the working day was what it should be,” she said. “Accordingly, as soon as the inspectors leave, everything goes back to the way it was: longer working days and mandatory weekend work.”
The order to work on weekends, she said, usually came not directly from FSIN but from the production site. A foreman would gather the convicts, make sure no one had phones to record the conversation, and then announce the new schedule: “We work on weekends. We work until such-and-such time. And whoever complains will make things worse for themselves.”
That is what makes a convict’s position in a correctional center fundamentally different from that of an ordinary worker. In a correctional center, an employer’s demand almost automatically becomes an FSIN demand. The administration begins applying pressure, and complaints or refusal to work can result in disciplinary penalties.
“Inspectors work in coordination with the employer. They are one single system,” Olga said. If a person refuses to work for pennies or complains about conditions, she said, the administration can begin “catching them on small things” to find grounds for punishment. Accumulating such penalties creates the risk of transfer to a penal colony.
Similar complaints have emerged in other regions. In Zelenograd, convicts in a correctional center said they worked without a proper schedule, faced overtime, and were threatened with tougher conditions if they reminded officials of their rights.
“We differ from undocumented migrants on a construction site only in that we are Russian,” forced laborers said.
Konstantin, a former prisoner who served his sentence in Kabardino-Balkaria in Russia’s north Caucasus, told the independent outlet Cherta that he was sent to sort household waste — eight hours in the heat at a rural dump that included hides of slaughtered cows and sheep, a terrible smell, large numbers of insects, and no ability to refuse the work.
Another person interviewed by the outlet, from the Voronezh Region in central Russia, worked at an agricultural complex growing mushrooms and said regular hired employees earned significantly more than convicts got from the correctional center.
These examples do not mean that people in every correctional center are forced to work overtime or are sent to the hardest jobs. Former convicts themselves also describe centers with decent working conditions and normal schedules. But all cases have one thing in common: a person cannot resign if they are unhappy with the conditions.
There is pay, but people support themselves
Officially, labor in correctional centers is paid. In any sentence, between 5% and 20% of a convict’s salary is withheld for the state, and the inmate is free to use the rest of the money. But unlike a penal colony, where prisoners have to be fed and issued uniforms, people in correctional centers are almost entirely self-supporting.
Convicts are given a bed and bedding, but they usually buy their food, clothes, shoes, hygiene products, medicine, and other everyday items while also reimbursing the correctional center each month for utilities and household services.
In Leninsk, in the Volgograd Region, Olga said, about 3,000 to 4,000 rubles ($35-$46) were withheld from her wages for utilities, and after all the deductions were made, convicts were typically left with about 9,000 to 10,000 rubles ($104-$116) a month to live on.
“And you have to take into account that this is not a colony: you need to dress yourself and eat something, because not all correctional centers provide food,” she said.
“This is not a colony: you need to dress yourself and eat something, because not all correctional centers have food”
Formally, if a convict has no money, the correctional center has to provide them with food, clothing, and shoes at the state’s expense. But in practice, Olga said, getting that support can be difficult.
“You go to the management and say: I have nothing to eat, you are supposed to provide me with food. And they say: ‘Well, where am I going to get it? You can see there is no kitchen,’” she said, describing life at a correctional center in the Moscow Region.
At the same time, Olga stressed that low pay is not an inevitable feature of correctional centers. In the Perm Region, where she worked at a private garment factory, the business was properly organized, and convicts’ wages could be comparable to ordinary wages outside the prison.
Olga earned about 40,000 to 50,000 rubles ($460-$580), while women who sewed well made up to 100,000 ($1,160), even after the deductions. “It was a fairly good place,” she said.
That contrast shows that the problem with correctional centers is not simply that they always pay poorly. With a decent employer, convicts can earn close to what they would outside prison. But if the employer is dishonest, the fact that a person is trapped means they are forced to survive on less than the national subsistence minimum.
What can lead to punishment in a correctional center
Under the Penal Enforcement Code, violations committed by people serving forced labor can lead to them being placed in an internal isolation cell inside the correctional center for up to 15 days. Olga said anyone sent there can only bring a minimum of belongings, and there is a ban on phones. “Not as frightening as in a colony, but the point is the same — to isolate you and show what they can do to you,” she explained.
The law separately defines “malicious violations,” which include refusal to work, disobeying the administration, participating in a strike or collective disobedience, possessing banned items, leaving the center without authorization, or returning more than 24 hours late. If a person is declared a malicious violator — for one “malicious” violation or for three ordinary violations within a year — the head of the correctional center submits a request to a court to transfer the person to a colony.
In practice, Olga said, these rules become a method of control. The administration may ignore minor violations for a long time, then use them against those who complain about an employer or refuse to work in poor conditions.
“They may treat you relatively well for a long time, but once you start demanding your rights, they begin finding fault with everything you do,” she said.
“Once you start demanding your rights, they begin finding fault with everything you do”
An everyday minor infraction can thus become part of a chain that ends in a person being packed off to a penal colony. “For those who came from a colony, that's the main fear,” Olga said. “They tell you: ‘if you don't want to work, you'll go back.’”
Who benefits from the new system
In public statements, FSIN describes correctional centers as a more humane alternative to colonies: a person is not completely isolated from society, and they can work, earn a salary, use a phone, and gradually return to normal life. In an explanatory note to the law expanding the use of forced labor, its authors wrote that such punishment allows convicts to maintain social ties, restore work skills, and compensate victims.
But this humanization also has an economic aspect. Under the Penal Enforcement Code, sections of correctional centers can be created directly at enterprises that use convict labor. The standard contract between a correctional center and a company describes the arrangement as a ready-made production scheme: the correctional center sends convicts, and the organization agrees to employ them at its site and report violations of labor discipline to the administration.
For businesses, this means access to workers whose minimal privileges depend on their successful fulfillment of assigned tasks. A convict cannot simply quit and leave for another employer, and as a FSIN representative told TASS, commercial entities are interested in creating such sections because people sentenced to forced labor are “fairly disciplined workers.”
“They are interested in doing their work well, because if they violate labor discipline or the procedure and conditions for serving their sentence, there is a risk that the punishment will be replaced with a harsher one — imprisonment,” the representative said.
The state additionally encourages businesses to take part in the scheme. Since 2026, organizations have been exempt from property tax on premises, territories, and other real estate they provide free of charge to house correctional centers.
The model is also convenient for FSIN. The agency does not need to build a traditional penal colony, as businesses provide part of the infrastructure while paying convicts enough that the state is not obliged to provide them with food, clothes, or medicine — 5% to 20% of their wages also go directly to the state.
In the end, businesses get workers whose discipline is backed by FSIN, while the agency gets infrastructure and a “contingent” — the official bureaucratic term used for prisoners and other people under state supervision — whose burden of support can largely be shifted onto the convicts themselves. At the same time, for FSIN and the state as a whole, this is a form of punishment that can be presented as humane resocialization.
A Gulag without isolation
The idea of correction through labor is not a new concept in the Russian penal system. In Soviet times, it was reflected even in the names of institutions, as camps and colonies were called “corrective labor institutions.” Soviet Russia’s Corrective Labor Code explicitly said that punishment should “correct and reeducate” convicts “in the spirit of an honest attitude toward labor.”
Under Stalin, this logic reached its extreme: the Gulag was not only a system of isolation and terror but also a vast economic mechanism. Prisoners built canals, railways, industrial facilities, and urban infrastructure. But directly comparing modern correctional centers with the Gulag would be inaccurate: the scale, conditions, and level of violence are not comparable.Today, supervision is as light as possible, as it is the system itself that stimulates the efficiency of the inmates’ labor.
The idea of correction through labor is not a new concept in the Russian penal system. In Soviet times, it was reflected even in the names of institutions, as camps and colonies were called “corrective labor institutions.” Soviet Russia’s Corrective Labor Code explicitly said that punishment should “correct and reeducate” convicts “in the spirit of an honest attitude toward labor.”
Under Stalin, this logic reached its extreme: the Gulag was not only a system of isolation and terror but also a vast economic mechanism. Prisoners built canals, railways, industrial facilities, and urban infrastructure. But directly comparing modern correctional centers with the Gulag would be inaccurate: the scale, conditions, and level of violence are not comparable.Today, supervision is as light as possible, as it is the system itself that stimulates the efficiency of the inmates’ labor.
The state does not need to fully isolate a person in order to control them. It is enough to link their place of residence, their type of work, their salary, and the threat of transfer to a penal colony into a single system. As a result, Correctional centers look like an updated version of the Soviet labor tradition — without the barracks of the Gulag, but with the same basic idea that a convict must work for the benefit of the state — and now, also, for Russia’s business sector.
Not humanization, but a pragmatic move by FSIN
Correctional centers may offer better conditions than penal colonies, but they are still a form of deprivation of liberty, no matter what the paperwork says. In the end, they create even more opportunities to exploit prisoner labor than colonies do, and FSIN directly describes people sentenced to forced labor as a convenient labor resource.
Putin’s war in Ukraine is draining prisoners from Russia’s penal colonies, and dozens of institutions have closed down due to the lack of inmates. That could have led to FSIN losing bureaucratic influence (and with it, staff and funding from the state budget). Instead, the agency’s leadership appears to have found an effective way out: it can now report growth in the number of institutions providing a more humane form of punishment, and it can do so in a way that certainly pleases Russian businesses.

articles.title: Suspect in Leipzig airport sabotage reportedly linked to Russian military intelligence
articles.body:
German investigators have identified two suspects in the sabotage attempt at Leipzig/Halle Airport, where a drone fitted with a detonator was found near a Ukrainian transport aircraft in early August. The suspects are Russian national Oleg L. and Belarusian national Andrei K., according to a report by German newspaper Welt am Sonntag. One of them, Oleg L., has ties to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, and was responsible for preparing the operation and handling its logistics.
German law enforcement officials investigating the attempted attack traced the operation to Russia’s GRU, with Welt am Sonntag citing investigative files obtained by the newspaper. Those materials indicate that Oleg L. appears to have overseen preparations and logistics for the operation. German security agencies believe he is a GRU officer.
The newspaper said Oleg L. entered Germany from Turkey through Berlin Brandenburg Airport. He later left the country from the same airport, flying to Serbia. Investigators believe he is now in Russia.
Welt am Sonntag also reported that German security agencies already knew of Oleg L.’s possible ties to Russian military intelligence when he entered the country, but did not place him under surveillance.
The suspected perpetrators planned to use three drones in the Leipzig airport sabotage operation. Two were destroyed during takeoff, while the third reached the Ukrainian aircraft. Investigators believe an explosion was avoided only because the detonator failed to function.
The second suspect is Belarusian national Andrei K. His DNA was found on an antenna that was used to control the drones. The DNA matched records in Finnish and Lithuanian police databases.
In Finland, he had been suspected of theft. He is also suspected of setting fire to a hardware store in the Polish city of Łódź in 2024.
The German publication Bild previously reported that a DNA trace found during the investigation of the Leipzig airport attack case matched DNA evidence from a 2024 arson attack on a DHL logistics center in Leipzig. The newspaper did not say whose DNA was found.
On Sept. 1, the German government formally accused Russia of carrying out a hybrid attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, where a drone with a detonator had been found near a Ukrainian transport plane on Aug. 5. At a news conference, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany would respond by closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and Russia’s consulate general in Bonn.
Russia, in turn, withdrew its consent for Germany’s consulate general in St. Petersburg to operate and shut down the country’s Goethe-Institut cultural centers nationwide.

articles.title: Houthis claim drone, missile strikes on airbase in Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
DOHA, September 14. /TASS/. Yemen’s Ansar Allah (Houthi) rebel movement claims to have conducted a series of ballistic missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid Air Base in the city of Khamis Mushait.
"Yemen’s Armed Forces carried out a large-scale operation against military and infrastructure facilities, including aircraft hangars, runways, ammunition depots and other targets at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait," Houthi military Spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on Telegram. He added that the attack involved "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones."
The situation in Yemen escalated sharply in early September when the rebel movement launched an offensive in the country’s southwest. At the same time, it began carrying out missile and drone strikes on Red Sea coastal areas and the outskirts of the city of Taiz, seeking to sever access routes to the port of Mocha and advance toward areas along the strategic Bab-el-Mandeb Strait.
On September 11, the Houthi military spokesperson announced that Ansar Allah units had begun an operation on Yemen’s west coast to push back Saudi forces. According to him, the operation was due to "attacks on civilians, villages and areas on the west coast by Saudi-backed forces, which have been going on for several years." Ansar Allah Political Bureau member Hizam al-Asad confirmed to TASS on September 12 that the Houthis had concluded an operation to take control of areas in western Yemen adjacent to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

articles.title: Tehran protests as US blocks Iran nuclear chief from IAEA meeting in Vienna
articles.body:
The United States has blocked Iran's nuclear chief from attending this week's UN atomic watchdog meeting in Vienna by opposing an exemption from so-called "snapback" UN sanctions, prompting protests from Tehran.
Iranian nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami had been due to attend and address this week's International Atomic Energy Agency General Conference, an annual meeting of IAEA member states that began on Monday.
At the opening, however, Iran said Austria had revoked Eslami's visa after initially granting it.
"The cancellation and so-called legal justification advanced for it are a stark indication of a political act and advanced formal politicisation of this organisation," Iran's ambassador to the IAEA told the conference.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the United States had pressured Austria into the move. In contrast, Iran and Russia said it formed part of a broader effort to prevent Iranian officials from obtaining visas for international travel.
The United States said it had objected to an exemption that would have allowed Eslami to travel despite sanctions reimposed under the so-called "snapback" mechanism at the UN Security Council.
Snapback sanctions
Eslami was among those targeted by sanctions lifted under a 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and major powers and the United States.
The deal unravelled after President Donald Trump pulled the US out of it in 2018, and Western powers triggered the "snapback" mechanism last year to re-impose those sanctions.
Last year, Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said the reimposition of sanctions "must not be the end of diplomacy".
Russia and China tried unsuccessfully last year, at the UN Security Council, to delay the sanctions snapback, warning it could escalate tensions in the Middle East.
Their draft resolution gained only four votes among the 15 council members.
Iran and allies, including Russia, do not recognise the reimposed sanctions.
US push
Austria said it had requested an exemption for Eslami.
"Austria, although being only the host state, submitted a request for an exemption to the travel ban to the Security Council sanctions committee, which was rejected," Ambassador Christian Ebner told the conference.
"As a consequence, Austria was obliged to deny one member of the Iranian delegation entry into its territory," he said.
US Ambassador Preston Wells Griffith III said his country had objected in New York to an exemption being granted, and that was why the application was denied.
"The United States objected to the exemption request, which, per the rules of the UN sanctions committee, resulted in the UN Security Council denying the request," he said.
"His (Eslami's) participation would have only resulted in Iran exploiting IAEA proceedings as a stage for propaganda while sidestepping substantive cooperation, undermining the credibility of the very body charged with verifying its nuclear commitments," he said, referring to a standoff over inspections.

articles.title: Ukraine: AfD questions German aid, Berlin remains committed
articles.body:
AfD puts pressure on German aid to Ukraine
September 14, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is standing firm on military aid for Ukraine in its war with Russia.
"We support Ukraine, and we will continue to support her, because she is also defending our freedom," Merz said on September 9 during a debate in the Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament.
He was reacting to Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel, who had urged him to "finally start pushing for peace talks, like the US is doing."
US President Donald Trump has indicated that he would make far-reaching concessions to Russia at such negotiations; critics in Germany have described that as dictated peace.
On the topic of high energy prices in Germany, Weidel said, "We need cheap natural gas from Russia. That is what we will work toward."
She insinuated that the Ukrainian government was responsible for blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany in September 2022. "They continue to reward the suspected masterminds of the attack in Kyiv with billion-dollar payments at the expense of Germany." A Ukrainian sabotage team is suspected to be behind the attack.
How pro-Russia the AfD is, despite its invasion of Ukraine, was shown clearly by its lawmaker Jürgen Koegel during the debate. He spoke of "valued President Vladimir Putin," who posed no threat of war to NATO.
East-west division in Germany over Ukraine aid
The AfD's position on the war in Ukraine is nothing new. However, since winning the state parliament election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6 by a large margin, gaining almost 44% of the vote, it has expressed it even more vehemently.
Combining the votes for the AfD, the socialist Left Party and the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), about 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that either oppose support for Ukraine or are skeptical of it.
According to one survey, citizens' concerns about peace in Europe influenced their votes. Those surveyed named this topic as their second-most important, after "social security" and far ahead of "immigration" or "environment and climate."
In addition, there is the result of an ARD Deutschlandtrend survey conducted shortly before the election. It showed an east-west divide on the question of military support for Ukraine. About 39% of western Germans (from the area which was West Germany prior to reunification) thought military assistance went too far, while it was 54% for eastern Germans — that is, people who live in the area which used to be the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR/DDR).
"The course that the German federal government is taking on Ukraine does not have majority support in the east," Johannes Varwick, a political scientist at the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt, told DW.
"I would not describe that as 'pro-Russia'; it comes from the desire to focus more on diplomacy rather than delivering ever more weapons to fuel a war which Ukraine cannot win."
Fear in Germany of Russian threats
On September 2, the German government blamed Russia for a failed attack with an armed drone in early August at Leipzig airport, a key hub for military aid to Ukraine.
Putin spoke of a "grave error," Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov even called the accusation the "start of a real war." The exchange of verbal blows marked a new level of escalation in an already tense relationship.
According to the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, most Germans (56%) see themselves currently either strongly or very strongly threatened by Russia. But it also showed that eastern Germans and AfD voters feel less threatened by Russia. The election results in Saxony-Anhalt also seem to reflect this.
Political scientist Sven Leunig from the Friedrich Schiller University Jena in the state of Thuringia has his own take on the reaction of eastern Germans, especially after the Leipzig incident.
"It is less a fundamental rejection of support for Ukraine, more a reaction based on fear," Leunig said. "They want to keep out of the conflict, so as not to be drawn further into it. That of course strengthens parties like the AfD, BSW and Left, who accommodate these sentiments."
Support for Ukraine is also coming under pressure for another reason. According to the AfD and BSW, the money Ukraine receives could be better spent on Germany's stretched social services. AfD lawmaker Gottfried Curio, for example, accused the German government of cutting social benefits and raising taxes "to keep on giving billions to foreign countries," to finance "foreign wars" such as in Ukraine.
Support for Ukraine is crumbling, but slowly
Chancellor Merz still believes he has political and public backing for his course. During the Bundestag debate, this was his response to the AfD's suggestion of resuming energy deliveries from Russia and ending German support for Ukraine: "This path that you depict is not supported by the majority in the German parliament and it is also not supported by the majority of the population of the Federal Republic of Germany. We will defend our freedom, also in the future."
But support for Ukraine, as shown in ARD Deutschlandtrend surveys over the years, is becoming less favored by the public. The share of people who think military support goes too far is growing, slowly but steadily, and is now 42%.
Leunig thinks the German government is not yet under pressure to reconsider its Ukraine policy: it still has "clear support" for the current course. "Plus, the threat coming from Russia is also becoming widely recognized. Of course, if public support weakens in the long-term, the government will have to react to that."
Is Ukraine 'another Afghanistan'?
His colleague Johannes Varwick, on the other hand, advises a course correction now, but not so much due to the mood in Germany: "Yes, we should stand with Ukraine, but standing by Ukraine does not mean fueling a futile war of attrition without a viable political strategy. That runs Ukraine into the ground, even if it is portrayed as 'pro-Ukraine'."
Critics have drawn parallels to Western intervention in Afghanistan, which after 20 years, billions of dollars spent and about 3500 western soldiers killed, ended with the Taliban retaking power.
But Leunig sees it differently. "I think both cases are not identical. In Afghanistan there was a direct military intervention by Western countries with ground and air forces. In Ukraine, the support is supplying weapons. But the public fear that the war will drag on for a long time, in this there is of course a parallel to Afghanistan, and that in the end Ukraine might still have to give up."
So far, however, there is no sign that the German government is rethinking its position. During a recent (September 10) visit from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, "Germany will stay the course during this time," despite the domestic debate.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Gulf states postpone strait of Hormuz talks with Iran as Yemen conflict intensifies
articles.body:
Gulf states have postponed a critical meeting with Iran on the future of the strait of Hormuz owing to a lack of Arab consensus and growing Saudi Arabian anger with Tehran for helping the Houthis loosen Riyadh’s grip in Yemen.
The stalemate over the vital waterway came as Houthi rebels launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets. A Houthi military spokesperson claimed its forces had attacked the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, hitting fighter-jet hangars, radar systems, runways and landing strips, ammunition depots and additional targets.
Last week, Tehran-backed militias in Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close a critical east-west pipeline that had been acting as a means for Riyadh to export oil after Iran effectively closed the strait of Hormuz.
The closure of the pipeline, the postponement of the Hormuz meeting, and the Houthis’ seizure last week of Yemen’s Red Sea coast – which gave the group control over another vital waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait – combined to drive up oil prices above $108 a barrel on Monday.
Also on Monday, the Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, held urgent discussions with the US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper in Jeddah to discuss “the latest developments in the region”, according to Saudi media. Sources told US media last week that the Saudi de facto ruler had sought military assistance from Donald Trump to help fight the Houthis. So far the US has provided only logistical and intelligence backing,
The Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting was postponed at the last minute, deferring a proposed agreement on a new temporary route for commercial shipping when the strait of Hormuz is reopened.
In a statement, Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, said the meeting had been delayed in the interests of consensus. “We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting co-operation in our region,” he wrote on X. He gave no further details.
The meeting would not have led to the immediate opening of the strait, since Tehran has set a series of other preconditions: including requiring the US to lift a blockade of Iran’s oil ports, the handing over of many frozen Iranian assets and a ceasefire in Lebanon.
But it would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member countries for two years. The planned agreement on a temporary route for ships to use would have formalised Iran’s control of the strait, since the entry route would have been entirely in Iranian waters.
Washington has not expressed publicly an opinion over the proposed deal, and some of Trump’s recent social media posts – claiming full US control of the strait – seemed to bear little relationship with what shipping companies have been reporting.
The atmosphere surrounding the meeting, in preparation for weeks, had been rapidly souring because of the advance by the Houthis in Yemen and the drone attack on the Saudi pipeline by an Iran-backed Shia militia in Iraq.
Vantor Technologies released high-resolution satellite images showing the damage to the east-west pipeline pumping station near Al Mesba’ah, Saudi Arabia. The station appears to be almost completely destroyed.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson denied any Iranian involvement in the pipeline attack, or on events in Yemen.
US military bases throughout the Gulf have been attacked by Iran in response to the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia, which backs the UN-recognised Yemeni government based in Aden, is trying to regain the initiative after Houthi forces swept down the west coast of Yemen from the port of Hodeidah last week and seized the Bab al-Mandab strait, a narrow waterway that links the Red Sea with Asia and is viewed as second in strategic importance to the strait of Hormuz.
It was claimed that a Saudi air bombardment was making it difficult for the Houthis to gain full control of the Yemen waterway or the strategic islands in the Red Sea.
The Houthi leadership says is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea but only Saudi-linked ships. It is also offering cut-price fees in the ports it controls on the west coast of Yemen in an effort to lure traffic away from the ports controlled by the Aden-based government in the south.
It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, but the group also operates independently of Tehran. The rebels ultimate aim is to oust Saudi Arabia from the country, and take full control of the territory.
Saudi Arabia has tried different tactics in handling the Houthis during the decade-long civil war in Yemen, including making concessions in the hope the highly ideological group would reach a power-sharing deal.
The Yemen government said preliminary tolls indicated that 150 civilians had been killed and 200 others injured in the course of the recent Houthi advance. About 85,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN.

articles.title: Finland does not intend to host nuclear weapons in peacetime — president
articles.body:
STOCKHOLM, September 14. /TASS/. Despite joining the French initiative on advanced nuclear deterrence, Finland does not intend to host nuclear weapons President Alexander Stubb has said.
"The French initiative does not replace or overlap with NATO's nuclear deterrence. Finland's primary objective is to act as part of NATO and the European Union. Finland does not intend to let nuclear weapons be deployed on its territory in peacetime," he wrote on the social network X.
Earlier on Monday, Finland decided to join the project promoted by France known as forward nuclear deterrence. As Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen has stated, the French initiative does not entail NATO-style collective defense obligations for participating countries.

articles.title: Russia wanted to cow Ukraine allies with railway drone attack, says top EU diplomat
articles.body:
Russia’s Sunday morning drone strike on a Warsaw-bound train near the Ukraine-Poland border was intended to push Western countries to stop their backing for Kyiv, the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday.
“This is clearly intended to frighten Western countries into ceasing their support for Ukraine, into refraining from going there to demonstrate their support,” Kallas told reporters after landing in Finland for an Arctic summit.
Kallas’ words were echoed by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, who said the strikes were designed “to intimidate Europeans, discourage them and above all to divide them.”
Advertisement
The drone hit the locomotive of a passenger train two kilometers from the frontier in Volyn region, Ukraine’s state rail operator confirmed.
Nobody was injured in the attack, but it happened shortly after a train carrying prominent Western officials and advisers had passed along the same line — prompting concerns that the diplomatic train may have been the real target.
Ukraine’s rail operator said it is “quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train.” Passengers included former U.K. Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former CIA chief David Petraeus and U.K. National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell.
The Russian defense ministry said in a statement that it had struck railway infrastructure in western Ukraine used to “transport military cargo” from Europe.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha responded to Sunday’s border strikes with a post on X stating that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces are “knocking directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” and urged Ukraine’s allies to “throw the full weight of your sanctions at Putin’s aggressive regime.”
Earlier this month, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned of upcoming threats to Europe’s borders following a Russian strike at a Moldova-Ukraine border crossing that killed two people.
“As you know, Russia has already resorted to provocative attacks on border crossings — for instance, in Moldova. We expect similar actions targeting border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” said Tusk.

articles.title: Katz says Lebanon's Ali al-Taher part of Israel-controlled zone
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Katz declares Ali al-Taher part of Israeli-controlled zone as attacks on Lebanon continue
Israeli forces opened fire on several people in southern Lebanon on Monday, damaging a municipal vehicle, as attacks continued across the region and Israel's defence minister declared a strategic ridge would become part of its so-called security zone.
The shooting took place near a landfill in Chaqra, in Bint Jbeil district, as Israeli military vehicles moved towards Wadi Slouki between Chaqra and the occupied border village of Meis al-Jabal. No injuries were reported.
Israeli forces also carried out an explosion in Bint Jbeil and earthworks in Mansouri, while artillery fire targeted Mansouri, Nabatiyeh al-Fawqa, Kfar Tebnit and Arnoun, the report said.
The latest attacks came after an Israeli patrol questioned the mayor of Kfar Shuba and confiscated his phone before releasing him.
Kfar Shuba municipality said mayor Qassem al-Qadri was questioned while visiting a water tank serving the town. He was later released and returned to his family.
The incident came as Israeli forces continued attacks and demolitions across southern Lebanon despite a truce agreement and ongoing US-mediated efforts to secure an Israeli withdrawal.
Israel declares strategic ridge part of security zone
Israel's defence minister Israel Katz said the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge would now be part of what Israel calls its "Yellow Line" and security zone in Lebanon.
Last week, Israeli forces detonated what they said were tunnels beneath the Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, a strategic highland long used by Hezbollah. The explosion was recorded as equivalent to a 4.1-magnitude earthquake.
Katz said Israeli forces would prevent Hezbollah or anyone else from returning to the area and warned that anyone approaching Ali al-Taher would be killed.
"Prime Minister Netanyahu and I have repeatedly made clear that we will not leave the security belt, and that the army will not withdraw or redeploy until Hezbollah is disarmed throughout Lebanon," Katz said.
The declaration came as Israel continued to maintain troops inside southern Lebanon and carry out airstrikes, artillery fire and demolitions in areas where residents are attempting to return.
Israeli forces had been systematically targeting Mansouri, a village in the Tyre district divided by the "Yellow Line", because Israel fears Hezbollah could reposition there.
On Monday, heavy gunfire was also reported around Shaqra and Baraachit as Israeli forces sought to prevent residents from returning, according to Lebanon's state-run National News Agency.
The violence has raised fears in Lebanon that Nabatiyeh and surrounding areas could face a similar fate to parts of southern Lebanon that remain under Israeli occupation. Ali al-Taher overlooks Nabatiyeh and provides Israeli forces with a strategic position over the city and surrounding areas.
Talks planned as attacks continue
The latest escalation comes as Lebanon and Israel prepare for another round of US-mediated talks.
The US embassy in Beirut said Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors will meet in Washington next week to discuss implementation of the trilateral framework, while the next round of formal Lebanese-Israeli talks will be held in Rome in October.
A US State Department official also confirmed to Reuters that the Rome talks would take place in October. The seventh round of negotiations in Rome in August ended without a breakthrough on key territorial issues.
The announcement came a day after Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said there were currently no new negotiations with Israel.
The talks are being planned while Israeli forces continue attacks across southern Lebanon, including airstrikes, artillery fire and the demolition of homes.
The Lebanese army said Israeli forces had failed to comply with the agreement, recording around 7,700 violations from the signing of the framework on 26 June last year. It also said Israeli forces had fired near army personnel and patrols.
Israel's offensive in Lebanon has killed more than 4,300 people since 2 March, according to Lebanese figures, while hundreds of thousands have been displaced.

articles.title: Finland says joining French initiative on European nuclear deterrence
articles.body:
Burak Bir
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Finland has decided to join France’s nuclear deterrence initiative which is significant for security in Europe, the Nordic country's defense ministry said Monday.
"The initiative is a form of bilateral cooperation between Finland and France," the ministry said in a statement, mentioning that both countries have been discussing the initiative both at the highest political level and at the level of officials.
In March 2026, French President Emmanuel Macron launched an initiative on the European dimension of France’s nuclear deterrence. Eight countries were then announced having joined the initiative, followed by Norway at a later stage.
"The French initiative will strengthen Europe’s increasingly active approach to defence. Its objective is to reinforce security and deterrence across Europe," said Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen.
Stressing that the French initiative does not replace or overlap with NATO’s nuclear deterrence, the statement recalled that NATO’s nuclear deterrence is based on nuclear-sharing arrangements and relies on the US' extended deterrent.
"It is ultimately the supreme guarantee of the security of the Alliance," it added.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb also confirmed that the initiative does not replace NATO's deterrence, adding that Finland's primary starting point is to act as part of NATO and the EU.
"Finland does not intend to station nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime," he said.
