articles.title: Russia loses about 1,700 troops, 74 artillery systems in past day - General Staff
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces eliminated about 1,700 occupying troops, 74 artillery systems, seven multiple rocket launchers, 2,124 operational-tactical-level drones, and 550 vehicles and pieces of special equipment over the past day, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces reported on its Telegram channel Monday morning.
"The enemy's total combat losses from February 24, 2022, to September 14, 2026, are estimated at: personnel - about 1,508,600 (+1,700); tanks - 12,345 (+1); armored combat vehicles - 25,331 (+1); artillery systems - 49,752 (+74); multiple rocket launchers - 2,127 (+7); air defense systems - 1,637 (+2); ground robotic systems - 2,615 (+12); operational-tactical-level drones - 516,441 (+2,124); vehicles and fuel tankers - 148,807 (+548); special equipment - 4,683 (+2)," the statement said.
The data is being updated.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill 6, injure 43 across Ukraine over past day, Donetsk Oblast among hardest hit
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill 6, injure 43 across Ukraine over past day, Donetsk Oblast among hardest hit
At least six people were killed and 43 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Sept. 14, with Donetsk Oblast among the hardest hit. The region has remained one of Russia’s main objectives since the beginning of the full-scale war and continues to be a key focus of Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Russian attacks killed three people and injured 13 others, Donetsk Oblast Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Two people were killed in Kramatorsk and one in Druzhkivka overnight.
Russian attacks continued across the region into the morning. In Sloviansk, one person was injured. In Kramatorsk, two people were killed and 10 others injured. One person was injured in Znamenivka. Another person was injured in Spasko-Mykhailivka. One person was also killed in Druzhkivka.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) also detailed the attack on Sloviansk.
"An airstrike damaged three homes. Debris and dry grass caught fire in one yard over an area of 100 square meters," the DSNS said, adding that intense drone activity disrupted firefighters' work.
The agency said two additional first-person-view (FPV) drone attacks sparked new fires, setting a car and an outbuilding ablaze.
Overall, the Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 drones. Air defenses shot down or intercepted 85 drones, while strikes were recorded at seven locations.
Two people were killed and 14 others were injured in Russian attacks on Kherson Oblast, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
One person was killed and four others were injured as Russian forces attacked Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Governor Ivan Fedorov said.
Five people, including a newborn, were injured in Russian attacks on Kharkiv Oblast, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. The overnight attack continued into the morning, when, at around 10 a.m. local time, a Russian drone struck a civilian vehicle, injuring a 62-year-old man.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian attacks injured six people, local authorities said. Four people were injured overnight, and two more people were injured in the early morning.

articles.title: Poland, Ukraine slam Russian strikes near border as 'escalation'
articles.body:
This handout picture taken and released by the Ukrainian State Emergency Service on September 13, 2026 shows firefighters spraying water at a train carriage damaged by a drone strike near the border with Poland. (AFP Photo)
The European Union’s top diplomat said on Sept. 14 that Russian strikes which hit a Warsaw-bound train near Ukraine’s border with Poland shortly after top Western figures passed through were meant to “scare” off Kiev’s backers.
“It is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support,” foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, urging Keiv’s backers to do “the opposite.”
Kallas’ remarks came a day after Poland and Ukraine denounced Russian strikes close to the Polish border that hit a Warsaw-bound train near a frontier checkpoint just after another train carrying several EU officials and British ex-PM Boris Johnson passed through.
Ukraine’s rail operator said Johnson and former CIA director David Petraeus, who were in Kiev for the annual Yalta European Strategy forum, had been traveling on two separate trains around the time the Warsaw-bound locomotive was hit on Sept. 13.
Petraeus told the New York Times in a telephone interview that he could hear Russian drones above followed by an explosion, prompting passengers to be quickly evacuated.
“For those who have not been under fire, this was terrifying. This is the act of a truly barbaric leader trying to terrorize Ukrainian civilians,” he added.
Johnson, who was traveling with several EU officials in a separate train, condemned the attack in a post on X.
“I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border,” he said.
“What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day, even on civilian railways.”
Poland and Ukraine said a Kiev-Warsaw passenger train was struck just two kilometers from the Polish border, but reported no casualties.
Warsaw has been one of Kiev’s main allies and, with Ukrainian airspace closed, trains to Poland have been one of the main routes out of the war-torn country, used by refugees.
The strikes came as U.S. President Donald Trump called on Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt attacks on Russian refineries, saying it was causing a shortage of diesel fuel and “there are plenty of other targets.”
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian oil refineries in a bid to hurt Russia’s war effort.
Zelensky said Moscow “deliberately” struck the locomotive.
“It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand,” Zelensky said.
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk chaired an emergency meeting in Warsaw following the strikes, warning he expected Russia to escalate the war “in the coming weeks.”
Speaking in Kiev, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said the “escalation” should lead to allies to “double” their support for Ukraine.

articles.title: ADF neutralizes 85 Russian drones overnight
articles.body:
ADF neutralizes 85 Russian drones overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this in a Telegram post.
Starting at 18:00 on September 13, Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 Shahed-type attack UAVs, including jet-powered ones, as well as Gerbera drones and Parody-type decoy drones launched from the directions of Orel and Kursk in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on September 14, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 85 drones.
Hits were recorded at seven locations. The attack is ongoing, and enemy UAVs remain in Ukrainian airspace.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukraine's air defense forces neutralized 310 of the 323 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine during the day on September 13.
Photo: Defense Forces

articles.title: Ukrainian Drone Strike in Sochi Wounds 5
articles.body:
Five people including a child were wounded in an overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Black Sea resort city of Sochi, local officials said Monday.
Emergency authorities said only one of the victims was hospitalized for their injuries. Three homes were also damaged as a result of the air assault, they added.
Sochi Mayor Andrei Proshunin said firefighters extinguished fires that had broken out from the attack. He warned people not to approach any drone debris.
Proshunin later announced the closure of Sochis beache’s due to the ongoing risk of drone strikes.
In the neighboring Rostov region, Governor Yury Slyusar said air defense systems intercepted 50 drones over the region. He reported damage to civilian infrastructure but said that no one was hurt.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 399 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday night and Monday morning.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian attack on a farm warehouse in the northern Chernihiv region killed three people and injured seven others, police said Monday.
The deadly strike came after Russia struck a passenger train near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday. A train carrying European officials was said to have passed through the area shortly before that attack.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot accused Russia of trying to scare and divide Europeans.
Reuters contributed reporting.

Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.

articles.title: Russian General’s Reported Death Sparks Confusion Over Another Milchakov’s Fate
articles.body:
The commander of Russia’s 51st Army, Lt. Gen. Sergey Milchakov, was likely killed in a Ukrainian strike on a military headquarters in Donetsk, according to the partisan movement Atesh.
Atesh said in a Telegram post that Milchakov, who heads the 51st Guards Combined Arms Donetsk Army of Russia’s Southern Military District, was likely killed on Aug. 26.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On that day, Ukrainian Defense Forces reportedly struck the main and reserve command posts of Russian forces in Donetsk.
“Russian military correspondents are sure that he was handed over by his own people, because they hit with aim. A very interesting version!” Atesh said.
There is currently no official confirmation of Sergei Milchakov’s reported death.
Confusion over two Russian commanders
The claim came as Russian media also reported the alleged death of Alexei Milchakov, commander of the Sabotage and Assault Reconnaissance Group (DSHRG) “Rusich,” a Russian far-right combat group that has fought in Ukraine since 2014.
The group and its commanders are under sanctions imposed by the EU, the US, and other countries.
Russian blogger Aslan Rubayev was among the first to report Alexei Milchakov’s alleged death.
“I just spoke with a colleague, he said that Alexei Milchakov died in the SVO (as the Russians call the war in Ukraine). Whatever it was, he is a great patriot of his homeland. I hope he is alive and this is a hoax,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian milblogger Yuriy Kotenok also reported the claim. However, the Russian outlet Mash, citing sources close to the “Rusich” commander, said Alexei Milchakov was alive and well.
Ukraine Sees Exponential Growth in Private Security Firms Providing Anti-Drone Protection
Strike on 51st Army headquarters
The strike on the headquarters of the 51st Army in Donetsk was reported in late August by the Ukrainian public channel Skadovsky Zakhysnyk and monitoring project Exilenova+. Neither report was officially confirmed at the time.
The 51st Army is part of Russia’s Southern Military District and was created in 2024 from the 1st Donetsk Army Corps, which until 2022 was subordinate to the so-called “People’s Militia” of the Russia-backed Donetsk People’s Republic.
Milchakov headed the 1st Donetsk Army Corps from 2022, replacing Lt. Gen. Roman Kutuzov, who was killed near Popasna, according to Russian military correspondent Semyon Pegov.
In 2024, Milchakov was awarded the title of Hero of Russia. He reportedly commanded Russian operations to capture Avdiivka, New York, and other settlements in the Donetsk region.
If confirmed, Milchakov would become the 23rd Russian general killed during the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia resumes mass launches of petrol-powered drones, threat of attack throughout the day
articles.body:
Russia resumes mass launches of petrol-powered drones, threat of attack throughout the day
The Air Force is warning of a threat of a massive attack by Russian strike drones throughout Monday 14 September, as the Russians are once again launching large numbers of UAVs powered by internal combustion engines.
Source: Colonel Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, during the national joint 24/7 newscast
Quote: "We are currently observing an attack by enemy strike UAVs on Odesa Oblast. The threat also remains, of course, for the northern regions. There is information that the enemy may attack today from both the north and the east. That is to say, a large quantity of enemy UAVs is available to be launched towards our country. Specifically, these are UAVs with internal combustion engines, non-jet-powered...
At present, the enemy has clearly expended large stockpiles of jet drones, having attempted to use them for strikes as much as possible in August. A certain number of conventional, classic Shaheds have evidently been accumulated... They have now been launched in several waves, primarily targeting western regions, likely because jet-powered ones lack the range to fly such long distances. A balance must be struck there between fuel capacity, warhead size, and so on. It is expected that these attacks may continue throughout the day."
Details: Ihnat added that defenders of Ukrainian airspace are doing everything possible to minimise Russian hits (which are currently around 10%, compared to an approximate 90% interception rate).
He emphasised that all available assets and personnel within the layered, integrated air defence system have been deployed to repel Russian air attacks.
Asked by a journalist about the reason for this shift in Russian tactics – deploying petrol-powered Shaheds again instead of jet-powered ones – the Air Force spokesperson noted: "Let's assume that the enemy is always planning an unexpected operation to catch our air defence off guard somewhere, utilising various types of munitions. This includes various types of missiles – ballistic, cruise and air-launched – as well as strike UAVs... The enemy is using all means available."

articles.title: Winter could be turning point in war in Ukraine – Polish Defence Ministry
articles.body:
Winter could be turning point in war in Ukraine – Polish Defence Ministry
Polish Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk has said that Russian strikes near the Polish border are an attempt to cut Ukraine off from military supplies. He warned that the coming months, particularly the winter, could prove to be a turning point in the war, potentially in Russia's favour.
Source: Tomczyk in an interview with TVN24, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Tomczyk said that Russia believes the coming period could become a turning point in the war and that Ukraine currently needs the maximum possible support from the Western world to withstand Russia's war and effectively defend itself against aerial attacks.
According to Tomczyk, the recent attacks on Ukraine's west are also a test for NATO. He said that, according to CIA intelligence, Russia's plans for the near future include scenarios involving European countries.
Tomczyk said he did not want to disclose any sensational details but warned that the scenarios included possible acts of sabotage similar to those seen in Germany, a potential escalation of hybrid warfare on a scale not witnessed before, and various types of operations in border areas, including in the Baltic states along NATO's frontier. He said these were very realistic scenarios that could escalate into something far more serious.
Background:
- On 13 September, Russia struck the locomotive of a passenger train near the Polish border. Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) suggested that the Russian drone may have been targeting a train carrying diplomats and politicians, whose passengers had to be evacuated. Those on board included former UK prime minister Boris Johnson and Günter Sautter, one of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's closest advisers.
- Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the coming weeks and months would be a period of very active Russian operations and that more serious attacks on Polish territory could not be ruled out.

articles.title: Five injured after Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Sochi
articles.body:
Five injured after Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Sochi
Ukraine’s military launched a drone attack on Krasnodar Krai overnight on September 14. articles.title: Russian Drone Strike Hits Kyiv-Warsaw Train Just 2 Kilometers From Polish Border
articles.body:
- Category

Russian Drone Strike Hits Kyiv-Warsaw Train Just 2 Kilometers From Polish Border
A Russian drone strike hit the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train in Ukraine’s Volyn region on September 13, approximately two kilometers from the Polish border.
According to state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia, no injuries were reported. Ukrzaliznytsia said a monitoring team had warned the train crew about the threat in advance.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The same Russian attack also struck infrastructure near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk international border crossing, one of the main road links between Ukraine and Poland.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha reported the strike near the Yahodyn crossing on September 13. Valentyna Chernysh, a spokesperson for the Volyn Customs Service, told Suspilne that falling drone debris caused a fire at a nearby gas station and several trucks parked at the site.
Border operations were temporarily suspended during the air raid alert while personnel and other people at the crossing took shelter. The Yahodyn-Dorohusk checkpoint later resumed normal operations.
Sybiha said the strikes near the Polish border amounted to Putin’s terror “knocking” directly on the doors of the EU and NATO and called on Ukraine’s partners to impose broader sanctions on Russia.
“Act now: throw the full weight of your sanctions at Putin’s aggressive regime. Make Moscow feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex,” Sybiha wrote.
Earlier, on September 12, Russia launched a large-scale missile and drone attack across Ukraine, killing at least four people and injuring civilians in Odesa, Kryvyi Rih, Zaporizhzhia, and the Kyiv region.

articles.title: Russian forces launch Kalibr missiles without sending launch vessels to sea — Navy
articles.body:
Russian forces launch Kalibr missiles without sending launch vessels to sea — Navy
Dmytro Pletenchuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Navy, made this statement during a television broadcast, according to Ukrinform.
“Even the launch of cruise missile carriers that fire ‘Kalibrs’ is taking place directly at their base, that is, right in the harbor. This is a trend that has been observed for the fourth consecutive month,” Pletenchuk noted.
He noted that the Russians use cruise missiles relatively rarely. According to him, there have been two such launches this month, and over the summer, the maximum number of launches was three.
Pletenchuk noted that Russia potentially has up to four vessels capable of launching cruise missiles from the Black Sea: two “Buyan-M” class surface ships and two “Varshavyanka” class submarines.
“Submarines, for example, aren’t that easy to deploy either. To do so, they need to submerge. I still can’t imagine how they could use them in exactly the same way they’re currently carrying out launches. Let’s not downplay the danger: we’re assuming the maximum—four launch platforms—but a more realistic figure would probably be two surface vessels,” Pletenchuk said.
As reported, the Air Defense Forces neutralized 85 out of 108 drones used by Russian invaders to attack Ukraine beginning on the evening of September 13.
Illustrative photo: Air Force

articles.title: Russia Recruits More Than 28,000 Foreign Nationals for War in Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Recruits More Than 28,000 Foreign Nationals for War in Ukraine
Russia has recruited more than 28,000 foreign nationals to join its war against Ukraine, including a substantial number of people from African countries, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) chief Oleh Ivashchenko.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In an interview with The Times, Ivashchenko said Ukrainian intelligence is working to disrupt Moscow’s efforts to recruit fighters abroad.
“We’re working to stop this, by passing information to the relevant security and intelligence services. We also conduct non-kinetic operations to inform the population in the relevant countries,” Ivashchenko said.
Beyond recruiting foreign nationals, Russia continues to receive military assistance from North Korea. HUR estimates that approximately 8,000 North Korean troops are currently deployed in Russia’s Kursk region, with their number potentially rising to around 50,000.
Russia’s reliance on foreign manpower extends across multiple regions. In an earlier interview with Ukrinform on September 7, Ivashchenko said Moscow was recruiting nationals from more than 40 countries as it seeks both to replenish battlefield losses and expand its forces for potential future military objectives.
“Today, Russia is using foreign nationals from more than 40 countries, including countries in Central Asia, Africa, and Latin America. They are primarily deployed in assault units. In intercepted communications, the Russians themselves call them ‘allies’ and often send them ahead of their own troops,” he stated.
Overall, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry estimates that Russia has recruited at least 2,982 nationals from 37 African countries into its armed forces, with approximately 486 reportedly killed in the war against Ukraine.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions blocked by a second judge – US politics live
articles.body:
EPA set to scrap power-plant pollution limits - reports
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is expected to repeal carbon pollution limits for coal- and gas-fired power plants, according to several outlets.
According to Bloomberg News, citing unnamed officials familiar with the matter, the EPA also plans to propose a separate rule repealing the federal finding that greenhouse gases from power plants specifically pose a threat.
The new measure is likely to be met with legal challenges from environmental groups. But, as the New York Times notes, if the move survives these battles, it could also prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.
As he returned from Ireland, Trump took some time on Truth Social to shout out the work being done on the White House facade – part of his ongoing obsession with renovating the residence.
“The White House was in very bad condition, both inside and out,” Trump wrote on social media. “Frankly, it was a ‘dump’ Past Presidents did not take care of it. I love renovating it during my spare time, which is not much.”
The president said that the exterior “skin” of the White House was “practically falling off” but is now “in better shape than when built in 1792”.
Trump also shared the first renderings of the new ballroom that was mired in legal challenges until the supreme court recently ruled could go ahead.
Johnson says Congress should not be in charge of AI guardrails, insists its tech companies responsibilities
During an interview with CNN on Sunday, Mike Johnson also said that it’s imperative that tech companies, not Congress, to guarantee the safety of their artificial intelligence products work. “We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that’s the challenge,” said the House speaker. “It’s national security balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe.”
This comes as both the issue of datacenter construction becomes a flashpoint ahead of the November midterms, and Donald Trump insists that any checks on AI development are ultimately a hinderance.
“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up,” the president said during a trip to Ireland over the weekend. Trump later said that AI is ultimately “going to be more good than bad” and “whoever wins with AI wins”.
Last week, however, three researchers at Anthropic warned that AI now has the potential to kill off humanity within the decade. Now, as my colleague Nick Robbins-Early reports, Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, issued a proposal at the weekend to slow down the technology’s advancement to ensure public safety.
In response, the OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis and xAI owner Elon Musk also posted support for Amodei’s proposal for slowing AI development.
Johnson says he will 'debate and discuss' Trump's $5k midterm pledge, says incentive needs approval from Congress
Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, said in interviews on Sunday that Donald Trump’s pledge to pay all US adult citizens $5,000 if the GOP win the midterm elections will require congressional approval. This, despite the president’s belief that he wouldn’t need both chambers to pass legislation to issue they payouts.
“I would assume, yes, he’d need Congress to act,” Johnson said in an interview with CNN on Sunday, while calling the incentive “a creative idea”. A reminder that the bill for doling out the $5,000 checks would amount to well over $1tn.
Speaking with NBC News, Johnson also said it was an idea that we’ll “process through Congress and talk through and debate and discuss”.
However, he did not say whether he supports the idea outright.
EPA set to scrap power-plant pollution limits - reports
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is expected to repeal carbon pollution limits for coal- and gas-fired power plants, according to several outlets.
According to Bloomberg News, citing unnamed officials familiar with the matter, the EPA also plans to propose a separate rule repealing the federal finding that greenhouse gases from power plants specifically pose a threat.
The new measure is likely to be met with legal challenges from environmental groups. But, as the New York Times notes, if the move survives these battles, it could also prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.
Donald Trump is in Washington today, after a weekend in Ireland meeting with leaders and various officials. He’ll be at the White House, but has no public events on his schedule. He’ll spend the day in closed-door meetings, but we’ll let you know if anything changes.
When Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a law erasing the words “climate change” from state statutes in May 2024 – colloquially known as the “don’t say climate change” law – Democrats were outraged.
Just six months later, many liberal politicians began to go quiet on the issue themselves. After Donald Trump won the 2024 election, mentions of the climate crisis started to disappear from Democrats’ rhetoric. As the 2026 midterms approach, that retreat is still shaping how some candidates talk about climate on the campaign trail.
The trend, known as “climate-hushing”, may reflect the limitations of Joe Biden’s climate policies, said Daniel Aldana Cohen, assistant sociology professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies climate politics and inequality. Green jobs and housing investments fell short of the climate movement’s desires, consumer incentives disproportionately benefited wealthier households, and Democrats struggled to effectively communicate their accomplishments. The president has since rolled back many Biden-era clean energy incentives and regulations.
The climate crisis, however, is still rearing its head around the country, fueling the heatwaves, wildfires and floods plaguing communities around the US. It also lurks behind issues animating voters, from datacenter expansion to rising home insurance rates. And while some pundits have concluded from their polling and research that Americans don’t want to hear about global warming, other surveys directlycontradict those findings.
“Maybe people don’t rank climate as their main or top issue … but nobody really experiences everyday life like walking around the world rank-ordering the things that they care about,” said Aldana Cohen, who is also founding co-director of the thinktank Climate and Community Institute that calls for “green economic populism”. “What’s important is to learn how to embed the climate issue organically amidst the other issues that people care most about.”
Leaders of the Kennedy Center who have sought to add president Donald Trump’s name to the storied institution say it is facing bankruptcy and possible closure in days, the Washington Post reports.
According to documents obtained by the paper, the center’s board of trustees is expected to vote on Tuesday on whether to close the main building of Washington’s performing arts center, due to financial and safety needs.
Officials warn in the documents that the center “could be unable to make payroll or pay routine maintenance contracts” within weeks, the Post reported.
Publicly recognizing Trump at the center, they argue in the 57-page pre-meeting packet, would help ensure fundraising help to keep it afloat.
“Trustees are being asked to choose among 10 texts that could be placed on the building’s exterior beneath its name,” to publicly credit Trump with the renovation, the Post reported.
The Democrats intend to train tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor the polls and counter possible voter intimidation under a new plan to protect November’s US midterm elections from anticipated interference from Donald Trump and his allies.
The nationwide initiative, dubbed the New Battlefield Project, will help state Democratic committees build up a vast coalition of volunteers to monitor the polls, push voters to cast their ballots early and create a network to respond to disinformation.
The Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), an arm of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), plans to train volunteers across 57 states and territories. It hopes to train volunteers for 25% of the nation’s 95,000 election day polling places, focusing on districts with competitive races.
These volunteers will wear blue vests to provide a visible presence intended to counter any voter intimidation, including by federal agents. Each state party has a trained election protection director.
The Trump administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to cities during the election, and some of the president’s allies have called on him to send immigration agents to the polls. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, previously said immigration agents’ job isn’t to patrol polling places, but they could go to polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant.
The president has personally made a series of interventions that have fanned fears that he could meddle in the upcoming elections, and even declare a national emergency in a bid to exert greater control over the process.
A second federal judge has prevented Donald Trump’s administration from implementing a new US Postal Service rule that would tighten mail-in voting requirements.
However, the US supreme court is still weighing the administration’s request to overturn a separate order blocking the rule. Late on Sunday, District Judge Carl J Nichols in Washington, DC, handed down a similar hold on the rule, which was issued 21 August.
“Plaintiffs have demonstrated that, absent an injunction, there is an increased risk that a significant number of otherwise appropriate absentee or mail-in ballots will ultimately not be counted in the upcoming elections,” Nichols wrote in issuing the preliminary injunction.
“The public has a strong interest in ensuring that doesn’t happen.”
Nichols in May had refused to issue an injunction because he ruled the lawsuit seeking one was brought too early. That was the high court’s reasoning late last month when it lifted an earlier freeze by Talwani.
But because the administration had just issued its rule to move ahead with Trump’s plan, the plaintiffs in Boston and Washington, DC, refiled their lawsuits. Talwani was nominated by former president Barack Obama and Nichols was nominated by Trump.
The new Postal Service regulations stem from an executive order Trump issued earlier this year. Election officials say it would be impossible to implement the changes this close to a general election.
In other developments:
Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the US hit a record on Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average.
British ministers face calls to act after US authorities secretly flew out of the UK a diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children. US officials reportedly raided the diplomat’s London flat in August before taking him to an American airbase and flying him out of the country, without warning the Metropolitan police.
A newly unveiled statue of the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk was vandalized at the Turning Point USA headquarters in Phoenix, Arizona. The statue was found with red spray-paint. A nearby poster memorial in front of the statue was vandalized with red paint as well.
A coroner in Pennsylvania announced the death of a 40-year-old woman associated with the state’s ongoing measles outbreak. The death appears to mark the third in the US state’s ongoing outbreak.Two previous deaths in the state were in infant children. In one case, the infant was born with a genetic defect that made her vulnerable to infection. The second infant child was infected with measles, and died of a ruptured spleen.
A Republican congressman said he had to swim to safety after a plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake late Saturday. Representative Tom Tiffany says he was returning from the La Crosse county Lincoln Day Dinner when the light aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau downtown airport. The pilot made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau. They both ended up in the water and swam to safety.
Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize a “public conversation” about AI management and safety in a closed-door Manhattan fundraiser last week. The comments by the former US president reportedly urged the party to create a sweeping framework for everything from a safety “slow-down” to domestic job losses and children’s wellbeing.

articles.title: Ukraine Blasts Key Russian Oil Refinery, Hitting Processing Unit and Fuel Tanks
articles.body:

Ukraine Blasts Key Russian Oil Refinery, Hitting Processing Unit and Fuel Tanks
Ukrainian forces struck the Slavyansk-EKO oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region overnight on September 13, damaging a key oil-processing unit and the facility’s storage tanks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) said the strike was carried out by operators from its Active Operations Department and Unmanned Systems Department in coordination with other Ukrainian Defense Forces as part of a joint long-range strike operation.
According to HUR on September 13, the attack hit a key oil-processing installation and the refinery’s tank farm. Footage published following the strike showed a large fire and thick smoke rising from the facility in Slavyansk-on-Kuban.
The Slavyansk-EKO refinery is one of Russia’s largest independent oil-processing facilities. HUR said the plant processes more than 4 million metric tons of crude oil annually.
The refinery is located in Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Russia’s Krasnodar region, approximately 70 kilometers northwest of the regional capital, Krasnodar.
The September 13 operation marks the latest Ukrainian long-range strike against Russia’s oil-processing infrastructure. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted refineries and other energy facilities that Kyiv says contribute to Russia’s ability to sustain its war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian drones also struck industrial and military-linked facilities in Russia on September 12, hitting areas near the Beriev aviation complex in Taganrog, which services A-50 surveillance aircraft and Tu-95 strategic bombers, as well as the KuibyshevAzot chemical plant in Tolyatti.

articles.title: Behind the killer robots of Ukraine's new warfare 'revolution'
articles.body:
In a cramped workshop near the front line in northeastern Ukraine, military mechanic "Chimera" is helping prepare his unit's robot forces for battle.
Lined up in a row, the four-wheeled unmanned vehicles known as "Hyenas" will crawl toward Russian lines with their payload of explosives and attack an enemy dugout or halt an advance.
Similar models have captured Russian prisoners, said Chimera, 44, who asked to be identified by his call sign.
"Imagine what 20 kilograms (44 pounds) of explosives is like: it's very powerful," he said. "Very powerful."
Workshops like this one, run by Ukraine's Third Army Corps, have sprouted up across the 1,200-km (745-mile) front as Kyiv's outmanned army seeks to gain the technological edge against Russia's unrelenting infantry assaults in the fifth year of war.
Unmanned ground vehicles are a critical new component of Ukraine's strategy to fight smarter by preserving the lives of its troops on a drone-saturated battlefield, where virtually any movement can prove deadly.
Most Ukrainian brigades and regiments feature unmanned systems units which are expanding to include UGVs as part of their forces.
Reuters visited Chimera's unit, NC13, a leader in employing UGVs to support battlefield assaults, to understand how the integration of these new weapons is shaping the future of land-based warfare.
New 'revolution'
In the workshop, a garage space is crammed with experimental drones, some with tracks and others wheeled. One is mounted with a hose for dousing fires; another is equipped with a rack to hold portable rocket launchers.
Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, who commands the Third Army Corps, described the gradual replacement of infantrymen with UGVs as the next "revolution" in warfare.
Considered one of Ukraine's premier forces, the corps wants to replace around one third of its frontline troops by the end of the year.
"The West slept through the (drone) revolution in many ways," he said, adding the infantry now performs just 10% of the tasks it did before the constant aerial threat appeared.
"If the West really wants to not just keep up with the times, but to get slightly ahead, it needs to think about the next revolution," said Biletskyi.
In frontline areas such as eastern Ukraine's "fortress belt" in Donetsk, ground drones can often be seen trundling to and from besieged cities with rations or ammunition, or spiriting away injured troops.
They have performed more than 50,000 logistics and evacuation missions this year, Kyiv's defense ministry said in June.
'Hunks of iron'
Inside a grey command center in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, the ground drone operators of NC13, formed last year, are manifesting Biletskyi's vision in real time, controllers in hand.
Parked in front of screens beaming a black-and-white feed from the battlefield, they sprayed a tree line with a machinegun mounted to a UGV.
Glowing screens and the din of digital chatter over Discord, the messaging platform team members use to communicate, lend the space the air of a gaming club.
Deputy commander "Bar" said his unit runs operations virtually every day.
In one, they loaded three bombs onto a trailer that was pulled onto a bridge used for enemy logistics, then blown up. In another, a machine-gun-mounted UGV suppressed an enemy assault while kamikaze drones rained on them from above.
"To me, it's a wonderful recipe," said the 23-year-old former bartender, referring to land and aerial drones working together. At least two prisoners have surrendered to NC13 UGVs, he added.
UGVs have their limits: they struggle with physical obstacles and cannot clear a building or a trench in the way an infantry team can. Nor are they produced widely enough to send in swarms the way aerial drones are, Bar said.
But they have already begun removing humans from a wide range of dangerous tasks.
"They don't need food, they don't need water, they don't need logs delivered to build shelters," he said. "Basically, we don't need to feel for them. It's a hunk of iron sent to do the job we used to send soldiers to do."
Room for 'creative' commanders
Though not a miracle weapon, ground drones are one more step toward the automation of warfare — which also includes AI analysis of battlefield data — that will free up humans to focus on planning and decision making, said Biletskyi.
They could shape new frontline tactics, with commanders more open to daring operations that would have otherwise led to heavy losses.
"War is a creative activity; it's an art," he said. "Otherwise, a commander is not called a commander — but a butcher."
Ukraine's former top general Oleksandr Syrskyi had faced criticism for what some service members described as a Soviet style of leadership that included a high tolerance for losses.
His younger successor, Mykhailo Drapatyi, is seen as a reformer expected to promote a more troop-friendly approach, partly through embracing new technology.
Biletskyi himself was promoted last month to help oversee the defense of Ukraine's Donetsk region, handing him a considerable new operational command.
Like most of NC13, deputy commander Bar is a former infantryman familiar with the brutality of ground fighting, having participated in major battles earlier in the war.
If UGVs had been widely used back then, he said, "a great number of my friends would still be alive."

articles.title: Finland to join French forward nuclear deterrence project
articles.body:
PARIS, September 14. /TASS/. Finland has decided to participate in France’s forward nuclear deterrence project, the leaders of the two countries said in a joint statement published by the Elysee Palace.
"Today, Finland has decided to join Forward Deterrence. This decision, in conformity with the two countries’ respective international obligations, is an important step for European security, and for bilateral cooperation," the statement said.
The statement added that the move does not conflict with the international obligations of either country. The Elysee Palace said the decision will create opportunities for "strategic signalling, as well as the ability to manage escalation below the nuclear threshold."
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen said in an interview with Kyodo in August that Helsinki is interested in discussing the extension of France’s ‘nuclear umbrella’ across Europe. She also said that Finland does not intend to deploy nuclear weapons, despite recent amendments to the country’s legislation allowing the import and storage of nuclear material.
French President Emmanuel Macron previously said that France intends to implement the concept of "forward deterrence," which includes joint exercises with partner countries as well as deploying elements of France’s strategic forces in other countries across the European continent. The French president also announced plans to increase the country’s nuclear arsenal, while Paris no longer intends to disclose the exact number of warheads.

articles.title: Trump downplays report China entities helped Iran before attack
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump downplays report China entities helped Iran before attack that killed US troops
US President Donald Trump on Sunday brushed aside a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three US troops there in July.
A recent report in the Wall Street Journal cited unnamed US officials about the attack in Jordan. Asked whether he would mention the issue at an upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump did not directly answer, and instead equated the surveillance activities of China and the United States.
"They basically do what we do," he told reporters aboard Air Force One. "When they say China spies on us, I say you're right and we spy on them too."
The Chinese and US presidents are expected to meet in the United States on 24 September, although China has yet to officially confirm that the meeting will take place.
Trump on Sunday reiterated his view that he has a good relationship with Xi.
"I think he's behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well," Trump said as he flew back to the United States after a weekend trip to Ireland.
The Wall Street Journal report, which Reuters could not immediately verify, said the US officials declined to identify the Chinese entities that supplied the imagery to Iran and did not allege direct involvement by Beijing.
Trump's comments appeared consistent with the administration's recent efforts to play down wide-ranging tensions between Washington and Beijing, despite US frustration over Beijing's close ties to Tehran.
At least 18 US service personnel have been killed and hundreds injured since the US-Israeli war with Iran began at the end of February.

articles.title: US wants to resume talks on Iran's nuclear program
articles.body:
The US wants to resume talks on Tehran’s nuclear program in its talks with Iran, CNN reported.
According to the TV channel, officials from US President Donald Trump’s administration have indicated in private conversations with representatives of Persian Gulf states that Washington would like to "refocus any future US-Iran negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program and not reopening the Strait [of Hormuz]."
For their part, Iranian representatives have made it clear to regional players that they will only be open to discussing their nuclear program after the Strait of Hormuz issue is resolved, including the lifting of the US blockade of Iranian seaports.
The US and the Israeli regime launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran, with Islamabad acting as mediator, signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran.
MNA

articles.title: Poland and Ukraine slam Russian strike on train near their border as 'escalation
articles.body:
The strike hit a Warsaw-bound train near to the border a short time after another train carrying various foreign dignitaries passed through the same track.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he expected Moscow to escalate the war in "in the coming weeks", following Russian strikes that hit a Warsaw-bound train in Ukraine, just two kilometres from its border with Poland.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she believed Russia's strike to close to the Polish border was designed to "scare" Western countries backing Kyiv.
"It is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," Kallas said, urging Kyiv's supporters to do "the opposite".
Meanwhile the country's foreign minister Radoslaw Sikorski urged allies to "double" their support for Ukraine, following what he also called an "escalation".
The train was at Yahodyn station when the strike occured. According to reports, only the train's engine was hit. Ukrainian authorities said all passengers were evacuated and no casualties were reported.
Shortly before the train was hit, a different train carrying senior EU officials and the former British prime minister Boris Johnson, passed through Yahodyn on the same line towards Poland on their way back from a conference in Kyiv.
At the time of the attack, on board a different train at the same station was the former CIA director David Patraeus. He told the New York Times that he heard Russian drones overhead and a subequent explosion, describing it as "terrifying".
Russia said it had hit "railway infrastructure used to transport military cargo" from European countries.
Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of "deliberately" striking the locomotive.
"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," Zelensky said.
Elsewhere, Russia's strikes on Ukraine on Sunday killed at least two people in the city of Kramatorsk.
Ukrainian officials also reported that 20 people, including two children, had been injured in the southern port city of Odesa.

articles.title: Russian strikes will cost Ukraine’s economy up to $10 billion this year, ministry says
articles.body:
Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year and plans to submit a three-part business support package to the Cabinet next week, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said on 12 September.
Russia has escalated its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine through 2026, striking first at power plants, substations, and residential blocks, then widening the target list to trains, factories, retailer warehouses, and medicine depots. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said on 28 August that Russia had destroyed about 90% of retail chains' food logistics, but that supply would shift to direct deliveries, with no shortage of basic foods expected.
Kravchenko said business is an absolutely important source of funding for the defense forces, and that it ensures critical goods are supplied and communities can function.
Three-part package aims to support businesses affected by Russian strikes
- The package has three elements, Kravchenko said. The first would extend the geographic coverage of existing damage compensation programs to include Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, and simplify the application process so affected companies do not wait months for support.
- The second would expand subsidized lending for large businesses, with loans of up to about $22 million (UAH 1 billion) and an interest-rate subsidy of about 5 percentage points. The loans could fund investment projects, including fortification and protection, as well as working capital.
- The third would expand the state's 5-7-9 lending program, which sets the borrower's rate at 5%, 7%, or 9% depending on the purpose of the loan and the size of the business, to suppliers whose large retail clients are losing money to strikes.
He said all three programs had been finalized and hoped businesses would begin receiving substantial support within the coming weeks. The package followed a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and discussions with businesses, he said.
Russian strikes have damaged logistics networks and businesses across Ukraine
An overnight strike on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast on 5 August killed 17 people and destroyed or damaged warehouses and distribution centers belonging to Rozetka, Epicentr, Nova Poshta, Silpo, and other major companies. Co-founder Iryna Chechotkina described Rozetka's warehouse complex in Brovary, valued at $70 million, as beyond repair. The same strike killed six Silpo employees.
Further strikes through early September hit Auchan, Nova Poshta again, Varus, Dnipro-M, and Coca-Cola.

articles.title: Ukraine's defence forces strike radar from S-400 Triumf system in Russia's Sochi
articles.body:
Ukraine's defence forces strike radar from S-400 Triumf system in Russia's Sochi
On 13 September and on the night of 13-14 September, units from Ukraine's defence forces struck a number of important military facilities belonging to Russia.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Quote: "In Sochi, Krasnodar Krai, Russia, a multifunctional 92N6 radar station from the S-400 Triumf surface-to-air missile system was struck."
Details: This concerns a multifunctional radar station that tracks aerial assets and guides surface-to-air missiles onto them. Within the S-400 system, this station is one of the key elements directly responsible for carrying out the air defence system's firing tasks.
Quote: "In the areas of the city of Kursk, Russia's Kursk Oblast, and the [temporarily occupied Ukrainian] city of Donetsk, storage, preparation and launch sites for attack drones were struck. In Novohrodivka, Donetsk Oblast – a drone unit ground control station. In Litizh, Trostenchik and Lipovka of Russia's Bryansk Oblast, enemy radar stations were struck."
More details: The General Staff also reported that a short-range navigation radio system belonging to the Russians was struck in the area of Saky airfield in temporarily occupied Crimea. Three Russian relay stations were also struck in Rokhmanove, Krasnyi Stiah and Kamin, Russia's Bryansk Oblast.
The General Staff said the extent of the damage caused is being assessed.
Background: Earlier, the General Staff reported that Ukraine's defence forces struck two Pantsir systems and a Russian defence-industry plant on 10 September and on the night of 10-11 September.

articles.title: Russian warship gets building-style camo after drone strikes
articles.body:
- A photo shared by military observer Massimo Frantarelli shows a Russian Parchim II-class corvette at Kronstadt painted to resemble a building, with anti-drone netting over its deck.
- The scheme follows Ukrainian drone strikes that damaged the corvette Boikiy in June and sank the patrol ship Purga in March, both near St. Petersburg.
Photos published by military observer Massimo Frantarelli show a Russian Navy corvette in Kronstadt painted to resemble a waterfront building, with outlines suggesting windows and doors on its hull, alongside netting rigged over the deck to blunt drone strikes.
The image, credited to M. Mishin and dated August 22, shows the ship at the Leningrad Naval Base, home to the Baltic Fleet.
Frantarelli identified the vessel as a Project 1331M corvette, known in NATO reporting as the Parchim II class, and suggested it could be either the Zelenodolsk or the Kazanets. He did not confirm which. Russia’s Baltic Fleet operates around six of these small anti-submarine corvettes, built in East Germany in the 1980s and displacing roughly 800 tons.
The ship is the latest in a string of Baltic Fleet vessels to receive improvised paint schemes and protective netting this year. Naval analyst H I Sutton, who tracks the pattern on his Covert Shores site, has documented Russian warships at Kronstadt painted with black bows and sterns, World War Two-style dazzle stripes, and checkerboard patterns since mid-2026. Two Project 22800 Karakurt-class corvettes, Mytishchi and Burya, appeared in July with similar disruptive paint and anti-drone netting, according to Sutton’s reporting.
The changes follow a series of Ukrainian drone strikes on the Baltic Fleet. On June 3, 2026, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces hit the corvette Boikiy while it sat in dry dock at Kronstadt, causing extensive fire damage. Ukrainian officials said the strike likely left the ship a write-off. In March, Ukrainian drones sank the patrol ship Purga at Vyborg, near St. Petersburg. Neither vessel had anti-drone netting installed at the time it was hit.
Sutton and other analysts say the paint jobs are not intended as traditional camouflage against aerial or satellite observation, since Kronstadt’s ship positions are already well documented. Instead, they appear aimed at confusing the operators of Ukrainian one-way attack drones, who often work from low-resolution video feeds, and any computer-vision software those drones use to identify targets.
The tactic has a wartime precedent. During World War Two, several navies used paint schemes intended to make warships blend into their surroundings when viewed from the air. Germany’s Tirpitz reportedly received a camouflage pattern during fitting-out at Wilhelmshaven meant to make the battleship’s hull resemble a waterfront building, complete with painted window and door outlines, to confuse Allied reconnaissance aircraft.
Ukrainian strikes on Black Sea Fleet vessels with similar paint schemes have continued to succeed despite the disruptive patterns.

articles.title: Russian Drones Just Miss Former CIA Director David Petraeus: a View From a Train Near the Polish Border
articles.body:
The third evacuation was different.
The first two times our train from Kyiv toward Poland stopped because of Russian drone attacks, passengers moved quickly but relatively calmly away from the cars. The third time, the urgency in the railway official’s voice had changed.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
People were shouting, “Run!”
So we ran.
We had been told to get at least 200 meters from the train, away from anything that might attract a Russian drone or send shrapnel flying if it were hit. We crossed a dark, marshy field, sometimes over old wooden planks. Then came the sound I will remember: the whine of a jet-powered drone somewhere above us.
I’m 85, and after running for a while my lungs went from burning to feeling as though they might burst. Eventually I couldn’t keep up with the younger passengers, but I kept moving.
We reached the edge of a lake, where people dispersed into bushes and under trees. The advice was to stay low, partly to reduce exposure to shrapnel and partly to be less visible from the air.
Some passengers were crying. A few small dogs looked as unhappy about the proceedings as the rest of us.
Two young women remained standing. Other passengers shouted at them in Ukrainian to get down. I didn’t need a translation. The tone was approximately: Sit down immediately or we will personally kill you before the Russians have a chance.
No one thought this was a drill.
Then we heard another explosion.
Ukraine Sees Exponential Growth in Private Security Firms Providing Anti-Drone Protection
My companion Clara Kaluderovic was receiving information from Ukrainian security contacts about drones in the area. At one point we were told that an interceptor had brought one down. Others were still somewhere nearby.
This happened after a week in Kyiv during which air-raid alerts had become almost part of the background noise. Ukrainians know this experience far better than I ever will. But for a foreign journalist, being hunted out of a train and into the bushes near the Polish border made something very clear: Russia’s effort to make normal life impossible does not stop at the front.
Railways matter enormously in Ukraine. With civilian airspace closed, trains are the principal arteries connecting Ukraine with Europe. Diplomats take them. Journalists take them. Aid workers take them. Families take them. So do Ukrainians leaving the country and Ukrainians determined to return.
Make those trains frightening enough and you begin to isolate Ukraine.
After one of the attacks we could see heavy smoke. Initially, from my angle, I thought a church near the railway had been struck. Later, after comparing photographs and talking with others, I learned that I had been wrong. The drone had hit the locomotive of a train standing beside ours, behind the church.
That correction matters. One obligation of eyewitness journalism is to distinguish what you thought you saw during chaos from what the evidence later shows. It was an exercise in humility.
We also saw damaged railway track. Another strike hit near a gas station. Trains began collecting in the area as movement toward the border stopped. At one point there were passenger trains around us and, beyond one of them, a long line of fuel cars.
Looking at the fuel cars I could see from my train window, sitting in a stationary railway carriage suddenly seemed considerably less attractive than it ordinarily does.
Gen. David Petraeus was also traveling in our group. Earlier in Kyiv, he had told me that Ukraine and Russia are “redefining the very nature of warfare.” He was talking primarily about drones, sensors, electronic warfare and the extraordinary speed at which battlefield technology is evolving.
Now we were experiencing one small part of that revolution ourselves.
The important question was not whether Russia knew precisely who was on our train. I cannot establish that, and speculation is not fact.
What can be established is the effect.
Hundreds of civilians were repeatedly driven from trains in the middle of the night. Rail traffic on one of Ukraine’s essential connections with Europe was disrupted. A locomotive was damaged. Railway infrastructure was hit. And passengers who had thought they were nearly safely across the border discovered that the war could follow them almost to Poland.
One Ukrainian woman I met while we were outside was surprised and seemed deeply appreciative that an American had come to Ukraine during the war. Of course I loved what she said, but, I found myself thinking the sentiment should run the other way.
Ukrainians have been living with versions of this for more than four years. For me, hiding under bushes while Russian drones passed nearby was extraordinary. For millions of Ukrainians, calculating where the nearest shelter is, listening for drones and waiting for the all-clear have become grotesquely ordinary.
Eventually, electricity returned to our carriage. My laptop began charging. Someone produced hot water and I made a cup of Earl Grey tea.
Civilization restored, at least temporarily.
Russia may be trying to persuade foreigners that traveling to Ukraine is too dangerous, too inconvenient and simply not worth it.
If that was the message, it failed with me.
I came away with more resolve and more energy than ever. I cannot wait to return to Ukraine.
And when I do, I intend to come back on that same rail line.

articles.title: Iran nuclear chief blocked by US from IAEA meeting in Vienna: State TV
articles.body:
Iran nuclear chief blocked by US from IAEA meeting in Vienna: State TV
- Iran's nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami was blocked from attending the IAEA annual conference in Vienna due to US opposition, forcing him to return to Tehran.
- Iran condemned Austria's visa refusal as unjustified and accused the US of pressuring Austria to bar Eslami.
- The US and Israel view Iran's nuclear programme as a threat, while Tehran denies seeking nuclear weapons, maintaining its IAEA membership and participation.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran’s nuclear chief was blocked from attending an annual conference on Sept 14 at the headquarters of the UN’s nuclear agency in Vienna due to opposition from the United States, Iranian state television said.
“Mohammad Eslami and his delegation took a regular flight to Vienna on Sept 12, but were blocked on the way because of obstructions by the United States,” the state broadcaster reported, saying he had returned to the capital Tehran.
He was due to attend the annual general conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the UN’s nuclear watchdog, which runs until Sept 18 in Austria.
He attended the conference in 2025 and delivered a speech there on behalf of Iran, a member state of the IAEA.
Tehran summoned Austria’s charge d’affaires in response to the decision to bar Eslami.
“The Austrian government’s refusal to issue visas to the delegation of the Islamic Republic of Iran is a completely unjustified decision,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said at a press conference in Tehran attended by AFP.
“It is clear to us that this incident occurred under American pressure, but that does not absolve the Austrian government of responsibility.”
A diplomatic source in Vienna, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Eslami was refused entry to Austria due to US pressure.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb 28, arguing that its nuclear programme posed a threat.
For decades, Western powers have suspected the Islamic republic of seeking to acquire nuclear weapons, a claim that Tehran categorically denies. AFP

articles.title: Social Democrats to call for official inquiry into purchase of F-35s from US
articles.body:
Social Democrats to call for official inquiry into purchase of F-35s from US
The left-wing Social Democratic Party says it will call for the creation of a parliamentary commission of inquiry (CPI) into the purchase of F-35 jets from the US. A parliamentary motion to this effect will be tabled following a debate in the parliamentary group.
The CPI will have to clarify a number of issues and ascertain whether there was individual misconduct or institutional failings within the relevant department, the party told the Keystone-ATS news agency on Sunday, confirming an article in the Sonntagszeitung.
The party also believes the CPI should investigate whether bidders were treated discriminatorily and whether the purchase and operating costs were deliberately distorted in favour of the F-35. It must also be clarified whether the defence ministry provided incorrect information regarding dependence on the supplier.
The matter is being pursued by Senator Franziska Roth, an expert on security policy. When asked about support from other parliamentary groups, the party replied that anyone wishing to restore confidence must ensure a “full clarification”.
More
F-35 jets: fixed-price scandal will have no immediate consequences
Last Thursday, former Social Democrat parliamentarian Pierre-Alain Fridez called for the creation of a parliamentary commission of inquiry, raising the suspicion that there is far more than simple misunderstanding behind the controversial information on the fixed price.
In an interview with Tamedia publications, he said he was convinced that those responsible had deliberately made false statements to secure approval for the purchase of the F-35 fighter jets.
The CPI is expected to receive the support of the Greens. But the chances of convincing the centre-right majority to set it up appear slim.

articles.title: Russia aims to 'scare' Western countries after strike near a train at Ukraine-Poland border: EU
articles.body:
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said that a drone attack near a train carrying European officials in Ukraine was intended to intimidate Western countries and discourage them from supporting Kiev.
"I think about that it is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," Kallas told reporters on Monday on the doorstep of the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi, Finland.
"The question for us is: What do we take from that message? I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine, and we are not scared off," she said.
Kallas argued that backing down would serve Russia's objective of forcing Ukraine into "submission."
"And like I've said several times, this is not their end goal. Their end goal is much more. So we have to stand firm on this," she added.
Her remarks came after German newspaper Der Spiegel reported that a privately chartered train traveling from Kiev toward Poland on Sunday, carrying European officials and former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, was evacuated following a nearby drone attack.
Kallas also highlighted growing security concerns in the Arctic, pointing to Russia's reopening of former Soviet military bases, missile exercises in the High North and China's increasing interest in the region.
She said the EU is preparing a new Arctic strategy with security at its core, which is expected to be presented in October.
Kallas said the EU must maintain a unified position on Arctic security and other issues affecting the region, adding that Greenland would probably not be discussed specifically.
US President Donald Trump repeatedly called for US control of Greenland during his presidency, calling it a historical and strategic necessity. However, both Danish and Greenlandic leaders firmly rejected the proposal, maintaining that Greenland "is not for sale."

articles.title: Zelenskyy reveals details of Canadian air defence assistance
articles.body:
Zelenskyy reveals details of Canadian air defence assistance
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has explained that Canada will not only purchase PAC-3 interceptors for Patriot systems but will also supply AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles and assist in procuring necessary equipment from other nations, emphasising that protecting Ukrainian airspace remains a key priority.
Source: European Pravda with a reference to Ukrinform
Quote: "The Prime Minister (of Canada, Mark Carney – ed.) announced the purchase of PAC-3 anti-ballistic missiles for Patriot systems worth CAD 350 million. This is an air defence package. Beyond that, we discussed AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles with him. These are relevant missiles that we also use for air defence in NASAMS anti-aircraft systems, which protect many different facilities, including energy infrastructure."
Details: According to Zelenskyy, Canada's air defence package will include "both funds and specific missiles".
Quote: "Furthermore, there are certain agreements requiring his (Mark Carney's – ed.) direct dialogue with other leaders who cannot sell something to Ukraine directly for various reasons."
Background:
- Last week, Zelenskyy and Carney signed a declaration establishing a 100-year partnership, which outlined the intention of both countries to elevate bilateral relations to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership.
- Zelenskyy also noted that Ukraine expects to sign a Drone Deal with Canada on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in late September.

articles.title: Fourth Russian attack on pharmaceutical warehouse this month: facility on fire in Odesa
articles.body:
Fourth Russian attack on pharmaceutical warehouse this month: facility on fire in Odesa
Russians have attacked a warehouse belonging to one of Ukraine's largest pharmaceutical distributors. Since the beginning of September, this is already the fourth warehouse storing pharmaceutical products to have been targeted by Russian forces.
Source: Ekonomichna Pravda sources in the pharmaceutical market
Details: The BaDM company's warehouse is located on the outskirts of Odesa, in the city's Khadzhybeiskyi district. A fire broke out on the warehouse premises following the attack, and the State Emergency Service is working at the scene.
The warehouse premises sustained significant damage. According to Ekonomichna Pravda sources in the pharmaceutical market, early reports indicate that there were no casualties.
Background:
- The attack on the BaDM warehouse is the fourth instance of Russian forces striking pharmaceutical market infrastructure.
- As a result of a Russian attack on 3 September, the Biokon logistics hub in the Boryspil district of Kyiv Oblast was damaged. It is considered the country's largest specialised pharmaceutical warehouse.
- On the night of 7-8 September, Russian forces attacked with two ballistic missiles a warehouse belonging to Optima-Pharm, one of Ukraine's largest pharmaceutical distributors, in Kyiv. The warehouse had already been destroyed by the Russians in 2025.
- On 13 September, Russian forces struck Universal Logistic, another of Ukraine's largest pharmaceutical warehouses.
