articles.title: Ukraine hits key S-400 radar station in Sochi
articles.body:
Ukraine hits key S-400 radar station in Sochi
As reported by Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this in a Facebook post.
On September 13 and overnight into September 14, Ukrainian Defense Forces units struck a number of important Russian military targets.
In Sochi, a 92N6 multifunctional radar station belonging to the S-400 Triumf SAM system was hit.
The 92N6 is a multifunctional radar station that tracks aerial targets and guides surface-to-air missiles toward them. As part of the S-400 system, the radar is one of the key elements responsible for carrying out the system’s air-defense missions.
In the areas of Kursk and temporarily occupied Donetsk, storage, preparation, and launch sites for Russian strike UAVs were hit. In Novohrodivka, Donetsk region, a UAV command post was struck.
Radar stations were hit in the areas of Lityzh, Trostenchyk, and Lipovka in the Bryansk region.
Near the Saki airfield in temporarily occupied Crimea, a short-range navigation radio system was hit.
Three repeaters were hit in Rokhmanovo, Krasny Styag, and Kamen in the Bryansk region.
The extent of the damage is being assessed.
As reported by Ukrinform, during a combat sortie in the Donetsk sector, a Su-27 fighter crew carried out a precision strike on Russian military positions, destroying two enemy D-30 howitzers.
Photo: Communications Group of the 426th Separate UAV Battalion

articles.title: Russia seeking to intimidate Poland, weaken support for Ukraine, former Polish DM says
articles.body:
Russia seeking to intimidate Poland, weaken support for Ukraine, former Polish DM says
Former Polish Defense Minister Janusz Onyszkiewicz said this in a comment to Ukrinform, responding to Russia’s recent strikes near the Ukrainian-Polish border.
“Russia is not yet prepared to launch an overt attack on Polish territory as a NATO member state that it could openly acknowledge. However, covert attacks are possible, in which Moscow would deny any involvement. This would be a continuation of its policy of intimidating Poland and the Polish people and fostering resistance within Polish society to supporting Ukraine in this Russia-Ukraine war,” Onyszkiewicz said.
He noted that Russia cannot achieve its goals in the war directly on the battlefield and will therefore seek to do so by influencing public sentiment and opinion in NATO countries, particularly Poland.
“Poland is geographically closest to Ukraine and may therefore be the most vulnerable to such intimidation,” the Polish expert emphasized.
Onyszkiewicz believes Russia’s efforts in Poland are focused on two main areas. The first involves intimidating Poland with the prospect of a conflict with Russia, including the consequences of providing military support to Ukraine, while the second is aimed at weakening support for Ukrainians among Polish society.
According to him, in this context Moscow is seeking to exploit a certain degree of war fatigue, the presence of a large number of Ukrainians in Poland, as well as Ukrainian-Polish disputes over historical issues.
“Russia is playing on two fronts. First, intimidation, and second, an attempt to fuel anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland,” Onyszkiewicz said.
At the same time, he noted that the Polish authorities are responding appropriately to acts of aggression against Ukrainians in Poland. According to him, those responsible for such incidents are quickly identified and held accountable.
The politician also described the growing anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from Poland’s far right as a negative development.
“This undoubtedly benefits Russia, although it is difficult to say that this is agent activity – at least for now. But there is no doubt that these actions benefit Russia and harm Poland, Europe and Ukraine,” he said.
The former Polish minister did not rule out the possibility that Russia could resort to armed provocations on Polish territory, but believes large-scale operations are unlikely.
“I think the likelihood of such attacks occurring is quite high. At the same time, I do not think they will be very large-scale,” he said.
According to him, Russia could attempt to carry out such attacks under a “false flag” in order to shift responsibility for them onto someone else, for example, Ukraine.
“Russia will claim that these are Ukrainian attacks, that the Ukrainians are deliberately carrying them out so that these actions can later be attributed to Russia,” the Polish politician said.
Onyszkiewicz put the likelihood of a Russian provocation in Poland at around 70%. In his view, one potentially convenient period for Moscow could be the run-up to Christmas, when any incident could have a particularly strong impact on public sentiment.
“Before Christmas could be a convenient time for this kind of action, as it could particularly painfully disrupt the atmosphere of anticipation of the holiday,” he explained.
At the same time, Onyszkiewicz believes the current Polish government will continue to strongly support Ukraine.
“As for the current government and the current ruling coalition, support for Ukraine will remain unwavering and will continue to be as strong as possible, including through concrete foreign policy actions,” he said.
At the same time, he believes public support for Ukraine in Poland could weaken somewhat.
“Public opinion may, under the influence of various factors, weaken, I think, but only to a limited extent,” the politician said.
He also did not rule out a significant change in the situation after Poland’s parliamentary elections in autumn 2027 if right-wing forces come to power.
“If the right comes to power after the next elections, this drift toward stronger anti-Ukrainian sentiment and weaker support for Ukraine could become more pronounced,” Onyszkiewicz said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said during an emergency meeting on the security situation in Poland the previous day that Poland must be prepared for increased Russian activity in the coming weeks and months, and that an escalation affecting Polish territory could not be ruled out.
Overnight on September 13, a Russian attack damaged a gas station in Volyn near the Yahodyn border crossing with Poland, as well as a locomotive near the Polish border.

articles.title: After 18 years flying Eagles, Barnes pilots get the F-35A
articles.body:
- The 104th Fighter Wing at Barnes Air National Guard Base officially received the F-35A Lightning II in a September 13, 2026 ceremony.
- The jet replaces the wing's F-15C/D Eagles, which were retired in October 2025 after 18 years of service at Barnes.
The Massachusetts Air National Guard’s 104th Fighter Wing formally welcomed the F-35A Lightning II to Barnes Air National Guard Base on September 13, 2026, marking the aircraft’s arrival after a transition process that began more than three years ago. The ceremony drew Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, military officials and representatives from Kenya and Paraguay, whose militaries partner with the Massachusetts Guard through the state partnership program.
The Air Force picked Barnes in April 2023 as the preferred site for a new F-35A squadron, a decision that became final in December 2024 after an environmental review. The F-35A replaces the wing’s F-15C/D Eagles, which the 104th flew for 18 years after the aircraft arrived at Barnes in 2007. The wing retired its last three F-15Cs on October 23, 2025, sending them to the Air Force’s aircraft storage facility at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona.
“For generations, men and women at the 104th Fighter Wing have answered the call, protected the skies, served our state, and defended our country,” Healey said. “The arrival of the F-35A represents a new chapter for this great military installation here.”
The Air Force plans to base 18 F-35As at Barnes. The wing has not said how many aircraft have arrived so far or when it expects to reach full operational capability with the new jets. U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. David Halasi-Kun, who led the wing through the early stages of the conversion before Col. Michael Glass took command in December 2025, said the shift to a fifth-generation aircraft would take considerable work from the unit.
“The F-35A brings with it incredible capabilities that will be able to support combatant commanders around the world, as well as continued defense of the United States from our 24-hour alert site,” Halasi-Kun said.
The F-35A is a single-engine, radar-evading fighter built by Lockheed Martin. Its sensor suite is designed to combine data from multiple onboard systems into a single picture for the pilot, a capability the Air Force calls sensor fusion, and it can carry precision-guided weapons for strikes against ground and air targets. The jet’s stealth shaping and coatings are intended to reduce its radar signature compared with older fighters like the F-15.
The 104th’s mission includes providing armed fighters on 24-hour alert to respond to airborne threats over the northeastern United States, a role known as Aerospace Control Alert that the wing has carried out with the F-15 for nearly two decades. Air Force Maj. Gen. Gary Keefe, the adjutant general of the Massachusetts National Guard, said the F-35A purchase secures that mission for the base well into the future.
“We are securing our role as a cornerstone of national security for the next fifty years and beyond,” Keefe said.
Some 104th pilots who flew the wing’s final F-15 sorties last October have since trained to fly the F-35A and returned to Barnes among the unit’s first F-35A pilots. U.S. Air Force Capt. Kyle Eckert, one of those pilots, said the shift from flying the last Eagles out of Barnes to flying the base’s first F-35As felt like a “full circle moment.”

articles.title: Talks mediated by India, Turkey on Black Sea navigation freedom ongoing – Polish FM
articles.body:
Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Radosław Sikorski has reported on ongoing talks mediated by India and Turkey regarding freedom of navigation in the Black Sea while discussing potential negotiation formats between Ukraine and Russia during the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) meeting held by Pinchuk Foundation in Kyiv on September 11–12.
"There are also negotiations run by the Indians over the freedom of shipping in the Black Sea and by the Turks," Sikorski said in the context that the question of negotiation platforms and intermediaries is not the main issue for ending the war unleashed by Russia against Ukraine.
"I'm of the view that if Putin is ready for a reasonable peace. He's just not ready yet," the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Poland noted.
According to him, negotiations and consultations between representatives of Ukraine and Russia are taking place constantly.
"Ukraine and Russia are negotiating the whole time a very difficult issue of swaps of prisoners of war and the bodies of fallen soldiers. So if, There were willingness on Russia's part to come to a solution. They could just broaden those talks, And actually they started very early on in the war with other baskets," Sikorski noted.
As Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure, and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk reported on September 13, as a result of systematic Russian strikes on port infrastructure and vessels, cargo handling in the Black Sea ports of Greater Odesa has dropped more than 15-fold since July 22.
In turn, Ukraine is also striking the Russian "shadow" fleet. Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Robert (Madyar) Brovdi recently reported that as part of the ten-week MoLoCHka operation, 285 vessels of the Russian "shadow" fleet have been neutralized in the Azov and Black Seas, including 16 units from September 1 to 11, 54 in August, and 215 vessels in July.

articles.title: UK sanctions on settlements unlikely to deter Israel: Caabu
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK settlement sanctions a policy shift but unlikely to deter Israel, says Caabu
The Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu) has warned against excessive optimism over the sanctions regime that the UK and several other European countries plan to impose on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Golan Heights saying the measures are unlikely to deter Israeli aggression and settlement expansion.
Caabu Director Chris Doyle described the British government's announcement of the forthcoming sanctions as reflecting a "major reset of the UK government policy" towards Israel, but added that he did not expect the Israeli government to respond to pressure to halt either settlement expansion or deadly violence against Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
In an interview with The New Arab, Doyle said the UK's acknowledgement of acts of ethnic cleansing committed by settlers in the occupied West Bank, together with its intention to impose sanctions on settlements there, represented a "transformation, shift of policy and change in substance" that "actually puts accountability into the equation that takes action that is sanctioning these settlements because they are illegal".
'Clear determination' to go forward
On the eve of Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's appearance before Parliament to announce the sanctions regime last week, Doyle attended a meeting with Stephen Doughty, Minister for the Middle East at the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO).
He said he emerged from the meeting with "the belief that there is a clear determination to move forward" and act "without hesitation" in dealing with Israel. He added that he believed that Miliband himself "is also serious" about implementing the measures that were announced.
Doyle also attached "legal significance" to Britain's acknowledgement that the Israeli occupation and presence in Palestine are illegal.
He added, however, that the anticipated British measures do not amount to the level of punishment Israel deserves for ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity, and the occupation.
But he said the measures showed that "the problem has at least been identified somewhat more truthfully, in the West Bank but also Gaza".
Therefore, he said, "the necessary measures to deal with this can be taken, maybe step by step", reiterating his view that the upcoming measures are "serious".
Doyle noted that the British government was "quite clear that they did not envisage a complete trade ban with Israel". Nonetheless, he asked: "who knows where things will be in six months, a year's time?"
Greater atrocities feared
Caabu considers the current British measures insufficient to punish Israel for settlement activity, even though it views them as "moving in the right direction".
"We have made our demands very clear," Doyle said. "We believe that there should be a full, complete ban on all dealings, all trade with settlements and financial services being offered to settlements".
He also argued that "the UK should not continue with business as usual in its relationship with the State of Israel" and that, "at a minimum, Britain should suspend the trade agreement with Israel, so that no Israeli products arrive (in the UK) under preferences".
"We should not be trading as usual with a state that is committing such serious violations of international law," he added.
Miliband's pledges included working to establish an operational sanctions regime within nine months. Doyle expressed optimism that the promised regime would not be weakened during the relevant ministries' review of the drafting process or because of exemptions for religious reasons mentioned in the ministerial statement.
He attributed the length of the process, as he understood it, to "ensuring that this ban cannot be challenged in the courts".
Despite Caabu's welcoming of the UK announcement, Doyle remained pessimistic about Israel's response and the likelihood of it changing its policies.
He said he was "certain this will not happen, under this government (led by Benjamin Netanyahu) or any likely government".
The Caabu director added that pressuring Israel enough to change its policies would necessitate "additional measures to prove that this (Israel's stance) cannot pass". He said that "when the (British) government is ready to implement the measures it announced, who knows what it might be prepared (to do) if Israel, for example, goes ahead with E1, conducts even greater atrocities in the West Bank?"
However, whatever Britain's capacity to act and influence, Doyle stressed that it would not be enough to "stop and deter Israel from continuing" its settlement programme, which he linked to the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. He added that "further international action, including by Britain, will almost certainly be required".
No to 'business as usual'
Doyle also hoped that the upcoming British measures would be a step towards reassessing overall relations with Israel, saying relations "should not continue as usual" following "Israel's serious violations of international law, including the genocide in Gaza".
He also hoped that Andy Burnham's government's towards the Middle East in general would be influenced by his experience of visiting the West Bank, which Caabu co-organised with the Labour Friends of Palestine group for Burnham and several MPs in September 2012.
Doyle said Caabu's activities had helped in "building a much better understanding of certain (Middle Eastern) issues within the British Parliament", including Syria and Lebanon, as well as raising debates over the US war on Iran and ways to address issues such as Islamophobia.
A parliamentary bloc against Israel
Caabu has sought over the past 59 years to "stimulate a debate on the Middle East and its issues based on accurate knowledge".
Its work has included hosting speakers from across the Middle East to address British politicians and providing opportunities for them to connect with influential British media outlets.
Doyle said this was "one of the reasons why you see, for example, a very strong parliamentary bloc demanding action against Israel regarding the atrocities it commits in Gaza, as well as in the West Bank, Lebanon, and its role in the war against Iran".
Caabu also continues to build relations with British MPs. At its most recent meeting with MPs in June, Doyle used maps and data to explain the dangerous consequences of Israel's new E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank. Extremist Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich has previously boasted that the project makes a Palestinian state impossible.
'Dehumanised' peoples
Despite its efforts, Caabu believes Britain's policy towards the Middle East, regardless of which party is in power, does not contribute sufficiently to conflict-resolution efforts or support for human rights and civil society in the region.
Doyle attributed this to a lack of "informed debate and rational policymaking" based on accurate information about countries in the region and developments there.
He cited the US-Israeli war on Iran, which began last February, as a clear example. Doyle said British officials "believed absolute nonsense" that prevailed within the administration of US President Donald Trump regarding the war, the fragility of Iran's ruling regime and the disposition of its people.
He said "there are many people in the British political system who shared these views, who genuinely believed, somehow, that the regime would be easily toppled", adding that they "still believe that some outfit had been toppled (and) there would have been some very pro-Western, reasonable government to take its place".
Doyle said very few people in Britain and the West "were certainly aware before the war, and perhaps still are now, of the type of state Iran represents, with all its different identity groups".
He attributed this to "a great deal (among the British and the West) of dehumanising the peoples of the region", which he said had led to "the widespread presuming that the people in Iran would not be able to put up a fight against the United States and Israel, and that Iran would not possess a reasonable, effective strategy to counter".
However, he said the Iranian leadership "proved that wrong, whether we like it or not".
Doyle said this reflected "a lot of very naive assumptions about the Middle East, [and] a lack of understanding of that, the differences between communities, the huge variety in terms of life, ways of life, different sects, ethnicities, and the like".
Caabu believes Arab countries themselves bear some responsibility for the lack of understanding of their positions in Britain, despite longstanding historical ties between the two sides.
'Honest and genuine' dialogue
Doyle said Arabs "can play a more effective role in trying to build an understanding of the region" in the West.
However, he said "in the Arab world, there needs to be more united positions on certain issues, and sometimes there needs to be a greater clarity to some of their positions on what is going on".
He also criticised the lack of Arab consensus, which he attributed partly to the absence of "a very honest dialogue, genuine dialogue, between Arab states".
He said there should be such dialogue "between Arab states and their partners, to build, construct, and develop more sophisticated and effective policy approaches".
At the same time, Doyle said the Arab world needed "a better understanding of both Europe and the United States".
He stressed that responsibility did not lie with governments alone, saying "there should be a collective effort" by civil society organisations and government institutions "to have an informed debate on all of these issues on the way forward, on many challenges".
